ACTION:
Temporary rule; closure.
SUMMARY:
NMFS closes the General category fishery for Atlantic bluefin tuna (BFT) for the remainder of the October through November time period. The General category may only retain, possess, or land large medium and giant
(
printed page 66289)
(
i.e.,
measuring 73 inches (185 centimeters (cm) curved fork length (CFL) or greater) BFT when the fishery is open. This action also waives the previously scheduled restricted-fishing days (RFDs) for the remainder of the October through November time period. With the RFDs waived during the closure, fishermen aboard General category permitted vessels and HMS Charter/Headboat permitted vessels may tag and release BFT of all sizes, subject to the requirements of the catch-and-release and tag-and-release programs. On December 1, 2026, the fishery will reopen automatically.
DATES:
Effective 11:30 p.m., local time, October 17, 2026, through November 30, 2026.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Becky Curtis,
becky.curtis@noaa.gov
,
or Larry Redd, Jr.,
larry.redd@noaa.gov
,
by email, or by phone at 301-427-8503.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Atlantic BFT fisheries are managed under the 2006 Consolidated Highly Migratory Species Fishery Management Plan (HMS FMP) and its amendments, pursuant to the Magnuson-Stevens Fishery Conservation and Management Act (Magnuson-Stevens Act;
16 U.S.C. 1801
et seq.
) and consistent with the Atlantic Tunas Convention Act (ATCA;
16 U.S.C. 971
et seq.
). ATCA is the implementing statute for binding recommendations of the International Commission for the Conservation of Atlantic Tunas (ICCAT). The HMS FMP and its amendments are implemented by regulations at
50 CFR part 635
. Section 635.27(a) divides the U.S. BFT quota, established by ICCAT and as implemented by the United States among the various domestic fishing categories, per the allocations established in the HMS FMP and its amendments. NMFS is required under the Magnuson-Stevens Act at
16 U.S.C. 1854(g)(1)(D)
to provide U.S. fishing vessels with a reasonable opportunity to harvest quotas under relevant international fishery agreements such as the ICCAT Convention, which is implemented domestically pursuant to ATCA.
Under § 635.28(a)(1), NMFS files a closure action with the Office of the Federal Register for publication when a BFT quota (or subquota) is reached or is projected to be reached. Retaining, possessing, or landing BFT under that quota category is prohibited on or after the effective date and time of a closure action for that category until the opening of the relevant subsequent quota period or until such date as specified.
NMFS recently published a final rule, which among other things, increased the BFT quota from 1,316.14 metric tons (mt) to 1,509.98 mt (not including the 62.5 mt ICCAT allocated to the U.S. to account for bycatch of BFT in pelagic longline fisheries in the vicinity of the management boundary and adjacent areas) (
91 FR 53526
, August 19, 2026). As described in § 635.27(a), the General category baseline quota is 815.4 mt. The General category baseline quota is suballocated to time periods. Relevant to this action, the baseline subquota for the October through November time period is 106 mt. On October 6, 2026, NMFS adjusted the October through November subquota to 192.9 mt (
91 FR 64302
, October 8, 2026).
Closure of the October Through November 2026 BFT General Category Fishery
Based on reported landings to date for the BFT General category October through November time period, NMFS has determined that the subquota for this time period is projected to be reached shortly. Therefore, retaining, possessing, or landing large medium or giant (
i.e.,
measuring 73 inches (185 cm) CFL or greater) BFT by persons aboard vessels permitted in the Atlantic Tunas General category and HMS Charter/Headboat permitted vessels (while fishing commercially) must cease at 11:30 p.m. local time on October 17, 2026. The BFT General category will automatically reopen December 1, 2026, for the December 2026 time period. This action applies to Atlantic Tunas General category (commercial) permitted vessels and HMS Charter/Headboat permitted vessels with a commercial sale endorsement when fishing commercially for BFT and is taken consistent with the regulations at § 635.28(a)(1).
Waiver for Remaining October Through November RFDs
On May 31, 2024 (
89 FR 47095
), NMFS published a final rule, which, among other things, implemented RFDs every Tuesday, Friday, and Saturday from July 1 through November 30 of each year. Since the fishery will be closed for the remainder of the October through November time period, NMFS has decided to waive the previously scheduled RFDs for the remainder of that time period.
With the RFDs waived during a closure, consistent with § 635.23(a)(7) fishermen aboard General category permitted vessels and HMS Charter/Headboat permitted vessels may tag and release BFT of all sizes, subject to the requirements of the catch-and-release and tag-and-release programs described at § 635.26(a). All BFT that are released must be handled in a manner that will maximize their survival, and without removing the fish from the water, consistent with requirements at § 635.21(a)(1). For additional information on safe handling, see the “Careful Catch and Release” brochure available at
https://www.fisheries.noaa.gov/​resource/​outreach-and-education/​careful-catch-and-release-brochure/​
.
Monitoring and Reporting
NMFS will continue to monitor the BFT fisheries closely. Per § 635.5(b)(2)(i)(A), dealers are required to submit landing reports within 24 hours of receiving BFT. Late reporting by dealers compromises NMFS' ability to timely implement actions such as quota and retention limit adjustments, as well as closures, and may result in enforcement actions. Additionally, and separate from the dealer reporting requirement, General and HMS Charter/Headboat category vessel owners are required per § 635.5(a)(4) to report their own catch of all BFT retained or discarded dead within 24 hours of the landing(s) or end of each trip, by accessing
https://hmspermits.noaa.gov
,
using the HMS Catch Reporting app, or calling 888-872-8862 (Monday through Friday from 8 a.m. until 4:30 p.m. E.T.).
After the fishery reopens on December 1, depending on the level of fishing effort and catch rates of BFT at that time, and after consideration of all the criteria specified at § 635.27(a)(7), NMFS may determine that additional adjustments are necessary to ensure available subquotas are not exceeded or to enhance scientific data collection from, and fishing opportunities in, all geographic areas. If needed, subsequent adjustments will be published in the
Federal Register
. In addition, fishermen may access
https://hmspermits.noaa.gov
,
for updates on quota monitoring and inseason adjustments.
Classification
NMFS issues this action pursuant to section 305(d) of the Magnuson-Stevens Act (
16 U.S.C. 1855(d)
) and regulations at
50 CFR part 635
, and this action is exempt from review under
Executive Order 12866
.
The Assistant Administrator for NMFS (AA) finds that pursuant to
5 U.S.C. 553(b)(B)
, there is good cause to waive prior notice of, and an opportunity for public comment on this action because it is impracticable and contrary to the public interest for the following reasons. Specifically, the regulations implementing the HMS FMP and amendments provide for inseason
(
printed page 66290)
retention limit adjustments and fishery closures to respond to the unpredictable nature of BFT availability on the fishing grounds, the migratory nature of this species, and the regional variations in the BFT fishery. Providing for prior notice and an opportunity to comment is impracticable and contrary to the public interest as this fishery is currently underway and, based on the most recent landings information, the available time period subquota is projected to be reached shortly. Delaying this action could result in BFT landings that exceed the adjusted October through November time period subquota, which may result in future potential quota reductions for other BFT categories or the 2027 General category quota, depending on the magnitude of a potential General category overharvest. Taking this action does not raise conservation and management concerns and would support effective management of the BFT fishery. NMFS notes that the public had an opportunity to comment on the underlying rulemakings that established the U.S. BFT quota, and the inseason adjustment and closure criteria.
For all of the above reasons, the AA also finds that pursuant to
5 U.S.C. 553(d)(3)
, there is good cause to waive the 30-day delay in effective date.

SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
We encourage written comments and suggestions from the public and affected agencies concerning the proposed information collection. Your comments should address one or more of the following four points:
—Evaluate whether the proposed information collection is necessary to properly perform ATF's functions, including whether the information will have practical utility;
—Evaluate the agency's estimate of the proposed information collection's burden for accuracy, including validity of the methodology and assumptions used;
—Evaluate whether the quality, utility, and clarity of the information being collected can be enhanced, and if so, how; and
—Minimize the information collection's burden on those who are to respond, including using appropriate automated, electronic, mechanical, or other technological collection techniques or other forms of information technology,
e.g.,
permitting people to submit electronic responses.
Overview of This Information Collection
Abstract:
Medical standards are part of the general requirement for specific positions in the federal government. Medical requirements are created for positions that involve arduous/hazardous duties or require a high standard of human reliability. Failing to meet an established medical standard or physical requirement means that the individual is not qualified for the position.
5 CFR 339.301
authorizes agencies to require a routine pre-appointment examination as part of qualifying for a position with specific medical standards. The Office of Personnel Management (OPM) identified the positions of criminal investigator (special agent), GL/GS-1811, and explosives enforcement officer, GS-1801, as having specific medical requirements. The qualification standard for Criminal Investigation series (special agent) and General Inspection, Investigation, Enforcement, and Compliance series (explosives enforcement officer) are published online in OPM's
General Schedule Qualification Standards.
These medical requirements are part of the basic prerequisites for both positions. ATF uses ATF Form 2300.10, Special Agent Medical Preplacement, to collect specific identifiable data, such as the name, address, telephone, social security number, and medical data, necessary to identify the applicant and to assess whether they meet the positions' qualification standards. The applicant completes the first part of the form, and the doctor/health care provider completes the second part. Applicants from outside ATF use the form to apply for these positions, and existing special agents and explosives enforcement officers who are applying for similar positions at ATF also use the form. The information on the form is used to determine medical suitability for these positions.

PRAComments@NCUA.gov
.

3133-0040.
(
printed page 66367)
Title:
Federal Credit Union Occupancy, Planning, and Disposal of Acquired and Abandoned Premises—
12 CFR 701.36
.
Type of Review:
Extension of a previously approved collection.
Abstract:
Section 107(4) of the Federal Credit Union Act authorizes a federal credit union (FCU) to purchase, hold, and dispose of property necessary or incidental to its operations. Section 701.36 of NCUA Rules and Regulations interprets and implements this provision of the FCU Act by establishing occupancy, planning, and disposal requirements for acquired and abandoned premises. It also prohibits certain transactions. In addition, this section includes provisions in which an FCU may seek a waiver from certain requirements of the rule. NCUA reviews written waiver requests and makes a determination on the request based on safety and soundness considerations.
Affected Public:
Private Sector: Not-for-profit institutions.
Estimated Total Annual Burden Hours:
160.
OMB Number:
3133-0061.
Title:
Central Liquidity Facility,
12 CFR part 725
.
Type of Review:
Extension of a previously approved collection.
Abstract:
Part 725 contains the regulations implementing the National Credit Union Central Liquidity Facility Act, subchapter III of the Federal Credit Union Act. The NCUA Central Liquidity Facility is a mixed-ownership Government corporation within NCUA. It is managed by the NCUA Board and is owned by its member credit unions. The purpose of the Facility is to improve the general financial stability of credit unions by meeting their liquidity needs and thereby encourage savings, support consumer and mortgage lending and provide basic financial resources to all segments of the economy. The Central Liquidity Facility achieves this purpose through operation of a Central Liquidity Fund (CLF). The collection of information under this part is necessary for the CLF to determine credit worthiness, as required by
12 U.S.C. 1795e(2)
.
Affected Public:
Private Sector: Not-for-profit institutions.
Estimated Total Annual Burden Hours:
119.
OMB Number:
3133-0141.
Title:
Organization and Operations of Federal Credit Unions—Loan Participation,
12 CFR 701.22
.
Type of Review:
Extension of a previously approved collection.
Abstract:
NCUA Rules and Regulations, sections 701.22 and 741.225, outline the requirements for a loan participation program. FICUs are required to execute a written loan participation agreement with the lead lender. Additionally, the rule requires all FICUs to maintain a loan participation policy that establishes underwriting standards and maximum concentration limits. Credit unions may apply for waivers on certain key provisions of the rule.
Affected Public:
Private Sector: Not-for-profit institutions.
Estimated Total Annual Burden Hours:
2,916.
OMB Number:
3133-0199.
Title:
Capital Planning and Stress Testing,
12 CFR 702
-E.
Type of Review:
Extension of a previously approved collection.
Abstract:
To protect the National Credit Union Share Insurance Fund (NCUSIF) and the credit union system, the largest Federally Insured Credit Unions (FICUs) must have systems and processes to monitor and maintain their capital adequacy. The rule requires covered credit unions to develop and maintain a capital plan and submit this plan to NCUA by March 31 of each year. The rule applies to all FICUs that report $10 billion or more in assets on their March 31 Call Report.
Affected Public:
Private Sector: Not-for-profit institutions.
Estimated Total Annual Burden Hours:
11,710.
OMB Number:
3133-0210.
Title:
Supervisory Stress Test Annual Data Collection,
12 CFR part 702, subpart C
.
Type of Review:
Extension of a previously approved collection.
Abstract:
The NCUA Board (Board) has determined, to protect the National Credit Union Share Insurance Fund (NCUSIF) and the credit union system, that the largest Federally Insured Credit Unions (FICUs) should have systems and processes in place to monitor and maintain their capital adequacy. Subpart C of part 702 of NCUA's regulations codifies capital planning and stress testing requirements for federally insured credit unions with $10 billion or more in assets (covered credit unions). Covered credit unions are further delineated by asset tiers. Tier I are credit union with $10 billion or more in total assets, but less than $15 billion in total assets; tier II are credit union with $15 billion or more in total assets, but less than $20 billion in total assets; and tier III are credit union with $20 billion or more in total assets. Tier II and III credit unions are required to conduct supervisory stress tests and section 702.306 (b) codifies that NCUA reserves the right to conduct stress tests of covered credit unions at any time and where both NCUA and a covered credit union have conducted the tests, the results of NCUA's tests will determine whether the covered credit union has met the requirements of this subpart. To facilitate NCUA's ability to conduct supervisory stress test on covered credit unions, section 702.306(d) requires that covered credit unions must provide NCUA with any relevant qualitative or quantitative information requested by NCUA pertinent to capital plans or stress test under this part.
Affected Public:
Private Sector: Not-for-profit institutions.
Estimated Total Annual Burden Hours:
224.

Comments submitted in response to this notice will be summarized and included in the request for Office of Management and Budget approval. All comments will become a matter of public record. 1. The Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (Commission) in this notice of proposed rulemaking (NOPR) proposes to amend its regulations to establish procedures for authorizing activities at liquefied natural gas (LNG) plants without the need for operators to file case-specific applications or for the Commission to issue case-specific orders under sections 3 or 7 of the Natural Gas Act (NGA).
[
1
]
This NOPR includes proposed revisions to Parts 2, 153, and 375 of the Commission's regulations.
I. Background
A. What is an LNG plant?
2. An LNG plant is a collection of facilities where natural gas is processed and cooled to about −260 °F until it becomes a liquid and is stored for later delivery, or where LNG is produced or delivered and stored for later regasification. Liquefying the gas dramatically reduces its volume (by about 600 times), making it easier and more economical to store and transport in bulk, especially by ocean-going marine vessels. Broadly, there are three types of LNG plants subject to the Commission's jurisdiction: (1) LNG export terminals; (2) LNG import terminals; and (3) LNG facilities that receive natural gas, produce and store LNG, and regasify it to deliver in interstate commerce.
3. For LNG export terminals, the LNG plant typically receives natural gas from a pipeline and processes it through a series of integrated systems—including feed-gas handling, pretreatment, liquefaction, and storage—to produce and store LNG. From there, the LNG is transferred to a marine vessel for export.
4. For LNG import terminals, the LNG plant typically receives LNG from a marine vessel and stores that LNG to regasify it in vaporization facilities, then sends out the natural gas to a pipeline or end user.
[
2
]
(
printed page 66493)
5. LNG plants operating in interstate commerce are typically peak shaving plants that receive and liquefy natural gas during low demand periods, store it as LNG, and then regasify the LNG and send out the gas to an interstate pipeline during peak demand periods.
6. An LNG plant is composed of two distinct categories of facilities: LNG facilities and auxiliary systems. LNG facilities are those components of an LNG plant that receive, unload, load, store, transport, gasify, liquefy, or process natural gas. LNG facilities include, but are not limited to:
[
3
]
(1) feed gas facilities, which include metering stations to receive natural gas; processing vessels to remove water and particulate matter; and compression, pressure regulation, and heating and cooling equipment;
(2) pretreatment facilities, which include equipment to remove carbon dioxide, sulfur compounds, mercury, water, or other impurities from the natural gas to safely and reliably liquefy the natural gas;
(3) natural gas liquid (NGL) facilities to extract or remove NGLs from natural gas,
[
4
]
store NGLs, and use them as part of refrigerant makeup in liquefaction facilities or fuel gas for fired equipment, or to transfer them to truck, rail, or marine loading facilities or send them out in pipelines;
(4) heavy hydrocarbon condensate facilities to extract or remove condensates from natural gas, store condensates, and transfer them to truck, rail, or marine loading facilities, or send them out through pipelines, or re-vaporize condensates to use as fuel gas;
(5) liquefaction facilities used to safely and reliably liquefy the natural gas into LNG and transfer it through piping prior to entering the LNG storage facilities;
[
5
]
(6) LNG storage facilities, including piping and valves used to fill the LNG tanks or vessels, and piping, valves, and in-tank pumps used to withdraw the LNG and transfer it to marine, truck, or rail loading or unloading transfer facilities or vaporization facilities;
(7) marine transfer facilities, including transfer arms, hoses, piping and valves, and other components used to unload or load marine vessels;
(8) truck and rail transfer facilities, including transfer arms, hoses, piping and valves, and other components used to unload or load truck or rail cars;
(9) vaporization or regasification facilities to convert the LNG back into natural gas prior to being sent out in a pipeline or to an end user;
(10) sendout gas conditioning facilities to meet pipeline quality specifications for the sendout gas; and
(11) sendout facilities, including sample stations and metering stations to measure the composition, flow, or other characteristics of the natural gas being sent out to a pipeline.
7. Auxiliary systems are those components of an LNG plant that are not LNG facilities but are necessary to support safe and reliable operation of the plant. Auxiliary systems include, but are not limited to:
(1) vapor handling systems to receive, process, and deliver boiloff gas from LNG containers, flash gas from process vessels, and any vapor generated or displaced from truck, rail, or marine transfer facilities;
(2) fuel gas systems to deliver natural gas to fired equipment;
(3) nitrogen and inert gas systems to unload, produce, and store nitrogen to create an inert nonflammable atmosphere where flammable fluids are handled;
(4) plant, utility, and instrument air systems to supply pneumatic pressure used by valve actuators and other equipment or tools;
(5) utility water systems to store and supply water used by power generation, boilers, heat exchangers, and other components;
(6) power generation and electrical systems, including any onsite main gas turbine, heat recovery steam generators, and emergency backup diesel engine generators, used to generate and supply power;
(7) emission control systems to reduce, control, capture, or transport air emissions;
(8) cathodic protection systems;
(9) relief valve and flare/vent systems used to safely and reliably discharge effluent from releases;
(10) security systems;
(11) spill containment systems used to contain any hazardous liquid spills from components and keep spill containment systems free of stormwater;
(12) passive protection systems, including cryogenic spill protection, vapor barriers, blast walls, passive fire protection, firewalls, radiant heat shields, foam glass blocks, or other systems to prevent cascading damage from hazardous fluid releases;
(13) hazard detection systems;
(14) hazard control systems used to extinguish or control fires;
(15) firewater systems;
(16) structural support systems;
(17) natural hazard mitigation used to monitor, measure, record, or protect LNG plant facilities and components from natural hazards; and
(18) emergency response systems, including any fire brigade buildings and apparatus, used to house and respond to hazardous fluid releases.
B. Existing Statutory and Regulatory Framework for the Commission's Authorization and Regulation of LNG Plants
8. The Commission regulates the siting, construction, expansion, and operation of LNG plants pursuant to sections 3 and 7 of the NGA. Section 3(a) provides for Federal jurisdiction over the siting, construction, expansion, and operation of facilities used to export or import natural gas.
[
6
]
Section 3(e)(1) states that “[t]he Commission shall have the exclusive authority to approve or deny an application for the siting, construction, expansion, or operation of an LNG terminal.”
[
7
]
And under section 7(c), the Commission issues certificates of public convenience and necessity for the construction and operation of natural gas and LNG facilities used for the transportation of natural gas in interstate commerce.
[
8
]
Under both section 3 and section 7, the Commission has the authority to include terms and conditions in any order authorizing an LNG plant.
[
9
]
9. The NGA also includes additional requirements that must be met prior to authorizing the construction of LNG terminals under section 3.
[
10
]
Consistent with section 3A(a),
[
11
]
the Commission promulgated regulations requiring LNG applicants to use a pre-filing process for an application for authorization to construct or modify an LNG terminal.
[
12
]
Section 3(f) requires that the Commission obtain the concurrence of the Secretary of War before authorizing the siting, construction, expansion, or operation of LNG terminals affecting the
(
printed page 66494)
training or activities of an active military installation.
[

149. The Commission estimates that the proposed tiered blanket authorization program will enable a subset of projects at LNG facilities to be implemented through either automatic or prior notice authorization while maintaining appropriate oversight and stakeholder engagement. As a result, the proposal would reduce the number of full applications and resultant information collection burden.
150. Natural gas companies and LNG operators file applications with the Commission so it can review the necessary information related to the construction, maintenance, and operation of facilities to provide service or to abandon facilities or service under sections 3 and 7 of the NGA and determine if the requested authorization meets statutory and regulatory requirements and should be granted. This NOPR proposal would provide entities with an opportunity to apply to participate in two new lower-burden filing approaches. To participate in the new approaches, entities must apply for and be granted a blanket authorization:
Application for Blanket Authorization
that includes a brief application, together with evidence that the applicant has the required safety systems, Emergency Response Plans, and appropriate environmental, engineering and operating procedures to support blanket activities.
The proposed lower-burden filing approaches are:
Prior Notice Filings
would include a description of the project, purpose, and justification, together with engineering and technical data, and an assessment of any capacity increases or footprint changes and any environmental or safety impacts. The prior notice filings also include evidence of landowner notification, the identification of affected agencies, as well as any environmental documentation.
Automatic Authorizations
that will not require prior filings or applications. These activities must be documented in a semi-annual operational report, which is already required for these projects.

160. This regulatory action proposes to establish procedures for authorizing activities at LNG plants without a case-specific authorization order from the Commission, which would have the effect of dramatically streamlining the approval of LNG infrastructure projects and would be deregulatory in nature. In particular, the proposed rule would reduce the number of projects subject to the case-specific application process in Part 153 Subpart B by approximately 3 projects per year; this streamlining would result in a burden reduction of 3%. We note that the proposed rule would not change the total number of projects that would be constructed, just the method for obtaining regulatory approval. The proposed rule would result in cost savings to the agency and LNG plant authorization and certificate holders for the projects that would be covered by the proposed rule because it would provide a more streamlined administrative process for project proposals that would otherwise require case-specific review under NGA
(
printed page 66514)
sections 3 or 7. As reflected in the tables above, we estimate that respondents would save 9,988 hours of effort, which the Commission estimates as a cost savings of $1,018,776. Moreover, faster approvals would result in additional cost savings and benefits to authorization and certificate holders and their customers. We seek comment on how to quantify those cost savings. Absent this rule, the activities proposed as eligible for an LNG blanket program would be subject to a less streamlined permitting process, resulting in increased administrative costs to the Commission and to authorization and certificate holders. This proposed rule, if finalized as proposed, is expected to be a deregulatory action under
E.O. 14192
(Unleashing Prosperity Through Deregulation).

(c)
Engineering compliance.
(1)
Facility Inspections.
Throughout the life of the replacements, modifications, and new components, systems, and facilities authorized under this subpart, the blanket authorization holder and its components, systems, and facilities shall be subject to regular Commission staff technical reviews and site inspections on at least an annual basis for LNG terminals and biennial basis for LNG plants in interstate service, or more frequently as circumstances indicate. Prior to each Commission staff technical review and site inspection, the blanket authorization holder shall respond to any specific data requests, including information relating to possible design and operating conditions that may have been imposed by other agencies or organizations. Up-to-date, detailed piping and instrumentation diagrams reflecting replacements, modifications, and new components, systems, and facilities and other pertinent information not included in the semi-annual reports described below, including events that have taken place since the previously submitted semi-annual report, shall be submitted as specified in data requests.
(2)
Semi-Annual Report.
Throughout the life of the replacements, modifications and new components, systems, and facilities authorized under this subpart, the blanket authorization holder shall file semi-annual operational reports with the Secretary to identify changes in design and operating conditions; abnormal operating experiences; applicable activities (
e.g.,
ship arrivals, quantity and composition of imported and exported LNG, liquefied and vaporized quantities, trucking quantities, boil off/flash gas quantities); and plant modifications, including future plans and progress thereof. Abnormalities shall include, but shall not be limited to, the following, as applicable:
(i) unloading/loading/shipping problems;
(ii) potential hazardous conditions from offsite vessels, transportation activities (
e.g.,
road, rail, air), or facilities adjacent to the plant site;
(iii) storage container stratification or rollover;
(iv) geysering;
(v) higher than predicted boil-off rates in storage containers;
(vi) storage container pressure excursions (high or low);
(vii) negative pressure (vacuum) within a storage container;
(viii) relative movement of storage container inner vessels;
(ix) cold spots on the storage containers;
(x) storage container vibrations and/or vibrations in associated cryogenic piping;
(xi) storage container settlement;
(xii) pipe movement including spring hanger position indicator(s) outside of normal range;
(xiii) significant equipment or instrumentation malfunctions or failures;
(xiv) non-scheduled maintenance or repair (and reasons therefor);
(xv) leaking or inoperative isolation valves;
(xvi) hazardous fluid releases;
(xvii) fires involving hazardous fluids and/or from other sources; and,
(xiii) adverse weather conditions and the effect on the plant and facilities.
(3) Semi-annual operational reports shall be submitted within 45 days after each period ending June 30 and December 31. In addition to the above items, a section entitled “Significant Plant Modifications Proposed for the Next 12 Months” shall be included in the semi-annual operational reports.
(4) Throughout the life of the replacements, modifications and new components, systems, and facilities authorized under this subpart, the blanket authorization holder shall notify Commission staff within 24 hours in the event the temperature of any region of an LNG storage container, including any secondary containment and embedded pipe supports, becomes less than the minimum specified operating temperature for the material, and specify procedures for corrective action.
(5) Throughout the life of the replacements, modifications, and new components, systems, and facilities authorized under this subpart, the blanket authorization holder shall report to Commission staff significant non-scheduled events, including safety-related incidents (
e.g.,
LNG, condensate, refrigerant, or natural gas releases; fires; explosions; mechanical failures; unusual over-pressurization; and major injuries) and security-related incidents (
e.g.,
unauthorized attempts to enter site, suspicious activities). If an abnormality is of sufficient magnitude to threaten public or employee safety, cause significant property damage, or interrupt service, notification shall be made immediately, without unduly interfering with any necessary or appropriate emergency repair, alarm, or other emergency procedure. In all instances, notification shall be made to Commission staff within 24 hours. This notification practice shall be incorporated into the LNG plant's Emergency Response Plan.
(6) In the event of an incident, the Director of the Office of Energy Projects has delegated authority to take whatever steps are necessary to ensure operational reliability and to protect human life, health, property, or the environment, including authority to direct the LNG facility to cease operations. Following the initial company notification, Commission staff will determine the need for a separate follow-up report or follow-up discussion in the upcoming semi-annual operational report. All company follow-up reports shall include investigation results and recommendations to minimize a reoccurrence of the incident.
(d)
Commencement.
Any authorized construction shall be completed and made available for service by the blanket authorization holder and any authorized operation, or service, shall be available within five years of the date the activity is authorized pursuant to § 153.105(h). The authorization holder may apply to the Director of the Office of Energy Projects for an extension of this deadline.
(e)
Reports.
The authorization holder shall file reports as required by this subpart.

(c)
Automatic authorization.
(1)
Abandonment.
Blanket authorization holders may abandon the following LNG facilities, auxiliary systems, and associated components that do not impact existing customers under contract and do not adversely affect the continued safety, reliability, or environmental protection of the remaining LNG facilities, auxiliary systems, or associated components:
(i) LNG facilities, auxiliary systems, or associated components that are degraded, obsolete, or soon to be obsolete;
(ii) LNG facilities, auxiliary systems, or associated components that are approaching, have reached, or have exceeded their design and service life;
(iii) LNG facilities, auxiliary systems, or associated components that may be unsafe to continue to operate; and
(iv) LNG facilities, auxiliary systems, or associated components that no longer offer services under contract.
(2)
Installation, construction, modification, or replacement.
Blanket authorization holders may install, construct, modify, or replace (in-kind or upgraded) components within existing LNG facilities and auxiliary systems provided that the new facilities will be:
(i) located within the footprint and the same vertical and horizontal extents of the existing facilities previously evaluated and authorized at the LNG terminal or plant by the Commission, or those previously reviewed and approved at the LNG terminal or plant by Commission staff as part of final design modifications;
(ii) spaced to allow for safe maintenance, access, and egress, and not increase confinement and congestion levels beyond those previously evaluated and authorized at the LNG terminal or plant by the Commission, or those previously reviewed and approved at the LNG terminal or plant by Commission staff as part of final design modifications; and
(iii) designed using components of the same (in-kind or upgraded) type as those that have been previously evaluated and authorized at the LNG terminal or plant by the Commission, or as those previously reviewed and approved at the LNG terminal or plant by Commission staff as part of final design modifications.

(i) result in an increase (or be associated with an increase) of the authorized capacity of an LNG terminal or plant;
(ii) result in an increase in frequency or size of LNG marine vessels at the LNG terminal beyond that previously evaluated in a U.S. Coast Guard Letter of Recommendation and considered by the Commission;

(a) design of basic process control systems (BPCS), safety instrumented systems (SIS), or applicable instrumentation and control systems;
(b) design and sizing scenarios for pressure and vacuum relief devices, including flare and vent systems;
(c) mechanical designs of components including fluid velocity, dynamic hydraulic surge from valve closures and pumps as well as flow and acoustic induced vibrations;
(d) minimum specification for design metal temperature (MDMT), maximum design temperature (MDT), maximum design pressures (MDP), maximum allowable operating pressure (MAOP), maximum allowable working pressure (MAWP) of components, and corrosion allowances;
(e) design and sizing for spill containment and impoundment systems;
(f) spacing and plant layout of LNG facilities and auxiliary systems;
(g) design of ignition controls including electrical area classification and building ventilation systems;
(h) design of hazard detection systems;
(i) design of emergency shutdown systems, and depressurization or blowdown systems;
(j) design of hazard control systems including layout and travel distance for portable extinguishers;
(k) design to mitigate impacts of cryogenic spills, overpressures, projectiles, fires, or other accidental or intentional external impacts that could increase risk to safety;
(l) design and location of cryogenic spill protection, vapor barriers, blast walls, blast resistant buildings or structures, fire walls, radiant heat shields, passive fire protection systems, or other passive protection systems to prevent cascading damage;
(m) design of firewater systems including firewater location, design densities, capacity, and coverage;
(n) design of structural components including any increases in loading from natural hazards and any larger LNG marine vessels;
(o) scalable procedures in Emergency Response Plans; and
(p) any other studies and/or reports applicable to the modifications.

Department of Energy
Federal Energy Regulatory Commission
[Docket No. PL26-3-000]
The Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC or Commission) has prepared a draft policy statement concerning the Commission's review of operational air emissions and associated air quality effects of proposed natural gas projects under the Natural Gas Act (NGA) and the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA). Pursuant to the policy described in the draft statement, the Commission would no longer ordinarily ask applicants to prepare or submit air dispersion modeling for compressor stations or liquefied natural gas facilities, nor require use of the results of such modeling in assessing the air quality effects of such facilities under the NGA and NEPA. Instead, the Commission would use other information submitted by applicants and identified by Commission staff, including but not limited to information on governing state and federal air quality regulations and applicants' compliance therewith, to analyze the air quality effects of proposed projects.
The draft policy statement, for which the Commission seeks comment, can be found in Docket Number PL26-3-000. Any person wishing to comment on the draft policy statement may do so. To ensure consideration of your comments before issuance of the final version, it is important that the Commission receive your comments on or before 5:00 p.m. Eastern Time on November 16, 2026.
The Commission specifically seeks comment on the optimal implementation of its new policy, as opposed to its legal justification. Instructions for filing comments are provided below.
For your convenience, there are three methods you can use to submit your comments to the Commission. In all instances, please reference the docket number (PL26-3-000) with your submission. The Commission encourages electronic filing of comments and has staff available to assist you at (866) 208-3676 or
FercOnlineSupport@ferc.gov
.
Please carefully follow these instructions so that your comments are properly recorded.
(1) You can file your comments electronically using the eComment feature on the Commission's website (
www.ferc.gov
) under the link to FERC Online. This is an easy method for submitting brief, text-only comments;
(2) You can file your comments electronically by using the eFiling feature on the Commission's website (
www.ferc.gov
) under the link to FERC Online. With eFiling, you can provide comments in a variety of formats by attaching them as a file with your submission. New eFiling users must first create an account by clicking on “eRegister.” If you are filing a comment on a particular project, please select “Comment on a Filing” as the filing type; or
(3) You can file a paper copy of your comments by mailing them to the Commission. Be sure to reference the docket number (PL26-3-000) on your letter. Submissions sent via the U.S. Postal Service must be addressed to: Debbie-Anne A. Reese, Secretary, Federal Energy Regulatory Commission, 888 First Street NE, Room 1A, Washington, DC 20426. Submissions sent via any other carrier must be addressed to: Debbie-Anne A. Reese, Secretary, Federal Energy Regulatory Commission, 12225 Wilkins Avenue, Rockville, Maryland 20852.
All of the information related to the draft policy statement and submitted comments can be found on the FERC website (
www.ferc.gov
) using the eLibrary link. Click on the eLibrary link, click on “General Search” and enter the docket number, excluding the last three digits in the Docket Number field (
i.e.,
PL26-3). Be sure you have selected an appropriate date range. For assistance, contact the Office of Public Participation at (202)502-6595 or
OPP@ferc.gov
.
The eLibrary link also provides access to the texts of all formal documents issued by the Commission, such as orders, notices, and rulemakings.
In addition, the Commission offers a free service called eSubscription that allows you to keep track of all formal issuances and submittals in specific dockets. This can reduce the amount of time you spend researching proceedings by automatically providing you with notification of these filings, document summaries, and direct links to the documents. Go to
https://www.ferc.gov/​ferc-online/​overview
to register for eSubscription.

Take notice that on October 2, 2026, Double E Pipeline, LLC (Double E), 910 Louisiana Street, Suite 4200, Houston, Texas 77002, filed an application under section 7(c) of the Natural Gas Act (NGA) and Part 157 of the Commission's regulations requesting authorization for its Texas Mainline Compressor Station Project (Project). The Project involves the installation of a new compressor station, consisting of two (2) natural gas-fired, turbine-driven centrifugal compressor units, totaling approximately 54,000 horsepower, along with associated piping, valves, controls, coolers, conditioning facilities, cathodic protection, and appurtenances in Loving County, Texas. The Project will create an additional 800,000 dekatherms per day of firm transportation service on Double E's existing pipeline system.
Double E states that the Project responds to a growing need for firm pipeline capacity that connects expanding natural gas output from the Delaware Basin, a producing area within the Permian Basin, to the Waha Hub, a highly liquid trading point also within the Permian Basin with expanding takeaway capability. Double E states that the Project will also strengthen the reliability and operational flexibility of the Double E system across Texas and New Mexico and give the system the capability to reverse the direction of flow on its mainline. Double E estimates the total cost of the Project to be $103,839,697 and proposes to use its existing recourse rates under Rate Schedule FTS as the applicable recourse rates for firm transportation service to be provided by the Project, all as more fully set forth in the application which is on file with the Commission and open for public inspection.

Department of Energy
Federal Energy Regulatory Commission
[Docket No. CD27-2-000]
(
printed page 66332)
On October 1, 2026, and supplemented on October 13, 2026, Zushi Renewables, LLC, filed a notice of intent to construct a qualifying conduit hydropower facility, pursuant to section 30 of the Federal Power Act (FPA). The proposed Arvin Edison Canal Hydrokinetic 1 Project would have an installed capacity of 40 kilowatts (kW) and would be located along the Arvin-Edison Water Storage District's Intake Canal, near Bakersfield, Kern County, California.
Applicant Contact:
Ryan Cook, 1115 Howell Mill Rd. NW, Atlanta, Georgia 30318, 614-619-0038,
ryan.cook@emrgy.com
.
FERC Contact:
Christopher Chaney, 202-502-6778,
christopher.chaney@ferc.gov
.
Qualifying Conduit Hydropower Facility Description:
The project would consist of: (1) four 10-kW modular hydrokinetic twin turbines, for a total capacity of 40 kW, and (2) and appurtenant facilities.
A qualifying conduit hydropower facility is one that is determined or deemed to meet all the criteria shown in the table below.
Table 1—Criteria for Qualifying Conduit Hydropower Facility
Statutory provision
Description
Satisfies
                             (Y/N)
FPA 30(a)(3)(A)
The conduit the facility uses is a tunnel, canal, pipeline, aqueduct, flume, ditch, or similar manmade water conveyance that is operated for the distribution of water for agricultural, municipal, or industrial consumption and not primarily for the generation of electricity
Y
FPA 30(a)(3)(C)(i)
The facility is constructed, operated, or maintained for the generation of electric power and uses for such generation only the hydroelectric potential of a non-federally owned conduit
Y
FPA 30(a)(3)(C)(ii)
The facility has an installed capacity that does not exceed 40 megawatts
Y
FPA 30(a)(3)(C)(iii)
On or before August 9, 2013, the facility is not licensed, or exempted from the licensing requirements of Part I of the FPA
Y
Preliminary Determination:
The proposed Arvin Edison Canal Hydrokinetic 1 Project will not alter the primary purpose of the conduit, which is for agricultural consumption. Therefore, based upon the above criteria, Commission staff preliminarily determines that the operation of the project described above satisfies the requirements for a qualifying conduit hydropower facility, which is not required to be licensed or exempted from licensing.
Comments and Motions to Intervene:
Deadline for filing comments, comments contesting whether the facility meets the qualifying criteria, and motions to intervene: November 16, 2026, 5:00 p.m. Eastern Time.
Anyone may submit comments or a motion to intervene in accordance with the requirements of Rules of Practice and Procedure,
18 CFR 385.210
and
385.214
. Any motions to intervene must be received on or before the specified deadline date for the particular proceeding.
Filing and Service of Responsive Documents:
All filings must (1) bear in all capital letters the “COMMENTS,” “COMMENTS CONTESTING QUALIFICATION FOR A CONDUIT HYDROPOWER FACILITY,” or “MOTION TO INTERVENE,” as applicable; (2) state in the heading the name of the applicant and the project number of the application to which the filing responds; (3) state the name, address, and telephone number of the person filing; and (4) otherwise comply with the requirements of sections 385.2001 through 385.2005 of the Commission's regulations.
[
1
]
All comments contesting Commission staff's preliminary determination that the facility meets the qualifying criteria must set forth their evidentiary basis.
For public inquiries and assistance with making filings such as interventions, comments, or requests for rehearing, contact the Office of Public Participation at (202) 502-6595 or
OPP@ferc.gov
.
The Commission strongly encourages electronic filing. Please file motions to intervene and comments using the Commission's eFiling system at
http://www.ferc.gov/​docs-filing/​efiling.asp
.
You must include your name and contact information at the end of your comments. For assistance, please contact FERC Online Support at
FERCOnlineSupport@ferc.gov
,
(866) 208-3676 (toll free), or (202) 502-8659 (TTY). In lieu of electronic filing, you may send a paper copy. Submissions sent via the U.S. Postal Service must be addressed to: Debbie-Anne A. Reese, Secretary, Federal Energy Regulatory Commission, 888 First Street NE, Room 1A, Washington, DC 20426. Submissions sent via any other carrier must be addressed to: Debbie-Anne A. Reese, Secretary, Federal Energy Regulatory Commission, 12225 Wilkins Avenue, Rockville, MD 20852. A copy of all other filings in reference to this application must be accompanied by proof of service on all persons listed in the service list prepared by the Commission in this proceeding, in accordance with
18 CFR 385.2010
.
Locations of Notice of Intent:
The Commission provides all interested persons an opportunity to view and/or print the contents of this document via the internet through the Commission's website at
http://www.ferc.gov/​docs-filing/​elibrary.asp
.
Enter the docket number (
i.e.,
CD27-2) in the docket number field to access the document. You may also register online at
http://www.ferc.gov/​docs-filing/​esubscription.asp
to be notified via email of new filings and issuances related to this or other pending projects. Copies of the notice of intent can be obtained directly from the applicant. For assistance, call toll-free 1-866-208-3676 or email
FERCOnlineSupport@ferc.gov
.
For TTY, call (202) 502-8659.
(Authority:
18 CFR 2.1
.)

Department of Energy

As separately announced in the Notices of Technical Conference issued in this proceeding on June 11, 2026, and August 7, 2026, the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (Commission) will convene its annual Commissioner-led Reliability Technical Conference, in the above-referenced proceeding, on Wednesday, October 21, 2026, from 10:00 a.m. to 2:40 p.m. Eastern Daylight Time, to discuss policy issues related to the reliability and security of the Bulk-Power System. The conference will be held in-person at the Commission's headquarters at 888 First Street NE, Washington, DC 20426 in the Kevin J. McIntyre Commission Meeting Room. The conference will be available to view online.
The purpose of this conference is to discuss policy issues related to the reliability and security of the Bulk-Power System. Attached to this Supplemental Notice is an agenda for the technical conference, which includes the technical conference program and expected panelists.
While the technical conference is not for the purpose of discussing any specific matters before the Commission, some discussions may involve issues raised in proceedings that are currently pending before the Commission. Any discussion on the merits of such proceedings will be curtailed. These proceedings include, but are not limited to:
PJM Interconnection, L.L.C

AGENCY:
Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service, USDA.
ACTION:
Proposed rule.
SUMMARY:
We are proposing to amend the regulations regarding the minimum maturation temperature for fresh (chilled or frozen) boneless beef and ovine meat from certain listed regions or countries affected with foot-and-mouth disease (FMD) from 4 °C to 2 °C. All other existing mitigations for the importation of beef from regions or countries affected with FMD would remain unchanged. This action is needed to align the regulations with the World Organization for Animal Health's standards for FMD minimum maturation temperatures, while continuing to protect the United States against the introduction of FMD.
DATES:
We will consider all comments that we receive on or before December 21, 2026.
ADDRESSES:
You may submit comments by either of the following methods:
Federal eRulemaking Portal:
Go to
www.regulations.gov
.
Enter APHIS-2023-0016 in the Search field. Select the Documents tab, then select the Comment button in the list of documents.
Postal Mail/Commercial Delivery:
Send your comment to Docket No.  APHIS-2023-0016, Regulatory Analysis and Development, PPD, APHIS, 5601 Sunnyside Ave. #AP760, Beltsville, MD 20705.
Supporting documents and any comments we receive on this docket may be viewed at
Regulations.gov
or in our reading room, which is in room 1620 of the USDA South Building, 14th Street and Independence Avenue SW, Washington, DC. Normal reading room hours are 8 a.m. to 4:30 p.m., Monday through Friday, except holidays. To be sure someone is there to help you, please call (202) 799-7039 before coming.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Dr. Lisa M. Dixon, National Director, APHIS Veterinary Services, Strategy and Policy, Animal Product Imports and Exports, 5601 Sunnyside Avenue, Beltsville, MD 20705; (301) 851-3373;
lisa.m.dixon@usda.gov
.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Background
The regulations in
9 CFR part 94
(referred to below as the regulations) prohibit or restrict the importation of certain animals and animal products into the United States to prevent the introduction of various animal diseases, including foot-and-mouth disease (FMD), African swine fever, classical swine fever, and swine vesicular disease. These are dangerous and destructive communicable diseases of ruminants and swine.
Under most circumstances, § 94.1 of the regulations prohibits the importation of live ruminants and swine and fresh (chilled or frozen) meat derived from ruminants and swine originating in, or transiting through, a region where FMD exists. Section 94.11 restricts the importation of ruminants and swine and their meat and certain other products from regions that are declared free of FMD but that nonetheless present a disease risk because of the regions' proximity to or trading relationships with regions affected with FMD. Regions that the Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service (APHIS) has declared free of FMD and regions declared free of FMD that are subject to the restrictions in § 94.11 are listed on the APHIS website at
https://www.aphis.usda.gov/​aphis/​ourfocus/​animalhealth/​animal-and-animal-product-import-information/​animal-health-status-of-regions
.
The regulations do allow for certain exceptions to the prohibitions contained in § 94.1. These exceptions include allowing the importation of fresh (chilled or frozen) beef from certain regions (Patagonia North A in Northern Argentina; Bahia, Distrito Federal, Espírito Santo, Goiás, Mato Grosso, Mato Grosso do Sul, Minas Gerais, Paraná, Rio Grande do Sul, Rio de Janeiro, Rondônia, São Paulo, Sergipe, and Tocantins in Brazil; Paraguay; and Uruguay), as well as ovine meat from Uruguay, subject to certain conditions. The conditions for the importation of boneless meat from these regions or countries affected with FMD are set out in § 94.29 of the regulations and require that:
The meat is beef from animals that have been born, raised, and slaughtered in the exporting regions of Argentina or Brazil or in Paraguay; or beef or ovine meat from Uruguay derived from animals that have been born, raised, and slaughtered in Uruguay.
Foot-and-mouth disease has not been diagnosed in the relevant exporting region within the previous 12 months.
The meat comes from bovines or sheep that originated from premises where FMD has not been present during the lifetime of any bovines and sheep slaughtered for the export of beef and ovine meat to the United States.
The meat comes from bovines or sheep that were moved directly from the premises of origin to the slaughtering establishment without any contact with other animals.
The meat comes from bovines or sheep that received ante-mortem and post-mortem veterinary inspections, paying particular attention to the head and feet, at the slaughtering establishment, with no evidence found of vesicular disease.
The meat consists only of bovine parts or ovine parts that are, by standard practice, part of the animal's carcass that is placed in a chiller for maturation after slaughter and before removal of any bone, blood clots, or lymphoid tissue. The bovine and ovine parts that may not be imported include all parts of the head, feet, hump, hooves, and internal organs.
All bone and visually identifiable blood clots and lymphoid tissue have been removed from the meat; with the exception of ovine meat from Uruguay that meets certain listed conditions.
The meat has not been in contact with meat from regions other than those listed as free of FMD.
The meat came from carcasses that were allowed to maturate at 40 to 50 °F (4 to 10 °C) for a minimum of 24 hours
(
printed page 66292)
after slaughter and that reached a pH below 6.0 in the loin muscle at the end of the maturation period. Measurements for pH must be taken at the middle of both
longissimus dorsi
muscles. Any carcass in which the pH does not reach less than 6.0 may be allowed to maturate an additional 24 hours and be retested, and, if the carcass still has not reached a pH of less than 6.0 after 48 hours, the meat from the carcass may not be exported to the United States.
An authorized veterinary official of the government of the exporting region certifies on the foreign meat inspection certificate that the above conditions have been met.
The establishment in which the bovines and sheep are slaughtered allows periodic on-site evaluation and subsequent inspection of its facilities, records, and operations by an APHIS representative.
The World Organization for Animal Health (WOAH) code article 8.8.24, Recommendations for importation of fresh meat of bovines from countries or zones infected with FMDV, where an official control programme exists and article 8.8.26,
Recommendations for importation of fresh meat of sheep and goats from FMD infected countries or zones where an official control programme exists
[
1
]
recommend that meat come from fresh deboned carcasses of bovine and sheep which, prior to deboning, have been submitted to maturation at a temperature greater than 2° C for a minimum period of 24 hours following slaughter and in which the pH value was less than 6.0 when tested in the middle of both the longissimus dorsi muscle as a mitigation for FMD.
As noted above, one of the requirements for the importation of fresh (chilled or frozen) boneless meat of bovine or ovine origin, from regions and countries in which FMD is known to exist, requires the meat to maturate at a temperature between 4 to 10 °C for a minimum of 24 hours after slaughter. We are proposing to amend the regulations to align with WOAH standards, and decrease the minimum maturation temperature to 2 °C. All other existing requirements for the importation of such meat would remain unchanged and would continue to provide interlocking safeguards to mitigate for FMD.
Executive Orders 12866 and 14192 and Regulatory Flexibility Act
This proposed rule has been determined to be not significant for the purposes of
Executive Order 12866
and, therefore, has not been reviewed by the Office of Management and Budget. As a proposed rule, it also is not subject to
Executive Order 14192
.
In accordance with
5 U.S.C. 603
, we have performed an initial regulatory flexibility analysis, which is summarized below, regarding the economic effects of this proposed rule on small entities. Copies of the full analysis are available by contacting the person listed under
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT
or on the
Regulations.gov
website (see
ADDRESSES
above for instructions for accessing
Regulations.gov
).
Based on the information we have, there is no reason to conclude that adoption of this proposed rule would result in any significant economic effect on a substantial number of small entities. However, we do not currently have all the data necessary for a comprehensive analysis of the effects of this proposed rule on small entities. Therefore, we are inviting comments on potential effects.
The regulations in
9 CFR part 94
prohibit or restrict the importation of certain animals and animal products into the United States to prevent the introduction of various animal diseases, including foot-and-mouth disease (FMD). This proposed rule would lower the minimum maturation temperature for the importation of meat from certain regions, as part of an overall system approach to address FMD risk. The current minimum maturation temperature does not align with international standards. All other existing requirements for the importation of such meat would remain unchanged and would continue to provide interlocking safeguards to mitigate for FMD.
The entities that could potentially be impacted by this proposed rule are businesses within the beef and ovine meat agricultural sector, including beef cattle ranching and farming, cattle feedlots, sheep farming, animal slaughtering and processing, and meat and meat product importing and wholesaling. The majority of businesses in these industries are considered by the Small Business Administration to be small entities.
The United States has the largest fed-cattle industry in the world. The U.S. is also the world's largest producer of beef, primarily high-quality, grain-fed beef for domestic and export use. Nevertheless, the United States is a net importer of beef, primarily purchasing beef destined for processing, which tends to be lower-value, leaner, grass-fed beef. The U.S. beef industry, which is comprised of over 600,000 farms and present in all 50 states, is roughly divided into two production sectors: Cow-calf operations and cattle feeding.
In 2024, U.S. beef consumption was about 29 billion pounds. The United States has a comparative advantage in producing higher-quality, grain-fed cattle, which results in higher-grading steaks, as well as lean beef trimmings and fat trimmings. Lean and fat trimmings are blended to make ground beef, which is by far the most consumed beef product in the U.S. By some estimates, between 50 percent and 55 percent of all beef in the U.S. is consumed in ground form. The corn-fed cattle in the domestic supply chain generate less lean beef trimmings than is necessary to satisfy the demand for ground beef. This results in a reliance on imported lean trimmings. Imports specifically of lean beef trimmings come largely from the countries affected by this proposed rule, as well as Australia and New Zealand. Lean beef imports also allow the U.S. beef industry to expand total beef production, add value by utilizing fat trimmings most efficiently, and export high-value beef products like primal cuts and steaks.
As this proposed rule makes no significant change that would affect the viability of exporting beef products from the affected countries, it is unlikely that there would be a significant increase in imports from this proposed rule. This proposed rule would not grant new market access for any countries or regions but would broaden the range of temperatures considered acceptable for the beef maturation process. Additionally, there is no evidence that the existing minimum maturation temperature is functioning as a barrier to trade.
This proposed rule would also marginally affect the requirements related to existing ovine meat imports from Uruguay, which currently represents less than one percent of annual U.S. lamb and mutton imports. The U.S. is a significant net importer of these products. Over the last five years, the U.S. has produced an average of 139 million pounds of lamb and mutton while importing an average of 335 million pounds. As with beef products, this proposed rule would not grant new market access for any producers of these products, nor is there any evidence that the existing minimum maturation temperature is functioning as a barrier to trade. As such, we do not expect any change in the trade of lamb and mutton from Uruguay as a result of this proposed rule.
While this proposed rule would have no direct impact on imports, we can
(
printed page 66293)
assume some hypothetical indirect impact to examine the welfare effects of such indirect impacts. To assess such a hypothetical change quantitatively, we used a range of 500 to 5,000 additional metric tons of imported beef products from the affected countries to compute impacts. In both scenarios, consumer welfare gains would outweigh producer welfare losses, with a positive net impact ranging from $192,000 to $1.92 million.
Executive Order 12988
This proposed rule has been reviewed under
Executive Order 12988
, Civil Justice Reform. If this proposed rule is adopted: (1) All State and local laws and regulations that are inconsistent with this rule will be preempted; (2) no retroactive effect will be given to this rule; and (3) administrative proceedings will not be required before parties may file suit in court challenging this rule.
Paperwork Reduction Act
This proposed rule contains no reporting or recordkeeping requirements under the Paperwork Reduction Act of 1995 (
44 U.S.C. 3501
et seq.
).

Accordingly, we propose to amend
9 CFR part 94
as follows:
PART 94—FOOT-AND-MOUTH DISEASE, NEWCASTLE DISEASE, HIGHLY PATHOGENIC AVIAN INFLUENZA, AFRICAN SWINE FEVER, CLASSICAL SWINE FEVER, SWINE VESICULAR DISEASE, AND BOVINE SPONGIFORM ENCEPHALOPATHY: PROHIBITED AND RESTRICTED IMPORTATIONS
1.

;

and

§ 94.29

AGENCY:

ACTION:
Notice.
SUMMARY:
The Institute of Education Sciences (IES) at the U.S. Department of Education (ED) is soliciting applications for new awards of the Fiscal Year (FY) 2027 From Seedlings to Scale and Transformative Research in Special Education grants programs, Assistance Listing Numbers (ALNs) 84.305J and 84.324T.
DATES:
Complete proposals must be submitted electronically through the
Grants.gov
“APPLY” function by 11:59:59 p.m. Eastern time December 11, 2026.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Akilah Nelson for the
84.305J
From Seedlings to Scale Grants Program. Telephone: (202) 804-7493. Email.
Akilah.Nelson@ed.gov
.
Courtney Pollack for the
84.324T
Transformative Research in Special Education. Telephone: (202) 987-0071.
Courtney.Pollack@ed.gov
.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
The FY 2027 application notices and instructions include program foci, requirements, and scientific peer review criteria for each competition listed below. IES is announcing the following competitions:
National Center for Education Research (NCER) Competition: From Seedlings to Scale Grants Program (ALN 84.305J)
. Under this competition, NCER will consider only Phase One applications that address the “C-STEP—Coordinating Systems to Translate Evidence into Policy and Practice” focus area.
National Center for Special Education Research (NCSER) Competition: Transformative Research in Special
(
printed page 66321)
Education (ALN 84.324T)
. Under this competition, NCSER will consider only Phase One applications that propose to research and develop transformative solutions to dramatically improve preservice teacher education systems so they can better attract, train, and retain preK-12 general and special education teachers who are prepared to provide high-quality instruction and substantially improve outcomes for students with or at risk for disabilities.
Maximum Award and Duration:
For the From Seedlings to Scale Grants Program (ALN 84.305J), the maximum Phase One award is $500,000 for a one-year project period. For the Transformative Research in Special Education (ALN 84.324T) program, the maximum Phase One award is $3,750,000 for a three-year project.
Eligible Applicants:
Institutions that have the ability and capacity to conduct scientifically valid research are eligible to apply. Eligible applicants include, but are not limited to, institutions of higher education and non-profit, for-profit, public, or private organizations and entities.
Program Authority:
20 U.S.C. 9501
et seq.

AGENCY:
Hydrocarbons and Geothermal Energy Office, Department of Energy.
ACTION:
Notice of request.
SUMMARY:
The Hydrocarbons and Geothermal Energy Office (HGEO) of the Department of Energy (DOE) gives notice (Notice) of receipt of a request (Request), filed on September 28, 2026, by Texas LNG Brownsville LLC (Texas LNG). Texas LNG asks DOE to amend its existing authorization to export domestically produced liquefied natural gas (LNG) to non-free trade agreement countries set forth in DOE/FE Order No. 4489 (as amended)—specifically, to extend its current export commencement deadline. Texas LNG filed the Request under the Natural Gas Act (NGA).
DATES:
Protests, motions to intervene, or notices of intervention, as applicable, and written comments are to be filed electronically as detailed in the Public Comment Procedures section no later than 4:30 p.m., Eastern time, November 19, 2026.
ADDRESSES:
Electronic Filing by email (Strongly encouraged):
fergas@hq.doe.gov
.
Postal Mail, Hand Delivery, or Private Delivery Services
(
e.g., FedEx, UPS, etc.
): U.S. Department of Energy (EX-31), Office of Global Energy Security, Hydrocarbons and Geothermal Energy Office, Forrestal Building, Room 3E-056, 1000 Independence Avenue SW, Washington, DC 20585.
Due to potential delays in DOE's receipt and processing of mail sent through the U.S. Postal Service, we encourage respondents to submit filings electronically to ensure timely receipt.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Jennifer Wade or Peri Ulrey, U.S. Department of Energy (EX-31), Office of Global Energy Security, Office of Strategic Resources, Hydrocarbons and Geothermal Energy Office, Forrestal Building, Room 3E-042, 1000 Independence Avenue SW, Washington, DC 20585, (202) 586-4749 or (202) 586-7893,
jennifer.wade@hq.doe.gov
or
peri.ulrey@hq.doe.gov
Christina Williams, U.S. Department of Energy (GC-76), Office of the Assistant General Counsel for Energy Delivery and Resilience, Forrestal Building, Room 6D-033, 1000 Independence Avenue SW, Washington, DC 20585, (202) 586-55281,
christina.williams@doe.gov
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
On February 10, 2020, in DOE/FE Order No. 4489, as amended,
[
1
]
DOE's Office of Fossil Energy (now known as the Hydrocarbons and Geothermal Energy Office)
[
2
]
authorized Texas LNG to export domestically produced LNG by vessel from the proposed Texas LNG Brownsville LLC Liquefied Natural Gas Export Project (Project), to be located at the Port of Brownsville, Texas, to any country with which the United States has not entered into a free trade agreement (FTA) requiring national treatment for trade in natural gas, and with which trade is not prohibited by U.S. law or policy (non-FTA countries), pursuant to Natural Gas Act section 3(a).
[
3
]
Texas LNG is authorized to export this LNG in a volume equivalent to 204.4 billion cubic feet (Bcf) per year (Bcf/yr) of natural gas for a term extending through December 31, 2050.
[
4
]
Under Order No. 4489, Texas LNG is required to “commence export operations using the planned Project no later than seven years from the date of issuance of this Order”—
i.e.,
by February 10, 2027.
[
5
]
In the Request, Texas LNG asks DOE to extend this export commencement deadline by five years, to February 10, 2032.
[
6
]
In support of this Request, Texas LNG states that, in the period since the issuance of Order No. 4489, Texas LNG has proceeded actively and diligently to develop the Project toward a positive final investment decision (FID).
[
7
]
Texas LNG states, however, that those good faith efforts have been “substantially frustrated” by extenuating circumstances outside of Texas LNG's control, most significantly due to six years of sustained litigation and remand proceedings challenging Federal Energy Regulatory Commission's (FERC's) authorization to site, construct and operate the Project by a joint group of opponents.
[
8
]
Texas LNG states that “[t]his uncertainty made it more difficult for Texas LNG to secure the long-term financing and commercial commitments necessary to reach FID and meet its current export commencement deadline.”
[
9
]
Texas LNG adds that, on August 21, 2025, the FERC granted Texas LNG's request for an extension of its existing construction and in-service deadline for the Project until November 22, 2029.
[
10
]
Texas LNG asserts that the requested commencement extension until February 10, 2032, will provide Texas LNG with additional time after FERC's current construction and in-service deadline to execute commercial commitments and begin exports.
[
11
]
Additionally, Texas LNG asks DOE to authorize an additional three-year make-up period at the end of its existing
(
printed page 66323)
export authorization term through December 31, 2050, consistent with recent DOE practice.
[
12
]
Additional details can be found in the Request, posted on the DOE website at
https://www.energy.gov/​sites/​default/​files/​2026-09/​Texas%20LNG%20DOE%20EOT%20Request.pdf
.
DOE Evaluation
In reviewing the Request, DOE will consider any issues required by law or policy under NGA section 3(a), DOE's regulations, and any other documents deemed appropriate.
Parties that may oppose the Request should address these issues and documents in their comments and/or protests, as well as other issues deemed relevant to the Request.
The National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA),
42 U.S.C. 4321
et seq.,
requires DOE to give appropriate consideration to the environmental effects of its proposed decisions. No final decision will be issued in this proceeding until DOE has met its NEPA responsibilities.
Public Comment Procedures
In response to this Notice, any person may file a protest, comments, or a motion to intervene or notice of intervention, as applicable, addressing the Request. Interested parties will be provided 30 days from the date of publication of this Notice in the
Federal Register
in which to submit comments, protests, motions to intervene, or notices of intervention. The public previously was given an opportunity to intervene in, protest, and comment on Texas LNG's long-term non-FTA application in this docket. Therefore, DOE will not consider comments or protests that do not bear directly on this Request.
Any person wishing to become a party to this proceeding evaluating Texas LNG's Request must file a motion to intervene or notice of intervention.
[
13
]
The filing of comments or a protest with respect to the Request will not serve to make the commenter or protestant a party to this proceeding, although protests and comments received from persons who are not parties will be considered in determining the appropriate action to be taken on the Request. All protests, comments, motions to intervene, or notices of intervention must meet the requirements specified by DOE's regulations in
10 CFR part 590
, including the service requirements.
Filings may be submitted using one of the following methods:
(1) Submitting the filing electronically at
fergas@hq.doe.gov
;
(2) Mailing the filing to the Office of Global Energy Security at the address listed in the
ADDRESSES
section; or
(3) Hand delivering the filing to the Office of Global Energy Security at the address listed in the
ADDRESSES
section.
For administrative efficiency, DOE prefers filings to be filed electronically. All filings must include a reference to “Docket No. 15-62-LNG” or “Texas LNG's Request for Extension” in the title line. Filings must be submitted in English to be considered.
[
14
]
For electronic submissions:
Please include all related documents and attachments (
e.g.,
exhibits) in the original email correspondence. Please do not include any active hyperlinks or password protection in any of the documents or attachments related to the filing. All electronic filings submitted to DOE must follow these guidelines to ensure that all documents are filed in a timely manner.
The Request, and any filed protests, motions to intervene, notices of intervention, and comments will be available electronically on the DOE website at
www.energy.gov/​hgeo/​regulation
.
A decisional record on the Request will be developed through responses to this Notice by parties, including the parties' written comments and replies thereto. Additional procedures will be used as necessary to achieve a complete understanding of the facts and issues. If an additional procedure is scheduled, notice will be provided to all parties. If no party requests additional procedures, a final Order may be issued based on the official record, including the Request and responses filed by parties pursuant to this Notice, in accordance with
10 CFR 590.316
.
Signed in Washington, DC, on October 15, 2026.
Amy Sweeney,
Director, Office of Global Energy Security, Office of Strategic Resources.

AGENCY:
