ACTION:
Notice of application.
SUMMARY:
Clear Power LLC (the Applicant or Clear Power) has applied for authorization to transmit electric energy from the United States to Mexico pursuant to the Federal Power Act.
DATES:
Comments must be submitted on or before November 19, 2026.
ADDRESSES:
Comments or requests for more information should be addressed by electronic mail to
Electricity.Exports@hq.doe.gov
.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Marina Fennel, (240) 702-6156,
Electricity.Exports@hq.doe.gov
.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
The United States Department of Energy (DOE) regulates electricity exports from the United States to foreign countries in accordance with section 202(e) of the Federal Power Act (FPA) (
16 U.S.C. 824a(e)
) and regulations thereunder (
10 CFR 205.300
). Sections 301(b) and 402(f) of the DOE Organization Act (
42 U.S.C. 7151(b)
and
7172(f)
) transferred this regulatory authority, previously exercised by the now-defunct Federal Power Commission, to DOE.
Section 202(e) of the FPA provides that an entity which seeks to export electricity must obtain an order from DOE authorizing that export (
16 U.S.C. 824a(e)
). On January 8, 2026, the authority to issue such orders was delegated to the DOE's Assistant Secretary for the Office of Electricity by Redelegation Order No. S3-DEL-OE1-2026.
On April 16, 2026, Clear Power filed an application (Application or App.) with DOE for renewal of export authority to transmit electric energy from the United States to Mexico for an additional five-year term. App. at 1. Clear Power was originally granted export authorization under Order No. EA-487 on December 9, 2020, which expired on December 9, 2025. Since Clear Power did not apply for renewal until after the expiration of the current export authorization, DOE is processing the application as a request for a new export authorization.
According to the Application, Clear Power is a limited liability corporation with its principal place of business in Folsom, California. The Applicant is a power marketer with “authorization from the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) to market electric energy and capacity at wholesale pursuant to market-based rate authorization.”
Id.
at 2. Clear Power states that it is a “wholly-owned subsidiary of the Alaywan Trust, which owns or is affiliated with entities that own or control a combined total of 18.0 MW (nameplate) of operating renewable generation facilities all located in the California Independent System Operator (CAISO) market.”
Id.
Clear Power “does not own or control any electric power generation, transmission distribution facilities” and “does not have a franchised service area”
Id.
at 3. Thus, the Applicant states that it has “no `transmission system' of its own on which power exports could have a reliability or stability impact.”
Id.
at 5. Clear Power “will schedule its exports from the U.S. in compliance with all applicable reliability criteria, standards and guides as are set out by the North American Electricity Reliability Corporation (NERC) (or any successor organization), the North American Energy Standards Board (or any successor organization) and regional reliability councils and as applied by U.S. transmission providers.”
Id.
at 5-6.
The existing international transmission facilities to be utilized by the Applicant have been previously authorized by Presidential permits issued pursuant to
Executive Order 10485
, as amended, and are appropriate for open access transmission by third parties.
See
App. at Exhibit C.
Procedural Matters:
Any person desiring to be heard in this proceeding should file a comment to the Application at
Electricity.Exports@hq.doe.gov
.
Comments concerning Clear Power's Application should be clearly marked with OE Docket No. EA-531. Comments will be posted along with the relevant application on the program website at
www.energy.gov/​oe/​pending-applications
.
A final decision will be made on the requested authorization after the environmental impacts have been evaluated consistent with the National Environmental Policy Act of 1969 (NEPA), as amended (
42 U.S.C. 4321
,
et seq.
), the DOE NEPA regulations at
10 CFR part 1021
, and the DOE's NEPA
(
printed page 66322)
Implementing Procedures (June 2026) and after DOE evaluates whether the proposed action will have an adverse impact on the sufficiency of supply or reliability of the United States electric power supply system.
Copies of this Application are available on the program website at
www.energy.gov/​oe/​pending-applications
or by emailing
Electricity.Exports@hq.doe.gov
.

AGENCY:
Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), DOT.
ACTION:
Final rule, administrative correction.
SUMMARY:
This action administratively corrects identified final rules published by FAA in the
Federal Register
between May and September 2026 so that certain published airspace designation amendments are transferred to the most-current revision of FAA Order JO 7400.11, which is incorporated by reference.
DATES:
Effective date 0901 UTC October 20, 2026. The Director of the Federal Register approves this incorporation by reference action under
1 CFR part 51
, subject to the next annual revision of FAA Order JO 7400.11.
ADDRESSES:
A copy of this final rule and all background material may be viewed online at
www.regulations.gov
using the FAA Docket number. Electronic retrieval help and guidelines are available on the website. It is available 24 hours each day, 365 days each year. An electronic copy of this document may also be downloaded from
www.federalregister.gov
.
A copy of FAA Order JO 7400.11, Airspace Designations and Reporting Points, may be viewed online or downloaded at
www.faa.gov/​air_​traffic/​publications/​
,
and subsequent amendments at
www.faa.gov/​air_​traffic/​publications/​airspace_​amendments/​
.

SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Authority for This Rulemaking
The FAA's authority to issue rules regarding aviation safety is found in Title 49 of the United States Code. Subtitle I, Section 106 describes the authority of the FAA Administrator. Subtitle VII, Aviation Programs, describes in more detail the scope of the agency's authority. This rulemaking is promulgated under the authority described in Subtitle VII, Part A, Subpart I, Section 40103. Under that section, the FAA is charged with prescribing regulations to assign the use of the airspace necessary to ensure the safety of aircraft and the efficient use of airspace. This regulation is within the scope of that authority as it makes the necessary updates to publication of airspace designations in the
Federal Register
made pursuant to
14 CFR part 71
within the National Airspace System.
History
The most-current revision of FAA Order JO 7400.11, Airspace Designations and Reporting Points (which lists Class A, B, C, D, and E airspace areas, air traffic service routes, and reporting points), is incorporated by reference annually in
14 CFR 71.1
as of September 15, and amendments to that revision of the Order are published as final rules throughout the following 12 months. Certain of these final rules are referred to as “effective date straddling amendments” because there is a mismatch between the effective date of the incorporated Order and the effective date of the amendment to the Order. These final rules are published in the
Federal Register
as amendments to the current revision of the Order, but contain effective dates that fall after the date when the next revision of the Order has been incorporated by reference and is effective (
i.e.,
they straddle the effective dates of the current and prospective Orders). This occurs because the effective date of airspace designations is typically delayed by approximately two months after publication of the final rule amendment to align with aeronautical charting cycles.
Incorporation by Reference
This action corrects the identified effective date straddling amendments by transferring the amendment to the currently incorporated revision of FAA Order JO 7400.11. These amendments will be manually integrated into a subsequent revision of FAA Order JO 7400.11.
For the availability of FAA Order JO 7400.11, see
ADDRESSES
.
The Rule
This action corrects certain final rules (the identified effective date straddling amendments) published under
14 CFR part 71
which are depicted on aeronautical charts.
Because these final rules were published while FAA Order JO 7400.11K was effective and incorporated by reference, but their effective dates fell while FAA Order JO 7400.11M was effective and incorporated by reference, these rules effectively crossed annual update cycles. As a result, these rules were not manually integrated into either revision of FAA Order JO 7400.11.
This action formally transfers these active amendments to FAA Order JO 7400.11M, Airspace Designations and Reporting Points, dated July 30, 2026, and effective September 15, 2026.
Accordingly, as this is an administrative correction to transfer the final rule amendments to the currently incorporated revision of FAA Order JO 7400.11, the FAA finds good cause under
5 U.S.C. 553(b)(B)
that publishing this action for prior notice and public comment is unnecessary, and also finds good cause for making this amendment effective in fewer than 30 days.
Regulatory Notices and Analyses
The FAA has determined that this regulation only involves an established body of technical regulations for which frequent and routine amendments are necessary to keep them operationally current. It, therefore: (1) is not a “significant regulatory action” under
Executive Order 12866
; (2) is not a “significant rule” under DOT Order 2100.6B, “Rulemaking and Guidance Procedure” (March 10, 2025); and (3) is expected to result in, at most, de minimis costs from compliance with applicable operating requirements or minor flight rerouting for operators choosing to navigate around the
(
printed page 66284)
controlled airspace. Since these amendments are routine and the expected impact to operators is de minimis, the FAA certifies that this rule, when promulgated, does not have a significant economic impact on a substantial number of small entities under the criteria of the Regulatory Flexibility Act.

AGENCY:

ACTION:
Proposed rule.
SUMMARY:
This proposed rule would implement section 6219 (Adjustments to Medicare Part D Cost-Sharing Reductions for Low-Income Individuals), section 6220 (Requiring Enhanced and Accurate Lists of (REAL) Health Providers Act), and section 6224 (Modernizing and Ensuring Pharmacy Benefit Manager Accountability) of the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2026.
DATES:
To be assured consideration, comments must be received at one of the addresses provided below, no later than 5 p.m. Eastern Standard Time on December 15, 2026.
ADDRESSES:
In commenting, please refer to file code CMS-4214-P. Because of staff and resource limitations, we cannot accept comments by facsimile (FAX) transmission.
Comments, including mass comment submissions, must be submitted in one of the following three ways (please choose only one of the ways listed):
1.

.

By regular mail.

3.

—Section 6224 of the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2026.

Inspection of Public Comments:

We post all comments received before the close of the comment period on the following website as soon as possible after they have been received:
http://www.regulations.gov
.
Follow the search instructions on that website to view public comments. CMS will not post on

Plain Language Summary:
In accordance with
5 U.S.C. 553(b)(4)
, a plain language summary of this proposed rule may be found at
https://www.regulations.gov/​
.
I. Executive Summary
A. Purpose
The primary purpose of this proposed rule is to amend the regulations for the Medicare Advantage (Part C) program and the Medicare Prescription Drug Benefit (Part D) program to implement section 6219 (Adjustments to Medicare Part D Cost-Sharing Reductions For Low-Income Individuals), section 6220 (Requiring Enhanced and Accurate Lists of (REAL) Health Providers Act), and section 6224 (Modernizing and Ensuring Pharmacy Benefit Manager Accountability) of the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2026 (CAA).
We note that, as with previous rules, any new marketing and communications policies in this rule are proposed to be applicable for all contract year 2028 marketing and communications, beginning October 1, 2027.
B. Summary of the Key Provisions
1. Adjustments to Medicare Part D Cost-Sharing Reductions for Low-Income Individuals (Section 6219 of the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2026)
CMS is proposing to implement section 6219 of the CAA that would reduce the generic drug copayment from $1 to $0 for full-benefit dual eligible individuals at or below 100 percent of the Federal Poverty Level, effective for plan years starting January 1, 2028.
2. REAL Health Providers Act (Section 6220 of the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2026)
CMS proposes to codify regulations to implement section 6220 of the CAA, titled the Requiring Enhanced and Accurate Lists of (REAL) Health Providers Act, which establishes new provider directory accuracy and accountability requirements for Medicare Advantage (MA) organizations beginning in contract year 2028. Specifically, CMS proposes requirements to implement this new law related to provider directory verification and maintenance standards, annual accuracy analysis and reporting, public reporting of accuracy scores, and cost sharing protections for enrollees who rely on inaccurate provider directory information. CMS also proposes to codify the statutory requirements for contract year 2029, including that CMS must publicly display provider directory accuracy scores in a machine-readable format and MA organizations must prominently display those scores in their provider directories. Through these proposed codifications implementing the REAL Health Providers Act, CMS seeks to promote provider directory accuracy and accountability among MA organizations to ensure that beneficiaries are provided with clear, accurate information on the network of providers available to meet their health care needs.
3. Modernizing and Ensuring Pharmacy Benefit Manager Accountability (Section 6224 of the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2026)
CMS has several proposals to implement section 6224 of the CAA, which established requirements related to pharmacy benefit managers (PBMs) and their affiliates specific to the Medicare Part D program. These proposals include new and enhanced requirements governing the remuneration that PBMs and their affiliates may receive for services in connection with the utilization of Part D drugs, data reporting by PBMs to Part D plan sponsors and CMS, transparency in
(
printed page 66409)
price guarantee arrangements between PBMs or their affiliates and Part D plan sponsors, disclosure by PBMs to Part D plan sponsors of the terms of certain agreements between PBMs or their affiliates and pharmaceutical manufacturers, and other requirements added by the CAA. CMS also proposes to define key terms related to such requirements and establish compliance and enforcement mechanisms, including disgorgement of funds to CMS for violations of the remuneration requirements.
C. Summary of Costs and Benefits
D. Conclusion
Finally, we are clarifying and emphasizing our intent that if any provision of this rule, once finalized, is held to be invalid or unenforceable by its terms, or as applied to any person or circumstance, or stayed pending further agency action, it shall be severable from this rule and not affect the remainder thereof or the application of the provision to other persons not similarly situated or to other, dissimilar circumstances. Through this rule, we propose provisions that are intended to and will operate independently of each other, even if each serves the same general purpose or policy goal. Where a provision is necessarily dependent on another, the context generally makes that clear (such as by a cross-reference to apply the same standards or requirements).
II. Implementation of Certain Provisions of the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2026
A. Adjustments to Medicare Part D Cost-Sharing Reductions for Low-Income Individuals (Section 6219 of the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2026) (§ 423.782)
In the Medicare Program, Medicare Prescription Drug Benefit Final Rule (
70 FR 4194
), CMS codified at § 423.782(a)(2)(iii)(A) and (B) the cost-sharing requirements for full-benefit dual eligible (FBDE) individuals with incomes that do not exceed 100 percent of the Federal Poverty Level (FPL) pursuant to section 1860D-14(a) of the Act, codified at
42 U.S.C. 1395w-114(a)
. Under these provisions, individuals are subject to cost-sharing for covered Part D drugs equal to the lesser of the following:
A copayment amount of no more than $1 for a generic drug, approved biological product, or preferred drugs that are multiple source, or $3 for any other drug in 2006.
For years after 2006, the amounts specified earlier are adjusted for the annual percentage increase in the Consumer Price Index (CPI) as of September of the previous year, rounded to the nearest multiple of 5 cents or 10 cents, respectively; or
Under § 423.782(a)(2)(i), the copayment amount charged to: noninstitutionalized full-benefit dual eligible individuals who have income above 100 percent of the FPL, individuals with income under 135 percent of the FPL for years prior to 2024, or individuals with income under 150 percent of the FPL for years 2024 and thereafter.
On February 3, 2026, the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2026 (CAA),
Public Law 119-75
, was enacted into law. Section 6219 of the CAA, titled “Adjustments to Medicare Part D Cost-Sharing Reductions for Low-Income Individuals,” amends section 1860D-14(a) of the Act to reduce the generic drug copayment from $1 to $0 for FBDE individuals with incomes that do not exceed 100 percent of the FPL, effective for plan years beginning on or after January 1, 2028. The provision also clarifies that the existing annual CPI inflation adjustment methodology applies only to plan years before 2028 with respect to generic drug copayments for this population.
Currently, for plan years before January 1, 2028, FBDE individuals with incomes that do not exceed 100 percent of the FPL as described in § 423.782(a)(2)(iii), are subject to a $1 copayment for generic drugs covered under Medicare Part D, adjusted annually for CPI. For plan year 2026, this amount is $1.60 for generic drugs and $4.90 for other covered Part D drugs, with no deductible, as reflected in the CY 2026 Resource and Cost-Sharing Limits for Low-Income Subsidy guidance issued October 31, 2025.
To implement section 6219 of the CAA, we are proposing to amend § 423.782(a)(2)(iii) to reflect that, for plan years beginning on or after January 1, 2028, the copayment for generic drugs for FBDE individuals with incomes that do not exceed 100 percent of the FPL is $0. First, we are proposing to amend § 423.782(a)(2)(iii)(A) to specify that the cost-sharing rules in that paragraph are applicable to plan years before January 1, 2028. Second, we are proposing to redesignate paragraph (B) in § 423.782(a)(2)(iii) as paragraph (C) and add new paragraph (B) to specify that for plan years beginning on or after January 1, 2028, the copayment for generic drugs for FBDE individuals with incomes that do not exceed 100 percent of the FPL is $0.
This proposal is a conforming change to existing regulatory text and would not alter the eligibility criteria, subsidy
(
printed page 66410)
structure, or any other cost-sharing parameters applicable to FBDE individuals. CMS is not proposing any changes to the copayment amounts applicable to the cost-sharing requirements for non-generic (brand-name) drugs or other covered Part D drugs for FBDE individuals. Specifically, the copayment for preferred multiple-source drugs and other covered drugs for FBDE individuals would continue to be adjusted annually for CPI in accordance with existing statutory and regulatory requirements. This proposal is narrowly tailored to implement the specific statutory directive in section 6219 of the CAA and does not introduce any discretionary policy changes.
We estimate approximately 6 million enrollees would be affected by these proposed changes, based on 2026 CMS enrollment data. We believe the proposed changes would impact the Medicare Trust Fund and individuals in two ways: elimination of the co-pay is expected to reduce out-of-pocket costs for affected enrollees, and the anticipated increase in generic drug utilization is expected to affect Medicare Trust Fund expenditures through transferring copay costs from the beneficiary to the Medicare program. This rule does not include a new collection of information; therefore, there is no change in paperwork burden to plans or individuals. Additional information is provided in the regulatory impact analysis in section IV.C.1. of this proposed rule.
B. REAL Health Providers Act (Section 6220 of the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2026) (§§ 422.2, 422.111, 422.120, 422.123, 422.124, 422.202, 422.504, 422.2265, and 422.2267)
On February 3, 2026, in section 6220 of the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2026 (CAA) (
Pub. L. 119-75
, H.R. 7148-484), Congress enacted the Requiring Enhanced and Accurate Lists of (REAL) Health Providers Act. The REAL Health Providers Act amends sections 1851, 1852, and 1857 of the Act to establish new provider directory accuracy and accountability requirements for MA organizations, effective January 1, 2028, which is the beginning of contract year 2028. These statutory requirements include provider directory accuracy standards, accuracy score reporting, verification requirements, public transparency, and enrollee cost sharing protections. CMS is proposing to codify regulations to implement the REAL Health Providers Act legislation through this proposed rule. In addition to the statutory authority of the REAL Health Providers Act, CMS is also relying on the statutory authorities of sections 1856(b)(1) and 1857(e)(1) of the Act to establish the standards needed to implement the REAL Health Providers Act that go beyond what is specifically addressed in section 6220 of the CAA. Section 1856(b)(1) of the Act provides that CMS shall establish by regulation other standards for MA organizations and plans consistent with, and to carry out, the Part C program. Likewise, section 1857(e)(1) of the Act authorizes CMS to specify additional contract terms as necessary and appropriate in the agreements that CMS enters into with each MA organization.
The REAL Health Providers Act directs the Secretary to strengthen requirements for the accuracy and public availability of provider directory information maintained by MA organizations offering specified MA plans. Existing regulations at § 422.111(m), finalized for plan years beginning on or after January 1, 2026, already establish a foundational framework requiring MA organizations to submit provider directory information to CMS/HHS for publication online in a format and manner determined by CMS (that is, on Medicare Plan Finder (MPF)), update that information within 30 days of becoming aware of a change, and attest to its accuracy no less than annually. As CMS explained when finalizing the § 422.111(m) requirements, these changes were intended to promote transparency and informed beneficiary choice by improving access to accurate online provider directory information for beneficiaries who are navigating their health care options (
90 FR 45140
). These goals closely parallel the enhanced accuracy and transparency requirements in the REAL Health Providers Act. Therefore, in implementing the REAL Health Providers Act, CMS intends to build directly upon, reinforce, and, where necessary, supplement this existing regulatory infrastructure, ensuring MA organizations have a clear and harmonized set of provider directory requirements, rather than creating a parallel, duplicative, or competing set of standards.
CMS is also actively developing a National Provider Directory (NPD), which is a centralized, standardized repository intended to serve as the authoritative public-facing platform for provider directory information across the entire health tech ecosystem. CMS expects that the provider directory data that it currently collects from MA organizations under the authority of § 422.111(m) will be compatible with and may ultimately feed into the NPD infrastructure. Accordingly, CMS's proposed implementation of the REAL Health Providers Act requirements, through the existing § 422.111(m) framework, as described here in this section, is intended to be a deliberate and forward-looking approach that will position MA organizations, CMS, and the public to realize the full transparency benefits of the NPD as it develops. CMS believes this integrated approach, leveraging existing regulatory requirements, building towards a centralized national directory, and now incorporating the enhanced statutory mandates of the REAL Health Providers Act to verify data accuracy, represents the most administratively sound and least burdensome path to ensuring beneficiaries have access to accurate, reliable, and readily available provider directory information.
Taken together, these layered requirements—the existing § 422.111(m) data submission framework, the developing NPD infrastructure, and the new REAL Health Providers Act requirements regarding accuracy, verification, cost sharing protections, and public reporting mandates—work to support the larger health tech ecosystem to form a cohesive and mutually reinforcing regulatory architecture designed to ensure that beneficiaries can rely on provider directory information when making critical health care decisions. For example, the REAL Health Providers Act establishes statutory accuracy and verification standards specific to MA organizations, the MPF effort builds near-term data infrastructure for plan comparison, and the NPD advances a broader multi-payer directory accessible to all. While each of these initiatives operates on a distinct timeline and authority, they are intentionally designed to complement and reinforce one another. The accuracy scoring and verification framework required under the REAL Health Providers Act, for example, will serve to strengthen the integrity of the underlying provider data that both MPF and the NPD will likely come to depend upon, helping to ensure a consistent and reliable foundation for the larger health tech ecosystem.
CMS's proposed regulatory changes align with the statutory requirements of the REAL Health Providers Act. The proposals impact various existing sections under
42 CFR part 422
, including §§ 422.2, 422.111, 422.120, 422.202, 422.504, 422.2265, and 422.2267. In addition, CMS is proposing to add two new sections: § 422.123—Provider directory accuracy requirements and § 422.124—Cost
(
printed page 66411)
sharing protections for reliance on incorrect provider directory information. CMS's proposals contained herein also consider feedback received from interested parties during the June 15, 2026, public meeting co-hosted by CMS and the Office of the National Coordinator for Health Information Technology (ONC), to gather input on implementing the REAL Health Providers Act. This virtual public meeting included participation from health care providers and suppliers, companies that specialize in relevant technologies (for example, provider data management, directory solutions, interoperability, verification tools, and data standards), health insurers (including MA organizations and other health plans), and patient advocates. CMS's proposals also considered written feedback from interested parties submitted after the public meeting.
During the June 15, 2026, public meeting, participants broadly supported CMS's efforts to improve provider directory accuracy while emphasizing the importance of implementing these requirements in a manner that minimizes administrative burden and promotes standardized, interoperable data exchange. Participants consistently identified provider practice locations, specialty information, acceptance of new patients, telehealth capabilities, and provider participation status as among the most challenging provider directory data elements to maintain accurately. Several participants recommended establishing standardized definitions for key provider directory information, which informed CMS's proposal to establish consistent provider directory information requirements and definitions.
Interested parties also expressed strong support for a centralized, authoritative source of provider directory information and encouraged CMS to leverage interoperability standards, existing CMS data sources, and emerging technologies to improve directory accuracy while reducing duplicative verification activities. These comments are consistent with CMS's proposed approach of building upon the existing provider directory submission framework under § 422.111(m), supporting the development of the NPD, and permitting the use of CMS-maintained data sources and verification methods. In addition, interested parties emphasized the importance of transparent, repeatable verification methodologies and encouraged CMS to recognize verification approaches that reduce burden on both MA organizations and providers.
Interested parties also discussed prioritizing provider specialty types with historically higher rates of directory inaccuracies, including behavioral health providers, and recommended that CMS focus verification and oversight efforts where they would have the greatest impact on beneficiary access to care. These comments informed CMS's proposals to identify high-inaccuracy provider specialty types and develop a weighted provider directory accuracy scoring methodology that considers both the relative importance of provider directory information to beneficiary access and the administrative burden associated with analysis. Finally, interested parties highlighted the importance of beneficiary protections when provider directory information is inaccurate, reinforcing CMS's proposal to implement the enrollee cost sharing protections established under the REAL Health Providers Act.
Overall, these proposals support the Administration's goals of improving health care transparency, strengthening beneficiary access to accurate provider information, ensuring that beneficiaries are protected when they rely on information furnished by MA organizations, and integrating with health tech ecosystem initiatives. Specifically, these proposed changes align with the June 24, 2019,
Executive Order 13877
, “Improving Price and Quality Transparency in American Healthcare to Put Patients First” (hereinafter referred to as
E.O. 13877
) and the February 25, 2025,
Executive Order 14221
, “Making America Healthy Again by Empowering Patients With Clear, Accurate, and Actionable Healthcare Pricing Information” (hereinafter referred to as
E.O. 14221
). Through these proposed codifications implementing the REAL Health Providers Act, CMS seeks to promote provider directory accuracy and accountability among MA organizations to ensure that beneficiaries are provided with clear, accurate information on the network of providers available to meet their health care needs.
1. Definitions (§ 422.2)
CMS is using the existing definition of “provider” under § 422.2 for purposes of this proposed regulation, unless otherwise indicated. Pursuant to § 422.2, a provider is (1) any individual who is engaged in the delivery of health care services in a state and is licensed or certified by the state to engage in that activity in the state; and (2) any entity that is engaged in the delivery of health care services in a state and is licensed or certified to deliver those services if such licensing or certification is required by state law or regulation.
To use consistent terminology throughout all impacted regulation sections, CMS proposes adding several new provider directory related definitions to § 422.2. The REAL Health Providers Act amended the disclosure requirements at section 1852(c) of the Act to add new subsection (c)(3) entitled “Provider Directory Accuracy.” The statute provides that the obligations under this subsection will apply to “specified MA plans” as defined in section 1852(c)(3)(C) of the Act. Thus, consistent with section 1852(c)(3)(C) of the Act, CMS proposes to define “specified MA plan” at § 422.2 as: (1) a network-based plan as defined in § 422.2—which includes MA plans that are coordinated care plans (for example, health maintenance organizations, provider-sponsored organizations, regional or local preferred provider organizations (PPOs), and specialized MA plans for special needs individuals), network-based Medicare Savings Account plans, or cost plans—or (2) an MA private fee-for-service (PFFS) plan that meets the access standards under § 422.114, in whole or in part, through entering into contracts or agreements with a network of providers. In other words, the proposed definition of “specified MA plan,” and the related proposed requirements for specified MA plans described in this proposed rule, would apply to all types of MA plans except non-network regional PPOs that meet access requirements substantially through the authority of § 422.112(a)(1)(ii) instead of written contracts. Likewise, the proposed definition of “specified MA plan” and the related proposed requirements for specified MA plans, would not apply to Program of All-Inclusive Care for the Elderly (PACE) plans.
In addition, section 1852(c)(3)(B) of the Act defines “provider directory information” as “information enrollees may need to access covered benefits from a provider with which such organization offering such plan has an agreement for furnishing items and services covered under such plan, such as name, specialty, contact information, primary office or facility addresses where items or services are furnished, whether the provider is accepting new patients, accommodations for people with disabilities, cultural and linguistic capabilities, and telehealth capabilities.” Accordingly, CMS proposes to define “provider directory information” at § 422.2 to conform with this section of the Act as “information enrollees may need to access covered benefits from a provider with which an
(
printed page 66412)
MA organization offering a specified MA plan has an agreement for furnishing items and services covered under such plan, including, at a minimum, all of the following: (1) provider name; (2) specialty; (3) contact information, including telephone number(s); (4) primary office or facility address(es) where covered items or services are furnished; (5) whether the provider is accepting new patients; (6) accommodations for people with disabilities; (7) cultural and linguistic capabilities; (8) telehealth capabilities; and (9) common ownership or control disclosure.”
This proposed regulatory definition captures all the elements of the statutory definition and includes one additional element—common ownership or control disclosure. CMS interprets the “such as” in section 1852(c)(3)(B) of the Act to mean that the data elements specifically listed in the statute are required, but not exhaustive of the types of information that may be considered “provider directory information” (that is, information that enrollees may need to access covered benefits from a contracted provider) for purposes of the requirements provided under the REAL Health Providers Act. CMS believes that common ownership or control disclosure is necessary to inform plan and provider choice because vertical integration may affect care delivery arrangements, referral patterns, and negotiated charges or payment arrangements. Greater transparency regarding common ownership or control may also be useful for beneficiaries, caregivers, State Health Insurance Assistance Program (SHIP) counselors, agents, brokers, researchers, and other entities assisting beneficiaries or evaluating MA provider networks. In the MA marketplace, provider networks are a central feature beneficiaries use to compare plan options, assess whether they can access preferred providers, and understand how care may be delivered within a plan's network. Information indicating that a network provider, provider group, facility, or supplier is under common ownership or control with the MA organization or its parent organization may provide important context about the relationship between the plan and the providers from whom enrollees may obtain covered services. For example, such information may help beneficiaries and those assisting them understand whether a plan's network includes providers that are part of the same corporate family as the MA organization, which may be relevant to evaluating provider choice, potential care coordination arrangements, referral pathways, and the structure of the network. CMS also believes that this information may promote broader transparency in the MA marketplace by allowing researchers, policymakers, and other interested parties to better assess the prevalence and effects of vertical integration across MA networks, including how common ownership or control relationships may relate to network design, access to care, utilization patterns, and beneficiary decision-making.
Under the proposed definition for “provider directory information” at § 422.2, CMS proposes for common ownership or control disclosures to include any network provider, provider group, facility, or supplier that is owned or controlled, in whole or in part, directly or indirectly, by the MA organization, by the MA organization's parent organization, by a subsidiary or affiliate of the MA organization, or by any entity that is under common ownership or control with the MA organization. CMS considers a provider to share ownership or control with an MA organization if the provider and the MA organization are directly or indirectly owned or controlled by the same parent organization, ultimate parent organization, holding company, or other controlling entity, regardless of whether the MA organization itself directly owns the provider. For example, an MA organization may be one subsidiary of a parent or holding company, while a physician group, hospital system, or other network provider may be owned by a separate subsidiary of the same parent or holding company. In this scenario, the MA organization may not directly own the provider, and the provider may not be legally organized under the MA organization itself. However, because both the MA organization and the provider are owned or controlled, directly or indirectly, by the same parent or holding company, CMS would consider the provider to be under common ownership or control with the MA organization for purposes of the proposed provider directory disclosure requirement. The provider directory disclosure could state: “This provider is under common ownership or control with [MA organization name or parent organization name].”
As another example, an MA organization's parent organization may own a health care services subsidiary, and that subsidiary may own, control, or partially own a provider group through one or more intermediate entities, and such provider group may be in the MA plan's network. The provider group may operate under a different trade name, may contract with multiple health plans, and may not be directly owned by the MA organization. Nevertheless, if the MA organization and the provider group are connected through indirect ownership or control by the same parent organization, affiliate, subsidiary, or other controlling entity, then CMS would consider the provider group to be under common ownership or control with the MA organization for purposes of the provider directory disclosure requirement. In that circumstance, the directory could identify the relationship using standardized language, such as: “This provider group is under common ownership or control with [MA organization name or parent organization name].” CMS solicits comments on the proposed model language that should be used in the disclosure statement and whether different versions of the statement would be necessary to accommodate different types of ownership or affiliations. With this proposed model language, CMS aims to capture these various business relationships appropriately but also provide the information in a simple and understandable manner for beneficiaries.
This requirement to disclose common ownership or control would not alter, or otherwise affect any existing or future standards, definitions, reporting obligations, or analyses related to MA bid development, medical loss ratio reporting, related-party disclosures, financial audits, or any other program integrity, payment, accounting, or oversight requirements outside of this provider directory disclosure construct. CMS solicits comments on whether these examples appropriately describe the types of direct, indirect, affiliate, subsidiary, parent, and common-control relationships that should be included in the proposed provider directory disclosure requirement, and whether additional examples or exclusions would be helpful for MA organizations, providers, beneficiaries, and other users of provider directory information.
CMS notes that the proposed provider directory element of “accommodations for people with disabilities” is referring to notations in the provider directory for provider listings in which accommodations for people with disabilities exist. Such accommodations may include physical accessibility features (such as accessible entrances with ramps, elevators, accessible exam rooms and tables, accessible medical equipment, and accessible parking), auxiliary aids and services, and other necessary accommodations. MA organizations must adhere to all current
(
printed page 66413)
federal laws and regulations concerning accommodations for people with disabilities, including Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act of 1973, Title II of the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) of 1990, and Section 1557 of the Affordable Care Act of 2010. Questions regarding this topic should be directed to the HHS Office for Civil Rights (OCR).
In addition, CMS notes that the proposed provider directory element of “cultural and linguistic capabilities” based on the language in the Act is similar to existing language at § 422.111(b)(3)(i). However, CMS proposes to adopt the terminology used by Congress for “cultural and linguistic capabilities” without retaining the additional language in current § 422.111(b)(3)(i) specifying that “each provider's” cultural and linguistic capabilities includes “languages (including American Sign Language) offered by the provider or a skilled medical interpreter at the provider's office.” In light of the intervening statutory requirement enacted by Congress, CMS believes it is appropriate to implement section 1852(c)(3)(B) of the Act using the terminology selected by Congress. This approach retains the requirement for MA organizations to include providers' cultural and linguistic capabilities in their provider directories and also reflects changes in Federal policy since publication of the April 12, 2023, Medicare Program; Contract Year 2024 Policy and Technical Changes to the Medicare Advantage Program, Medicare Prescription Drug Benefit Program, Medicare Cost Plan Program, and Programs of All-Inclusive Care for the Elderly final rule.
Executive Order 14151
, “Ending Radical and Wasteful Government DEI Programs and Preferencing,” directed agencies, consistent with applicable law, to review Federal policies and regulations adopted in furtherance of prior diversity, equity, inclusion, and accessibility initiatives and to align agency actions with the policies established by that order. CMS recognizes that providers may have a variety of cultural and linguistic capabilities that could be included in an MA organization's provider directory. Therefore, by removing this additional language, CMS is providing added flexibility regarding the types of cultural and linguistic capabilities that MA organizations can include in their provider directories. As proposed, CMS intends to allow MA organizations to include information beyond the examples identified in § 422.111(b)(3)(i). This flexibility would allow MA organizations to highlight capabilities that respond to the specific needs of their enrollees and help beneficiaries identify providers who can meet those needs.
CMS also proposes to add a definition for “provider directory” to § 422.2, which would pull together provider directory categories of information (§ 422.111(b)(3)(i)(A), (b)(3)(i)(B), and (b)(12)) and be defined as “for specified MA plans, as defined in this section, the publicly available listing, maintained and distributed by an MA organization pursuant to § 422.2267(e)(11), of providers that are currently contracted and participating in that MA plan's provider network, and containing the information under § 422.111(b)(3)(i)(A), (b)(3)(i)(B), and (b)(12).” CMS's proposed definition for “specified MA plan” would apply here. Note that CMS is proposing to include the cross-reference to § 422.111(b)(3)(i)(B) in this proposed definition of “provider directory,” which eliminates the need to refer to “provider directory information” in this definition because CMS's proposed changes to § 422.111(b)(3)(i)(B) (discussed in section II.B.11. of this proposed rule) include a cross-reference to the definition of “provider directory information.”
Finally, CMS proposes to define “provider directory accuracy score” at § 422.2 as “the score reflecting the accuracy of provider directory information calculated and reported in accordance with § 422.123(d).” Regarding the cross-references to §§ 422.111(b)(12) and 422.123(d) in these two proposed definitions, these are two new proposed sections of the regulation which CMS discusses in sections II.B.4., II.B.5., II.B.6., and II.B.11. of this proposed rule. CMS solicits comments on these proposed changes to definitions at § 422.2.
2. Provider Directory Verification Requirements (§§ 422.123(a) and (b), 422.2265(b)(3) and (b)(15), and 422.111(h)(2))
The REAL Health Providers Act's addition of section 1852(c)(3) of the Act establishes new provider directory requirements for plan year 2028 and subsequent plan years, in which each MA organization offering a specified MA plan shall, for each specified MA plan offered by the organization, do the following: (1) maintain, on a publicly available internet website, an accurate provider directory that includes provider directory information; (2) not less frequently than once every 90 days (or, in the case of a hospital or any other facility determined appropriate by the Secretary, at a lesser frequency specified by the Secretary but in no case less frequently than once every 12 months), verify the provider directory information of each provider listed in such directory and, if applicable, update such information; (3) if the organization is unable to verify such information with respect to a provider, include in such directory an indication that the information of such provider may not be up to date; and (4) remove a provider from such directory within 5 business days if the organization determines that the provider is no longer a provider participating in the network of such plan.
To implement these new requirements of section 1852(c)(3) of the Act, CMS proposes to add new § 422.123—Provider directory accuracy. Within new proposed § 422.123, paragraph (a) would set forth the applicability of the section to each MA organization offering a specified MA plan for contract year 2028 and subsequent contract years. Although the statute uses the term “plan year,” the customary term that CMS uses is “contract year,” therefore, CMS proposes language using the term “contract year” throughout the proposed regulations. To codify section 1852(c)(3)(A)(i) of the Act, CMS proposes to amend § 422.2265(b)(3) to require that an MA organization's website includes an accurate provider directory for each specified MA plan that includes provider directory information for each provider that is currently contracted and participating in the plan's provider network. CMS also proposes a slight modification to the existing regulatory language at § 422.2265(b)(3), which currently reads: “A PDF or copy of a printable provider directory.” To ensure greater clarity in terminology, CMS proposes to revise this phrase to read as follows: “a PDF or otherwise printable electronic copy of the provider directory.” Section II.B.3. of this proposed rule includes a more detailed discussion of the proposed requirements for updating this version of the provider directory.
In conjunction with the proposed changes at § 422.2265(b)(3), and in line with the January 31, 2025,
Executive Order 14192
, “Unleashing Prosperity Through Deregulation,” CMS is taking the opportunity to streamline existing regulations. CMS proposes to make conforming changes to § 422.111(h)(2) to cross-reference §§ 422.2265, 422.120(a), and 422.2267(d) and remove duplicative information that is already addressed by the aforementioned regulations. Specifically, at § 422.111(h)(2), CMS proposes to require MA organizations to
(
printed page 66414)
have a publicly available internet website that complies with the website requirements in §§ 422.2265 and 422.120(a) and state that posting copies of required materials on the website does not relieve the MA organization of its responsibility to provide hard copies to enrollees upon request in accordance with § 422.2267(d) or when required by CMS. This proposed change would remove the existing reference to § 422.111(b) in § 422.111(h)(2) and replace it with a reference to the website requirements at § 422.2265. All the contents of a plan description under § 422.111(b) are already required on MA organizations' websites per § 422.2265, except existing § 422.111(b)(9), the quality improvement program. To preserve this requirement, CMS proposes to add a new paragraph (b)(15) to § 422.2265 to require an MA organization's website to include a description of the quality improvement program required under §§ 422.152 and 422.111(b)(9). The proposed change to § 422.111(h)(2) would also remove duplicative information about hardcopy requirements for required materials (such as the evidence of coverage, provider directory, and summary of benefits) and instead include a cross-reference to these requirements which are already outlined at § 422.2267(d).
To codify section 1852(c)(3)(A)(ii) and (iii) of the Act, CMS proposes to add new § 422.123(b) to set forth the new provider directory verification requirements. Aligning with the statute, at new proposed § 422.123(b)(1), CMS proposes to require each MA organization offering a specified MA plan to verify the provider directory information of each provider listed in that specified MA plan's provider directory not less frequently than once every 90 days, except in the case of hospitals and other facilities as listed in § 422.116(b)(2)(i), (iv), and (v)—that is, acute inpatient hospitals, critical care services (intensive care units), and surgical services (outpatient or ambulatory surgery center). For these excepted hospitals and other facilities, CMS proposes to require each MA organization offering a specified MA plan to verify the provider directory information of these entities not less frequently than once every 12 months. The statute provides CMS with discretion to impose verification requirements for hospitals or any other facility determined appropriate by the Secretary at a lesser frequency than once every 90 days (as is the case for other providers) but at a frequency no less than once every 12 months. At this time, CMS is proposing a 12-month verification frequency for these entities. CMS selected these three types of entities because CMS believes that data for these specific entities is generally more static, as they may not move locations as often as other providers or facilities given their size and facility requirements, therefore, verifying the information at least every 12 months is sufficient for these types of entities. This policy approach would also limit some of the burden associated with verification on both MA organizations and these facilities. In addition, CMS's proposed reference to hospitals and other facilities listed in § 422.116(b)(2)(i), (iv), and (v) is appropriate because MA organizations are familiar with this list of facilities for purposes of network adequacy. CMS seeks comments specifically on the proposed selection of other facilities listed in § 422.116(b)(2)(i), (iv), and (v) for the 12-month verification requirement. For all providers listed in the provider directory, CMS proposes that the MA organization must comply with the appropriate verification frequency (90 days or 12 months) and update the provider directory in accordance with CMS's updating requirements, if updates are needed. Provider directory updating requirements are discussed in section II.B.3. of this proposed rule.
Next, at new proposed § 422.123(b)(2), CMS proposes to require the MA organization to use one or more CMS-specified provider directory verification methods to meet the provider verification requirements, including verification using internal plan information, verification via telephone or email, verification using provider attestations, verification using data sources maintained by CMS, claims data, or other verification methods specified by CMS. By including internal plan information as a proposed CMS-specified provider directory verification method, CMS is referring to information such as current, accurate provider rosters or recent claims information. Regarding data sources maintained by CMS, CMS means provider data repositories, such as the National Plan and Provider Enumeration System (NPPES), and provider directory databases, such as the NPD, that are maintained by CMS. By including claims data, CMS is referring to data containing information on recent claims between the contracted provider and the MA organization.
By including data sources maintained by CMS and other verification methods specified by CMS in this proposed list, CMS would retain the flexibility to specify additional acceptable, CMS-approved verification methods in technical guidance. CMS is aware that this is a space where technology and the use of artificial intelligence is quickly evolving and CMS's work on the NPD is ongoing, and including this flexibility in proposed § 422.123(b)(2) would enable CMS to respond more quickly to advancements in verification methods, ultimately providing MA organizations with more options for meeting their provider directory verification obligations. CMS would provide technical guidance as necessary.
CMS anticipates that MA organizations may need to use more than one verification method to verify all the elements of provider directory information in the proposed provider directory verification requirements. For example, CMS recognizes that MA organizations may be accustomed to using NPPES. However, NPPES has both benefits and limitations, including the fact that certain provider directory information may not be available in NPPES, such as whether a provider is accepting new patients. As such, there will likely be a need for MA organizations to supplement use of NPPES with other verification method(s) to verify all the elements of provider directory information that CMS requires. In addition, CMS is also actively developing the NPD, which is intended to be a centralized, standardized repository meant to serve as the authoritative public-facing platform for provider directory information across the entire health tech ecosystem. CMS anticipates that once the NPD is fully operational, MA organizations might be able to use this source for verification, as it falls under the category of a data source maintained by CMS.
CMS issued guidance through the Health Plan Management System (HPMS) on January 3, 2020, and June 29, 2022, about the use of NPPES for determining the accuracy of provider directory data in CMS's various monitoring and enforcement activities. In the January 3, 2020, HPMS memorandum, CMS stated that the agency, in its monitoring and enforcement activities, would employ discretion should it uncover errors in directories that are consistent with NPPES data that has been updated or certified between January 1 and April 30, 2020, so long as any errors identified are corrected within 30 days. In the June 29, 2022, HPMS memorandum, CMS stated that it would continue to use discretion while monitoring and reviewing organizations' online provider directories for compliance and enforcement action and that during
(
printed page 66415)
compliance reviews, if CMS finds an error in an organization's online provider directory and the error matches the information in NPPES, then that error will not be considered an “error” for purposes of compliance so long as the organization contacts the provider, whose information was incorrect, within 30 days to encourage the provider to correct their information in NPPES. By proposing to include NPPES as one of the verification methods that MA organizations may use to verify provider directory information, and also because there would be other verification methods that MA organizations may use, CMS would not need to continue to use this discretion for compliance and enforcement actions if these provisions are finalized as proposed. Also, since issuing these memoranda, the landscape related to provider directories in MA has shifted due to the REAL Health Providers Act and CMS's efforts to develop the NPD. Therefore, if these provisions are finalized as proposed, CMS intends to rescind this previously issued guidance (in both the January 3, 2020, and June 29, 2022, HPMS memoranda) regarding MA organizations' usage of NPPES for purposes of verifying provider directory accuracy.
CMS notes that, in developing the proposal for the 90-day/12-month provider directory verification requirement at new proposed § 422.123(b)(2), CMS considered limiting which verification method(s) may be used by MA organizations for which provider directory elements. Including such limitations may potentially impose additional burden on MA organizations. At this time, CMS is not proposing any such limitations on MA organizations' use of the proposed verification method(s) for fulfilling their 90-day/12-month provider directory verification obligations as described in new proposed § 422.123(b)(1)(i) and (ii). However, as discussed in section II.B.5. of this proposed rule, at new proposed § 422.123(d)(3)(i), CMS is proposing to limit what verification method(s) may be used by MA organizations to evaluate the accuracy of certain provider directory data elements for purposes of calculating the estimated provider directory accuracy score (please refer to that section of this proposed rule for a more detailed discussion). CMS solicits comments on the considerations and proposals surrounding limiting verification approaches, for both new proposed § 422.123(b)(2) and (d)(3)(i). In addition, CMS intends to identify certain best practices in technical guidance, such as which verification methods might be more appropriate or reliable for the proposed 90-day/12-month provider directory verification requirement, depending on the particular provider directory data elements being verified.
To implement section 1852(c)(3)(A)(iii) of the Act, at § 422.123(b)(3), CMS proposes to require that if the MA organization is unable to verify provider directory information with respect to a provider during the applicable verification cycle, then the MA organization must include in the provider directory a clear indication that the information of such provider may not be up to date. An example of language that CMS believes would be sufficient for this proposed indicator is: “The provider's information may not be up to date.” If § 422.123(b)(3) is finalized as proposed, then CMS intends to update the Medicare Advantage and Section 1876 Cost Plan Provider Directory Model and Instructions with similar template language for the indicator. If the MA organization subsequently verifies or updates the information, then the MA organization must remove or revise the indicator consistent with CMS's provider directory updating requirements.
Finally, per existing statutory authority under section 1856(b)(1) of the Act to establish by regulation other standards for MA organizations consistent with, and to carry out, the Part C program, CMS is proposing, at new proposed § 422.123(b)(4), to require that each MA organization offering a specified MA plan must include a term in their contract with each contracted provider for a specified MA plan, obligating the contracted provider to maintain current and accurate provider directory information as defined in proposed § 422.2. The purpose of this new proposed contract requirement is to ensure that when the MA organization verifies provider directory information in accordance with proposed § 422.123(b), the information the MA organization obtains from each contracted provider is more likely to be current and accurate. This proposed contract requirement is intended to improve the reliability of the data that MA organizations obtain directly from their contracted providers, specifically the type of data collected using the first four CMS-specified verification methods outlined at proposed § 422.123(b)(2)(i) through (iv), which are internal plan information, telephonic verification, email verification, and provider attestations. CMS believes that this proposed provider contract term is necessary to assist MA organizations in carrying out successful verification efforts, which would ultimately support the broader effort to ensure accurate provider directories.
In summary, to implement several aspects of the REAL Health Providers Act, CMS is proposing the provider directory accuracy applicability requirement at new proposed § 422.123(a), verification requirements at new proposed § 422.123(b), proposed changes to the website requirement at § 422.2265(b)(3), a streamlining of existing regulations at § 422.111(h)(2), and a preservation of the existing requirement for a description of the quality improvement program on an MA organization's website at new proposed § 422.2265(b)(15). CMS solicits comments on these proposed changes.
3. Provider Directory Updating Requirements (§§ 422.123(c) and 422.2267(e)(11)(iv))
Implementation of the REAL Health Providers Act presents CMS with the opportunity to streamline other existing provider directory regulations, including rules around updating provider directories. After considering the proposed layout of the new rules for provider directory accuracy, CMS determined it would be prudent to move the existing updating requirements for provider directories to new proposed § 422.123, for purposes of logic and ease of reading. Therefore, CMS is proposing to move the updating requirements from § 422.2267(e)(11)(iv) to new proposed § 422.123(c). CMS is not changing the basic 30-day provider directory updating requirement, but CMS is proposing some changes in order to implement certain requirements of the REAL Health Providers Act. The current provider directory regulations apply to MA plans with provider networks, all of which are included in the proposed definition of “specified MA plan.”
The MA organization will still be required to update both the online provider directory and the PDF or otherwise printable electronic copy of the provider directory (as specified in proposed § 422.2265(b)(3)) within at least 30 days of receiving information requiring update, except that a provider must be removed from the directory no later than 5 business days after the MA organization determines that the provider is no longer participating in the specified MA plan's network. CMS is proposing to move this requirement to new proposed § 422.123(c)(1). This proposed 5-business-day updating requirement would apply to both the online provider directory and the PDF or otherwise printable electronic copy of the provider directory (as specified in proposed § 422.2265(b)(3)). In other
(
printed page 66416)
words, if this requirement is finalized as proposed, MA organizations would be required to update the PDF or otherwise printable electronic copy version of their provider directory within 5 business days, but this would not mean printing new physical hardcopies since the PDF or otherwise printable electronic copy of the provider directory is required to be posted on the MA organization's website. This 5-business-day updating requirement would apply to PDF or otherwise printable electronic copy of the provider directory posted on the MA organization's website and would not require an MA organization to mail a revised physical hardcopy directory to an enrollee within 5 business days. As discussed further later, for enrollees who have requested a physical hardcopy provider directory, CMS is separately proposing at § 422.123(c)(2) to require MA organizations to send a quarterly addendum containing updates to the provider directory. This quarterly addendum would provide a regular mechanism for keeping enrollees who rely on a previously furnished physical hardcopy directory informed of subsequent directory changes without requiring MA organizations to mail a revised physical hardcopy directory each time an update is made.
To codify section 1852(c)(3)(A)(iv) of the Act, at § 422.123(c)(4) CMS proposes to require that the MA organization must remove a provider from the provider directory no later than 5 business days after the date on which the MA organization determines that the provider is no longer participating in the network of the specified MA plan. This would be the only proposed exception to the 30-day provider directory updating requirement at new proposed § 422.123(c)(1).
In addition, although the REAL Health Providers Act does not include a specific timeframe for updating physical hardcopy provider directories, CMS would like to take the opportunity through this proposed rule to further clarify the policies regarding physical hardcopy updates via addenda. Currently, § 422.2267(e)(11)(iv)(B)(2) states that hardcopy directories that include separate updates via addenda are considered up to date. CMS has reconsidered this policy and determined that it would be beneficial to specify a regular cadence for updating physical hardcopy directories to avoid ambiguity or misinterpretation by MA organizations. Specifically, CMS proposes to require MA organizations to send a quarterly addendum containing updates to all enrollees who have requested a physical hardcopy provider directory. Sending a quarterly update only to those enrollees who have requested a physical hardcopy directory would meet the requirements for keeping physical hardcopy directories updated and avoid the need for MA organizations to mail updated physical hardcopy directories on a monthly basis, thus reducing burden. This policy would be a supportive beneficiary protection because it would keep enrollees informed with a predictable and regular cadence of updates if they are accustomed to using a physical hardcopy directory, and it would protect enrollees from making a misinformed decision based on an outdated version of the physical hardcopy directory. CMS proposes to add this requirement regarding the quarterly addendum for physical hardcopy provider directories at new proposed § 422.123(c)(2).
In addition, while CMS believes it is unlikely for plans or agents/brokers to use physical hardcopy directories at marketing events (and instead refer to or show prospective enrollees the online provider directory), CMS clarifies that if plans or agents/brokers do plan to distribute physical hardcopy directories, then they would need to print out the PDF or otherwise printable electronic copy of the provider directory that exists on the MA organization's website and use that current, up-to-date version if needed for physical distribution to prospective enrollees. This would ensure that prospective enrollees have access to the most updated provider directory that exists at that time.
Furthermore, due to the point-in-time nature of physical hardcopy directory updates and the fact that if CMS finalizes the proposed quarterly addenda policy then enrollees receiving a physical hardcopy directory would only receive four updates per year, CMS proposes to require that MA organizations include a disclaimer on the physical hardcopy provider directory that recommends beneficiaries check the online provider directory or contact the MA organization for the latest updates. CMS proposes to add this requirement at new proposed § 422.123(c)(3). CMS believes this type of disclaimer is essential to keep all beneficiaries (both prospective enrollees and current enrollees) informed and aware that the online directory is likely the most reliable version because of the ease and timeliness of making electronic updates. This would ensure that all beneficiaries have access to the most current and accurate information about the plan's provider network.
These proposed changes related to provider directory updating requirements at new proposed § 422.123(c) would replace and supplement existing updating requirements at § 422.2267(e)(11)(iv). Accordingly, CMS is proposing to amend § 422.2267(e)(11)(iv) to require that the provider directory be verified and updated in accordance with § 422.123(b) and (c) (for contract year 2028 and subsequent contract years).
In summary, CMS is proposing several changes to the provider directory updating requirements, including moving existing updating requirements from § 422.2267(e)(11)(iv) to § 422.123(c)(1), implementing section 1852(c)(3)(A)(iv) of the Act at § 422.123(c)(4), adding new requirements related to physical hardcopy directories at § 422.123(c)(2) and (c)(3), and updating § 422.2267(e)(11)(iv) to refer to § 422.123(b) and (c). CMS solicits comments on these proposed changes.
4. Provider Directory Accuracy Analysis and Sampling Methodology (§ 422.123(d)(1) and (2))
In addition to provider directory verification and updating requirements, the REAL Health Providers Act establishes new requirements regarding provider directory accuracy. Section 1857(e)(6)(A) of the Act requires that beginning with plan years beginning on or after January 1, 2028, each MA organization must conduct an annual analysis estimating the accuracy of the provider directory information of each specified MA plan using a random sample of providers included in such provider directory. Further, section 1857(e)(6)(A)(i)(I) and (II) of the Act states that this sample shall include a random sample of each specialty of providers with a high inaccuracy rate of provider directory information relative to other specialties of providers, as determined by the Secretary, and one type of specialty may be providers specializing in mental health or substance use disorder treatment. CMS believes it is important that the provider directory accuracy analysis focus on a blend of provider specialty types including those that are known to have a high inaccuracy rate, as required by the statute, but to further include other provider specialty types that do not fall within the high inaccuracy rate criteria. Following this process allows CMS to continue to test and identify areas of inaccuracy as they apply to provider specialty types.
To implement the new requirements of section 1857(e)(6)(A) of the Act, CMS proposes to add new § 422.123(d)(1) to establish the annual accuracy analysis requirement and § 422.123(d)(2) to set

CMS's proposed definitions for “provider directory information” and “specified MA plan” at § 422.2 would apply here. When determining provider specialty types with high provider directory inaccuracy rates, at new proposed § 422.123(d)(2)(i), CMS proposes that CMS will consider all provider specialty types included in the Medicare specialty codes and National Uniform Claim Committee (NUCC) taxonomy and may consider other provider specialty types and providers furnishing supplemental benefits.

At new proposed § 422.123(d)(2)(iii), CMS proposes to require that MA organizations identify the sampling frame as consisting of provider records in the provider directory with a unique provider, address, and phone number. Thus, when considering the universe of possible provider records that may be chosen for the sample, each provider record that could be selected in that universe would need to be a unique provider at a specific address and phone number. This means that, for example, a provider could be included in the sample at one address but not at another address. Similarly, if there is a case where a provider has two different phone numbers at the same address, then one provider/address/phone combination could be selected to be in the sample, but not the other. CMS proposes this approach for the sampling frame because CMS is aiming to ensure that a provider record constitutes a single, unique listing in the provider directory, and CMS believes that using the unique provider, address, and phone number constitutes a single, unique listing. When determining a unique provider for their sampling frame, CMS recommends that MA organizations use the provider's National Provider Identifier (NPI) because the NPI uniquely identifies the provider. CMS notes that a notice that the provider information may be outdated, per the proposed requirement at new proposed § 422.123(b)(3) as discussed in section II.B.2. of this proposed rule, does not mean that records associated with the provider would be excluded for purposes of sampling. A provider with such a notice would still be considered part of the sampling frame. CMS seeks comments on this proposal.
CMS is also considering identifying the sampling frame for MA organizations as consisting of provider records that contain a unique provider and address. CMS identified a drawback to this approach because there may be cases where a provider has the same address but different phone numbers, potentially creating confusion for MA organizations when they are determining their sampling frame. CMS seeks comments on whether the proposed identification of the sampling frame as a provider record in the provider directory with a unique provider, address, and phone number is appropriate or whether only a unique provider and address would be needed to identify a unique provider record. CMS also seeks comments on other data elements that may be necessary to identify a unique provider record for the sampling frame.
CMS is proposing that MA organizations would create a sample set for purposes of the proposed accuracy analysis methodology as described in new proposed § 422.123(d)(2)(iv). At new proposed § 422.123(d)(2)(iv)(A), CMS proposes to require that MA organizations use a simple random sample with 65 percent of the sample made up of any providers in the provider directory except those with provider specialty types with high provider directory inaccuracy rates identified in § 422.123(d)(2)(ii), and 35 percent of the sample made up of providers with provider specialty types with high provider directory inaccuracy rates identified in § 422.123(d)(2)(ii). In its current proposal, CMS proposes only one provider specialty type with high provider directory inaccuracy rates at § 422.123(d)(2)(ii)(A), the provider specialty type of mental health or substance use disorder treatment. Therefore, if finalized as proposed, the 35 percent portion of the sample would be made up of only providers in the mental health or substance use disorder treatment provider specialty type. If there are more provider specialty types that CMS incorporates as provider specialty types with high provider directory inaccuracy rates, then CMS would include in regulation the portion of the 35 percent of the sample that should be made up of each provider specialty type. If this were to occur, CMS anticipates an even split in the sample amongst provider specialty types with high provider directory inaccuracy rates but will consider whether certain provider specialty types should make up more of the sample than others. CMS seeks comments on the proposed sampling methodology at new proposed § 422.123(d)(2)(iv). In addition, CMS intends to release annual technical guidance with additional information regarding its sampling methodology.
CMS is also considering stratified sampling based on county type as a way to create a sample set. CMS is considering assigning counties into two groups, one containing Large Metro, Metro, and Micro counties and a second group with Rural counties and Counties with Extreme Access Considerations (CEAC). CMS is considering defining a proportion of records that should come from each grouping. CMS is also considering using a three-group stratification of Large Metro and Metro counties making up one group, Micro counties making up a second group, and Rural and CEAC counties making up a third group, or having all five county types representing separate strata. CMS understands that the dynamics associated with each county type are different, but sampling this way may also introduce complications. For example, a specific provider may serve MA plan enrollees in both a Rural and Micro county, introducing additional steps into the sampling methodology. Due to CMS concerns about the possible additional layer of complexity and the consideration of administrative burden on MA organizations and providers, CMS has not proposed stratified sampling based on county type at this time but CMS is still actively considering this approach. CMS seeks comments about whether CMS should include any of these alternative approaches in the sampling methodology or consider other alternative approaches.
In the proposed sampling methodology described in § 422.123(d)(2), CMS is also considering specifying a number or percentage of records that must be included in the sample. CMS is concerned with ensuring that conducting accuracy analysis on the sample is not overly burdensome (that is., that the sample is not too large) but also that there are enough records in the sample to ensure that the accuracy scores calculated are meaningful (that is, that the sample is not too small). CMS seeks comments on the number or percentage of records that should be included in the sample.
CMS is considering whether the proposed sampling methodology described in § 422.123(d)(2) should specify a maximum number or percentage of records that may be incorporated in the sample. CMS understands that provider networks for specified MA plans vary considerably depending on the size of the MA organization, the number of plans offered, and where an MA organization operates, among other considerations. Conducting an accuracy analysis may be more burdensome for some MA organizations than for other MA organizations, some may prefer to use a larger sample size, and some may prefer to use a smaller sample size. MA organizations that are able to conduct provider directory accuracy analysis using a larger sample size may find that they can increase their accuracy score this way relative to an MA organization who prefers to use a smaller sample size, or they may find that using a larger sample size decreases their score while increasing the associated burden. Large differences in the sample sizes used by MA organizations may affect the comparability of the resulting accuracy scores. CMS is seeking comments about whether CMS should have a maximum
