Specifically, CMS is seeking comments on such issues as, whether there should be different considerations based on the size of MA organizations or in which types of counties MA organizations operate (Large Metro, Metro, Micro, Rural, CEAC); whether there are other differences between MA organizations that CMS should consider when determining the maximum number or percentage of records in the sample; and how CMS can help to ensure that there is a level playing field among all MA organizations. While CMS has not proposed a specific value in regulation at this time, CMS seeks comments on what values for a maximum number or percentage may be appropriate as part of the sampling methodology CMS intends to adopt, as well as comments on the considerations discussed previously.
In addition, CMS is considering whether the proposed sampling methodology described in § 422.123(d)(2) should specify a minimum number or percentage of records both for each provider specialty type with high provider directory inaccuracy rates at § 422.123(d)(2)(ii) and for an overall minimum number or percentage of records that must be in the sample. As noted earlier, CMS is interested in balancing the need to ensure that the sample is large enough to be sufficient to calculate the accuracy scores but also not so large as to be overly burdensome for MA organizations. Some smaller MA organizations or MA organizations with plans in rural areas may have fewer providers in their networks than other MA organizations. Considering both goals of having enough of a sample for a meaningful accuracy score calculation and minimizing administrative burden on MA organizations and providers, CMS seeks comments on what the minimum number or percentage of providers for each provider specialty type with high provider directory inaccuracy rates should be. While CMS has not proposed a specific value in regulation at this time, CMS seeks comments on what values for a minimum number or percentage may be appropriate as part of the sampling methodology CMS intends to adopt, as well as comments on the considerations discussed as part of the sampling methodology CMS intends to adopt.
Since the provider directory accuracy score must be reported for each specified MA plan, as discussed in section II.B.6. of this proposed rule, CMS's understanding is that the sample that supports the accuracy score will also need to be drawn at the plan level. However, to limit the burden on both MA organizations and providers, CMS intends to require that MA organizations consolidate their samples across the MA organization. For example, if a provider appears in multiple samples because they are contracted to participate with multiple MA plans, and the MA organization chooses the verification method of email (as described later), then using that verification method one time would be sufficient for each sample the provider appears in, and there would be no need to email the provider multiple times.
As part of the annual provider directory accuracy analysis and sampling methodology that CMS proposes to implement in § 422.123(d)(1) and (d)(2), CMS is considering also setting parameters governing when MA organizations must draw samples for purposes of the proposed annual accuracy analysis. CMS is considering the possibility that the MA organizations would be required to draw samples on a specified date, or dates, each year. This would ensure that results are directly comparable across plans, would reduce the risk of gaming, and would simplify the ability of beneficiaries to compare provider directory accuracy across plans. CMS also recognizes that there may be certain disadvantages to this approach, including operational constraints related to a specific date, the potential for MA organizations to focus on accuracy efforts for a known date rather than maintaining accuracy on an ongoing basis, and that such an approach limits flexibility for MA organizations. Alternatively, CMS could allow MA organizations to choose the date on which they draw their samples for their specified MA plans. This approach would provide operational flexibility and may reduce the administrative burden associated with sampling, but it would reduce the comparability across plans, increase the risk of gaming, and may increase oversight complexity for CMS. CMS is also considering some hybrid approaches, such as defining a window (for example, one quarter) and randomly assigning a date to an MA organization within that quarter or announcing the date on which the sample should be pulled with minimal advance notice. While CMS has not proposed a specific timeframe for the sample drawing in regulation at this time, CMS seeks comments on these considerations as part of the annual provider directory accuracy analysis and sampling methodology that CMS intends to adopt.
In summary, CMS is proposing to codify the provider directory accuracy analysis requirement at new proposed § 422.123(d)(1) and the sampling methodology for such analysis at new proposed § 422.123(d)(2). CMS solicits comments on these proposed changes.
5. Provider Directory Accuracy Score and Scoring Methodology (§ 422.123(d)(3) and (4))
Section 1857(e)(6)(B)(i) of the Act requires that the Secretary shall specify plan verification methods, such as using telephonic verification or other approaches using data sources maintained by an MA organization or using publicly available data sets, that MA organizations may use for estimating accuracy scores of the provider directory information of specified MA plans offered by such organizations.
To implement these statutory requirements, first CMS proposes to require that MA organizations must estimate an accuracy score reflecting the accuracy of the provider directory information. Furthermore, CMS proposes that the accuracy score must be: (1) estimated using the verification methods specified in new proposed § 422.123(b)(2) for specified provider directory elements, (2) based on the verification results for the random sample specified in new proposed § 422.123(d)(2)(i) and (d)(2)(ii) using the sampling methodology specified in new proposed § 422.123(d)(2)(iii), and (3) represented in the form of a letter grade. CMS proposes to add these provider directory accuracy score requirements at new proposed § 422.123(d)(3).
At new proposed § 422.123(d)(3)(i), CMS proposes to limit what verification method(s) may be used by MA organizations to estimate the provider directory accuracy score, such that certain provider directory elements may only be verified using certain verification methods. CMS notes that this proposed limitation of verification method(s) for certain provider directory elements only applies to MA organizations' verification methods for purposes of estimating the accuracy score at new proposed § 422.123(d)(3), not to the verification methods for the 90-day/12-month verification at new proposed § 422.123(b)(2). At new proposed § 422.123(d)(3)(i)(A), CMS proposes to limit the verification method “internal plan information” to be used only to confirm network participation status (that is, that the provider is currently contracted and participating in that MA plan's provider
(
printed page 66422)
network) and specialty because it is possible that internal plan information may be dated and contain information about a provider that is not current (for example, an old address). At new proposed § 422.123(d)(3)(i)(B) and (d)(3)(i)(C), CMS proposes to limit the use of the methods “telephonic verification” and “email verification” to the following provider directory elements: specialty; contact information; primary office or facility address(es); whether the provider is accepting new patients; accommodations for people with disabilities; and telehealth capabilities. CMS believes that direct interaction with the provider through telephone or email communication is the most effective way to verify the accuracy of these provider directory elements. CMS has not proposed using telephone or email communication to verify network participation status because telephone and email communication are two verification methods that may cause a higher burden on providers, so considering that network participation can be verified using other verification methods, CMS has not proposed to include that here. Further, CMS proposes that the verification method of provider attestations at new proposed § 422.123(d)(3)(i)(D) would not be limited to any specified provider directory elements. That is, MA organizations would be permitted to use provider attestations to verify any provider directory element. Lastly, CMS proposes that the verification method of claims data at new proposed § 422.123(d)(3)(i)(E) may be used to confirm the provider directory elements of network participation status and specialty. At this time, CMS has not proposed any provider directory elements that can be verified for the purposes of the accuracy score with the verification method “data sources maintained by CMS.” CMS may revisit this verification method with the development of the NPD and may incorporate the NPD as a verification method that may be used for one or more provider directory elements. CMS seeks comments on, for purposes of the accuracy score, whether there are data sources maintained by CMS that commenters recommend for use as reliable sources for any of the provider directory data elements. Finally, if CMS specifies other verification methods in technical guidance, as noted in new proposed § 422.123(b)(2)(vii), then CMS will identify which provider directory elements the verification method may be used for, for purposes of estimating the accuracy score at new proposed § 422.123(d)(3).
CMS understands that certain verification methods depend on a response from a provider, and a provider may not respond. If a provider does not respond to one verification method, another verification method may be used, but it is possible that an MA organization could exhaust the possible verification methods for a specific provider directory data element for their specified MA plan. As part of the sampling methodology that CMS proposes to implement in § 422.123(d)(2), CMS may implement a process for an MA organization to move on to another permitted verification method. For example, a possibility may be that if a provider did not respond within 7 business days, including at least one reminder, then the MA organization may consider that verification method exhausted and move on to another. In the event that all possible verification methods are exhausted for a particular record, CMS seeks comments on whether an MA organization should incorporate a new record into its sample to replace the non-response. The ability to add additional records into the sample if there are non-responses would prevent the sample from becoming so small as to be insufficiently comparable to the samples of other specified MA plans. However, MA organizations may also choose to oversample in order to ensure that sufficient providers respond, which may increase the administrative burden on MA organizations and providers. CMS also understands that some provider specialty types may be more difficult to receive responses from than others, and therefore seeks comments on whether there should be requirements to fill the sample with the same type of provider as a non-responding provider. Given the possibility of non-response, CMS is also considering implementing a minimum response rate that each MA organization must meet for a specified MA plan and requests comments on what that minimum response rate should be. CMS also seeks comments on the provider non-responses and how they should be considered in the sampling methodology and verification methods.
The next provision of the REAL Health Providers Act that CMS is implementing is the provider directory accuracy scoring methodology. Section 1857(e)(6)(B)(ii) of the Act states that with respect to each verification method, the Secretary shall specify a methodology for MA organizations to use in estimating such accuracy scores, and that each such methodology shall take into account the administrative burden on plans and providers and the relative importance of certain provider directory information on enrollee ability to access care.
To describe the proposed provider directory accuracy scoring methodology, CMS will use an example throughout this section. This example is simplified for purposes of illustrating the scoring methodology. For each element in the proposed definition of provider directory information, Table II.B.3 indicates the results of the verification process the MA organization for MA plan Y would follow pursuant to the proposed sampling and verification methodology described in new proposed § 422.123(d)(2) and (d)(3):
(

CMS proposes using a binary system of “accurate” and “not accurate” for each provider directory data element. Some of the data elements consist of multiple parts that make up the data element. For example, a provider's address may consist of a first address line, a second address line, a city, a state, and a zip code. A provider directory data element should only be considered “accurate” if all of the parts of that provider directory data element are correct. For example, if a provider's address has the correct first address line, city, and state, but wrong second address line and zip code, then the address would be considered “not accurate.” CMS notes that a difference in the address such as the use of the comment abbreviation “st” instead of “street” or “ct” instead of “court” would not prevent an address from being considered accurate as such differences would be considered non-material. CMS proposes this method because the aim of the accuracy score analysis is to see how correct each of the various elements are in the provider directory, and this means that each of the multiple parts that make up the data element must be correct for the whole data element to be correct.
CMS is considering offering a “partial” score if at least half of the multiple parts that make up the provider directory data element are correct. In that methodology, a score of “not accurate” would be 0, and a score of “accurate” would be 1, and if it was partially correct, the score would be “0.5.” In the address example mentioned previously, since 3 of the 5 parts of the data element were correct, that record would receive a score of 0.5 rather than 0. Some drawbacks of this approach are that it may unnecessarily complicate the scoring methodology and perpetuate inaccurate provider directory information. CMS did not propose this methodology but CMS is still actively considering this approach. CMS seeks comments on whether a score should be included for partial accuracy of any of the provider directory data elements.
CMS is also considering a confidence scoring approach to determine the accuracy or inaccuracy of a given provider directory data element. Using a confidence scoring approach, a score of “accurate” or 1 would be assigned to a provider directory data element if such data element matched least two or more verification methods, a score of “partially accurate” or 0.5 would be assigned if a provider directory data element matched at least one verification method, and a score of “inaccurate” or 0 would be assigned if a provider directory data element did not match any attempted verification methods. A concern that CMS identified is that this confidence scoring approach would be more burdensome because it would require validation against multiple sources. CMS has not proposed this methodology, but CMS is still actively considering this approach. CMS seeks comments on whether a confidence scoring approach should be used.

CMS is proposing these weights to emphasize the accuracy of certain elements in the provider directory to focus the attention of MA organizations on specific elements most significant to ensuring beneficiaries can access care. CMS proposes a weight of 40 percent for network participation status (that is, per proposed § 422.2, that the provider listed in the directory is a provider with which the MA organization offering the MA plan has an agreement for furnishing items and services covered under such plan) because this is the most foundational piece of information in a provider directory. Beneficiaries expect that the providers listed in the directory are in the MA plan's network, and, as such, beneficiaries expect to be able to access care from these in-network providers at in-network cost sharing. An error in network participation status can lead a beneficiary to unknowingly receive out-of-network care, which may result in higher costs and undermine continuity of care.
CMS proposes a weight of 20 percent for both contact information and primary office or facility address. Beneficiaries and caregivers may frequently rely on contact information from the directory to call the provider to schedule an appointment, and an incorrect phone number creates an immediate barrier for a beneficiary to access care. Beneficiaries and caregivers also need an accurate primary office or facility address to physically reach the provider, so an incorrect address would create an immediate barrier to receiving care. Also, beneficiaries may choose which provider to schedule an appointment with based on the proximity of the address to their home or other places they frequently visit. If the address information is inaccurate, then a beneficiary may inadvertently call or schedule an appointment with a provider at an address that they cannot easily access.
CMS proposes a weight of 10 percent for the provider's specialty. Accurate specialty information helps beneficiaries identify the provider for the beneficiary's particular health care needs. Inaccurate specialty information may lead the beneficiary to contact several providers before one with the correct specialty can be identified, which may slow the beneficiary's access to needed care.
CMS proposes a weight of 3.5 percent whether the provider has accommodations for people with disabilities and has telehealth capabilities. These elements provide important information to beneficiaries as they seek access to care. Beneficiaries with disabilities may need certain accommodations, and knowledge of which providers can accommodate them is integral to their decision making. Knowledge of a provider's telehealth capabilities allows beneficiaries to choose a provider that offers the option for telehealth appointments. While these two elements with the proposed weight of 3.5 percent are meaningful and important for beneficiaries to access needed care, the potential for harm if any of these elements are incorrect is more limited because beneficiaries can still identify and contact providers even if these elements are inaccurate in the provider directory. Also, the accommodations for people with disabilities provider directory element affects a subset of the overall beneficiary population, which justifies a lower proposed weight relative to the universally applicable elements.
CMS proposes a weight of 3 percent for whether the provider is accepting new patients. This element shares a lot of similarities with whether the provider has accommodations for people with disabilities and has telehealth capabilities discussed previously. This is also an element which provides important information to beneficiaries as they seek access to care. Knowing whether a provider is

accepting new patients may help beneficiaries identify providers that may have available appointments. In addition, while this element is also meaningful and important for beneficiaries to access needed care, the potential for harm if this element is incorrect is more limited because beneficiaries can still identify and contact providers even if this element is inaccurate in the provider directory. CMS proposes a weight of 3 percent rather than 3.5 percent proposed for whether the provider has accommodations for people with disabilities and has telehealth capabilities because of the three elements, CMS believes whether the provider is accepting new patients may be an element that could change more frequently than other elements and therefore may be a challenging provider directory element for MA organizations to collect and maintain. Recognizing the possible additional burden associated with collecting and maintaining this element for both MA organizations and providers, CMS proposes a slightly lower weight than the other two similar elements. Further, as a practical matter, CMS also wanted to ensure the proposed weights added up to 100 percent, and the most straightforward way to do that was to use weights of 3.5 percent for two elements and 3 percent for one element.
Given these weights, CMS's proposed provider directory accuracy scoring methodology (also described in Table II.B.5) is that first, the MA organization would need to sum the number of accurate records for each element across all providers in the specified MA plan's sample and then divide the number of accurate records for each element by the number of providers in the sample to determine the Accuracy Percentage per Element. Then, CMS proposes that the MA organization would need to multiply the Accuracy Percentage by Element by the Element Weight in Table II.B.5, to determine the Weighted Score per Element. In the example earlier, the accuracy percentage for the element “Network Participation Status” is
5 divided by 6, or 5/6 = 0.833333
and then the weighted score for that element would be
0.833333 multiplied by 0.4, or 0.833333 * 0.4 = .333333.
To determine the Final Composite Score, CMS proposes that the MA organization would need to sum the Weighted Score per Element. Then, CMS proposes that the MA organization would need to multiply the Final Composite Score by 100 to convert to a percentage, then round to the nearest whole number to determine the Rounded Composite Score. As a result, CMS proposes that, to determine the final Provider Directory Accuracy Score, the MA organization would need to convert the Rounded Composite Score to the appropriate letter grade. CMS proposes that 90 percent to 100 percent would be equivalent to a grade of “A,” 80 percent to 89 percent would be equivalent to a grade of “B,” 70 percent to 79 percent would be equivalent to a grade of “C,” 60 percent to 69 percent would be equivalent to a grade of “D,” 50 percent to 59 percent would be equivalent to a grade of “E,” and 49 percent and below would be equivalent to a grade of “F.” Table II.B.5 illustrates this calculation for MA plan Y's scores in the example.
In this example, for MA plan Y, the accuracy score would be a “C” because the Rounded Composite Score is 73 percent. Note that while Table II.B.5 only includes 6 decimal places, CMS proposes that MA organizations should not round to the nearest whole number until they get to the Final Composite Score calculation. That calculation should then be rounded to the nearest whole number and be represented in the form of a percentage as the Rounded Composite Score. CMS is proposing these requirements for the provider directory accuracy scoring methodology in new proposed § 422.123(d)(4).
In developing this proposal, CMS considered a scoring methodology approach that incorporated the proposed verification requirements, described at new proposed § 422.123(b), into the accuracy score. As seen in Table II.B.6, the results from the accuracy of the provider directory information may be different on the date that the sample is drawn as compared to the date of the 90-day verification.

CMS is considering a methodology in which the MA organization use both records of provider directory accuracy data when they develop the accuracy score. This may provide additional incentives for MA organizations to ensure their verification activities are thorough and also not unduly penalize MA organizations if through most of the year the provider directory information is correct but happened to be incorrect when the sample was drawn. A possible drawback for this approach is that MA organizations could choose the exact timing that they conduct their verification as long as it is consistent with CMS requirements at new proposed § 422.123(b), which may introduce opportunities for gaming, and the resulting accuracy scores may also be less of a direct “apples-to-apples” comparison between specified MA plans given these differences. CMS considered several different ways to incorporate the verification results into the accuracy score methodology. For example, CMS considered incorporating the most recent verification for the provider and also considered incorporating the results from all of the 90-day and 12-month verifications that the MA organization completed. Additionally, CMS considered whether the verification results should be weighed equally with the sample, whether the sample should be weighed more than the verification results, or whether the verification results should be weighed more than the sample. For example, CMS considered requiring that only verification results that used the same verification method as the sample could be included. CMS has not proposed incorporating the verification results into the accuracy score at this time because a more complex scoring methodology may increase the burden on MA organizations and providers, but CMS is still actively considering these approaches and interested in comments on whether CMS should consider an accuracy scoring methodology that incorporates the verification results.
CMS is also considering whether certain provider specialty types with high provider directory inaccuracy rates should be weighed in the accuracy score more so than other provider specialty types and whether certain provider specialty types, regardless of whether it is considered a provider specialty type with high provider directory inaccuracy rates, should be weighed in the accuracy score more so than other provider specialty types. A drawback of either of these approaches is that they would likely add additional complexity into the provider directory accuracy scoring methodology. CMS has not proposed either of these approaches but is still considering them and seeks comments on whether accuracy scores should be calculated differently for provider specialty types with high provider directory inaccuracy rates or if scores for certain provider specialty types should be calculated differently regardless of whether it is considered a provider specialty type with high provider directory inaccuracy rates.
CMS is further considering whether geographical considerations should be part of the scoring methodology. CMS is considering whether records in the sample with an address in a rural or CEAC county should have different weights associated with the provider directory data elements or whether some provider directory data elements should not be included in the scoring methodology for records in the sample with an address in a rural or CEAC county. CMS is also considering whether specified MA plans with 75 percent or more of their service area in rural and CEAC counties should have a different scoring methodology than other plans. CMS recognizes that a drawback of this approach may be that it represents less of a direct “apples-to-apples” comparison among specified MA plans and also that it may add additional complexity to the scoring methodology. CMS has not proposed different scoring methodologies based on geographic considerations but is still actively considering this approach. CMS seeks comments on whether different scoring methodologies would be appropriate and if so, how the scoring methodology should differ and what criteria should be used to identify which scoring methodology an MA organization should use when determining its accuracy score for a specified MA plan.
In alignment with the statute, as CMS developed this proposed accuracy scoring methodology, CMS considered the relative importance of certain provider directory information on enrollee ability to access care and the administrative burden of verification on MA organizations and providers. As described at new proposed § 422.123(d)(4), CMS proposes to have a weighted provider directory accuracy scoring methodology, in which provider directory information elements are weighed according to their relative importance for beneficiary access to care. By choosing to weigh specific pieces of information, CMS emphasizes the accuracy of certain elements of provider directory information over others.
In summary, CMS is proposing to codify the provider directory accuracy score requirements at new proposed § 422.123(d)(3) and the provider directory accuracy scoring methodology requirements at new proposed § 422.123(d)(4). CMS solicits comments on these proposed changes.

6. Provider Directory Accuracy Reporting to CMS (§ 422.123(d)(5))
Section 1857(e)(6)(A)(ii) of the Act requires that beginning with plan years beginning on or after January 1, 2028, each MA organization must submit to the Secretary a report containing the results of the analysis conducted under clause (i), including an accuracy score for such provider directory information (as determined using a plan verification method specified by the Secretary under subparagraph (B)(i)).
CMS proposes to codify this requirement at new proposed § 422.123(d)(5)(i), requiring that the MA organization must submit to CMS an annual provider directory accuracy report containing the results of the accuracy analysis for its specified MA plans. CMS proposes that the report must contain the provider directory accuracy score for each specified MA plan. In addition to this basic statutory requirement, CMS is considering requiring additional elements for the annual provider directory accuracy report so that CMS can monitor MA organizations' implementation of the new provider directory accuracy requirements and can issue updated technical guidance taking into account the experience and burden of MA organizations. Furthermore, CMS is also aware of section 6220(b)(3) of the CAA, which states that the Comptroller General of the United States (or the Government Accountability Office, GAO) shall conduct a study and corresponding report including an analysis of the use of cost sharing protections; the trend in provider directory information accuracy scores submitted to CMS, both overall and among providers specializing in mental health or substance use disorder treatment; provider response rates by plan verification methods; administrative costs to providers and MA organizations; and other items determined appropriate by the Comptroller General (or GAO). Therefore, as CMS considers what reporting data to collect from MA organizations, CMS is bearing in mind what information the GAO may be interested in for purposes of the GAO study and corresponding report. Specifically, in addition to the provider directory accuracy score, CMS is considering requiring that the annual provider directory accuracy report also contain elements, including but not limited to provider specialty type response rates by verification method or other sampling data by provider specialty type (including possibly requiring reporting based on the NUCC provider taxonomy code set), estimated administrative costs to the MA organization, estimated administrative costs to the MA organization's contracted providers, and data on the use of cost sharing protections. CMS requests comments on whether these additional reporting elements should be required. CMS will take into account commenters' feedback and may finalize the collection of these additional data elements in the final rule should such an outcome be supported.
In addition, regarding timing for MA organizations' annual submission of the provider directory accuracy report, at new proposed § 422.123(d)(5)(ii), CMS proposes that the report must be submitted not later than the first Monday in April of the year following the contract year being measured, in a form and manner specified by CMS. In proposing this date, CMS intends to give MA organizations at least three months to compile the required information and complete their provider directory accuracy report for the previous contract year. CMS solicits comments specifically on this proposed annual reporting deadline and whether it provides MA organizations with sufficient time. CMS also solicits comments on all aspects of these proposed changes regarding provider directory reporting at new proposed § 422.123(d)(5).
CMS is also considering whether to require that the annual provider directory accuracy analysis and resulting provider directory accuracy score be independently reviewed and certified by a qualified third party prior to submission to CMS. CMS believes that an independent review could promote consistency in the application of the sampling methodology, strengthen confidence in the reported accuracy scores, and provide an additional safeguard against variability in implementation across MA organizations. Similar to other CMS reporting requirements that require independent certification or attestation, the third party would be responsible for evaluating whether the MA organization's analysis was conducted in accordance with CMS requirements and that the reported results reasonably reflect the underlying provider directory information.
CMS seeks comments on whether an independent third-party certification requirement should be adopted, the qualifications such entities should possess, whether certification should be performed under generally accepted attestation or audit standards, and whether CMS should establish independence requirements comparable to those used for other CMS certification and reporting requirements.
7. Exception for Specified MA Plans With Low Enrollment
Section 1857(e)(6)(C) of the Act specifies that the Secretary may waive the requirements of paragraph (e)(6) “Provider Directory Accuracy Analysis and Reports,” in the case of a specified MA plan with low enrollment (as defined by the Secretary). CMS is considering whether to implement this statutory authority to exempt low-enrollment specified MA plans from the annual provider directory accuracy analysis and reporting requirements. Since the statute allows the Secretary to define what low enrollment means, CMS is contemplating various approaches for this definition if the low-enrollment exception were to be implemented. One approach might be to use a threshold for low enrollment that is already used in other areas of the MA program. For example, CMS could potentially apply similar criteria as the existing minimum enrollment threshold for MA plans, such as 500 enrollees for non-special needs plans (non-SNPs) and 100 enrollees for SNPs. Alternatively, CMS could apply similar criteria as is currently used for the Star Ratings threshold, which is 30 enrollees.
Considering these approaches, if CMS implements the low-enrollment exception so that specified MA plans with low enrollment do not have to complete the annual provider directory accuracy analysis and report, then some of the administrative burden on smaller plans may be eased, though all MA organizations offering specified MA plans, including low-enrollment plans, would still be subject to the verification and updating requirements in proposed § 422.123(b) and (c). There would also be a consistency in approach in terms of other areas of the MA program in which low enrollment thresholds are used. However, CMS believes that provider directory accuracy is important for all specified MA plans, regardless of the number of enrollees. It is important to balance the burden on specified MA plans and the need for enrollees to have accurate provider directories to ensure they can access care. CMS is inclined towards making the annual provider directory analysis and reporting requirements applicable to all specified MA plans, regardless of enrollment size, in which case CMS would not implement an exception to these new requirements for specified MA plans with low enrollment. CMS strongly supports the idea that accurate provider directories are important regardless of the plan size. In addition, the fact that

10. Enrollee Cost Sharing Protections When Provider Directories Are Inaccurate (§§ 422.124 and 422.202(f))
Section 1852(d) of the Act establishes provider directory cost sharing protections for enrollees who rely on incorrect provider directory information. Specifically, if a provider is in the provider directory of a specified MA plan on the date an enrollee makes an appointment, but at the time of the appointment when the item or service is furnished by the provider, it is determined that the provider is no longer in-network, then the MA organization must limit enrollee cost sharing to the lesser of the in-network or otherwise applicable cost sharing amount. These protections take effect beginning in contract year 2028 and apply to all subsequent contract years.
To implement the new cost sharing protections contained within section 1852(d) of the Act, CMS proposes to add new regulations at § 422.124, which would outline the scope of the protections, and the process enrollees must follow to access them. The protections would apply under proposed § 422.124(a) and (b) when an enrollee receives services from an out-of-network provider who was listed as in-network in the specified MA plan's directory on the date the appointment was made, and those services would otherwise be covered. In such cases, the MA organization would limit the enrollee's cost sharing to whichever amount is less, the in-network or otherwise applicable cost sharing amount. To initiate the process, the enrollee or their authorized representative would submit a request for the cost sharing protections to the MA organization, which would treat the request as an organization determination or reconsideration request per § 422.124(c). The MA organization would then determine eligibility by: (1) confirming the date the appointment was made per § 422.124(d); and (2) verifying whether the provider appeared in the specified MA plan's online directory on that date per § 422.124(e). If the MA organization cannot obtain the documentation necessary to make that determination from provider documentation, attestation, or a provider directory archive, the protections would be applied in the enrollee's favor per § 422.124(f). Once the MA organization confirmed that the protections apply, the lower cost sharing would be reflected in the enrollee's bill and maximum out-of-pocket (MOOP) calculation consistent with § 422.124(g).
Regarding the scope of the protections, CMS proposes to add § 422.124(a) and (b) providing that the cost sharing protections would apply if an enrollee in a specified MA plan is furnished an item or service from a provider that is not participating in the MA plan's network, but that provider is listed in the MA plan's provider directory as defined in § 422.2 on the date the appointment is made. The protections apply if the item or service would otherwise be covered under the MA plan if furnished by an in-network provider. In such cases, the MA organization offering the MA plan must ensure that the enrollee pays no more than the lesser of either: (1) the amount of cost sharing that would apply if the provider had been participating in the network of the plan; or (2) the amount of cost sharing that would otherwise apply.
CMS proposes adding § 422.124(c) to require the MA organization to apply the provider directory cost sharing protections without requiring an enrollee request when the MA organization knows or reasonably should know that the protections apply. In other words, if an enrollee or authorized representative references the use of incorrect provider directory information when requesting an organization determination or reconsideration for an out-of-network cost sharing bill but does not appear to be aware of the provider directory cost sharing protections, the MA organization must inform the enrollee of the available protections and evaluate whether the protections apply to the claim or claims. CMS also proposes to permit an enrollee or the enrollee's authorized representative to request application of the protections verbally or in writing to their MA organization. CMS proposes at § 422.124(c)(1) that such requests would be processed as organization determinations or reconsideration requests, as applicable, consistent with subpart M of this part. Consistent with current practice, when an enrollee or provider believes an item or service may not be covered, or could be covered only under specific conditions, a pre-service organization determination should be requested from the MA organization. If the item or service is denied, the standardized
(

denial notice must include information about the enrollee's appeal rights.
To confirm the date on which the appointment was made, CMS proposes to require at § 422.124(d) that MA organizations include a term in each provider contract for a specified MA plan obligating the provider to supply documentation of the earliest date on which the enrollee's appointment was scheduled, regardless of any subsequent rescheduling. For example, if an enrollee makes an appointment on April 12, 2028, and reschedules the appointment on May 15, 2028, the MA organization would look at the provider directory on April 12, 2028, to see if the provider was listed as in-network. At § 422.124(d), CMS proposes that acceptable documentation would include a paper or electronic record from the provider's scheduling system or confirmation sent to the enrollee or their authorized representative from the provider. If a record of the date the appointment was made is not reasonably obtainable, a signed attestation from the provider, accompanied by any available corroborating information such as a calendar entry, a referral record, electronic communications, or a phone log, if available would be sufficient to show the approximate date the appointment was made. CMS proposes that this contract term survives the expiration or termination of the contract between the MA organization and the provider for not less than 10 years, beginning on the date the contract expiration or termination becomes effective, thereby ensuring that providers who were previously participating in the specified MA plan's network remain obligated to supply documentation regarding the date on which the enrollee's appointment was made, even after departing from the network.
In order to verify the accuracy of the provider directory, at § 422.124(e) CMS proposes to add a requirement that the MA organization would determine whether the provider was listed as an in-network provider in the specified MA plan's online provider directory on the date the appointment was made by referencing archived electronic provider directory data maintained online by the MA organization. Archived provider directory data must be sufficient to identify whether any provider was listed in the specified MA plan's online directory at any point on a given date, retained for not less than ten years consistent with § 422.504(d), and made available to CMS upon request within 5 business days. If the archived provider data provided indicates that the provider in question was listed in the specified MA plan's online provider directory at any point during a given day, whether in the morning or later in the afternoon, the provider would be considered to have been listed in the online directory for that entire day for the purpose of determining whether the cost sharing protections apply. In addition, a notice that the provider information may be outdated, per the requirement at new proposed § 422.123(b)(3) in this proposed rule, would not affect an enrollee's eligibility for the cost sharing protections.

CMS is seeking comments on whether, under this proposed framework, an enrollee who uses the most current physical hardcopy directory available (that is, a physical hardcopy version with up-to-date addenda) to schedule an appointment—even if that physical hardcopy differs from the online directory on the date of the appointment—should qualify for the cost sharing protections described in proposed § 422.124. CMS also solicits comments on the duration of the proposed data retention requirement and whether MA organizations should be required to publicly post daily versions of their provider directories instead of being made available to CMS upon request within 5 business days as proposed. CMS believes that inclusion of such a requirement may be necessary to ensure accuracy and ease the review of archived provider directories. Finally, CMS seeks public comment on whether formatting requirements for archived provider directory information should be established, such as through a log of provider updates or removals or another auditable archive sufficient to identify the directory status of a provider on a given date.
CMS proposes at § 422.124(f) that if the MA organization is unable to obtain documentation demonstrating the date on which the appointment was scheduled or is unable to verify archived provider directory data within the applicable standard or expedited organization determination timeframes provided under

,
the
provider directory cost sharing protections must be applied in favor of the enrollee. This default application may be reversed only if the MA organization is able to clearly demonstrate that the cost sharing protections do not apply.
To apply the cost sharing protections, at § 422.124(g)(1) CMS proposes that if the MA organization collects cost sharing from an enrollee in excess of the amount permitted under the provider directory cost sharing protections, and the protections apply, the MA organization must refund the excess amount to the enrollee consistent with § 422.270(b). Additionally, when the protections apply and a refund is issued, at § 422.124(g)(2) CMS proposes that MA organizations treat that cost sharing as in-network cost sharing for purposes of any applicable MOOP limit, consistent with § 422.100(f)(4).
The purpose of the cost sharing protections created by the REAL Health Providers Act is to protect MA enrollees who rely on the provider directory of a specified MA plan to schedule an appointment with an in-network provider and later discover that the provider is out-of-network. The following example illustrates a scenario when the cost sharing protection would apply. An MA enrollee needs to see a cardiologist, checks their MA plan's online provider directory, and finds Dr. Smith listed as an in-network provider. On January 5, 2028, they schedule an appointment with the provider's office for March 6, 2028. The enrollee receives items and services from Dr. Smith on March 6, 2028, and subsequently receives an EOB reflecting cost sharing at the out-of-network rate, higher than the in-network rate the enrollee expected. The enrollee contacts their MA organization to see why the bill is so high and explains that the doctor was listed on their plan's provider directory at the time the appointment was made. The MA organization educates the enrollee about the provider directory cost sharing protections and offers to determine whether the enrollee qualifies. The enrollee agrees and the MA organization works with the enrollee's provider's office to confirm the appointment was made on January 5, 2028, and verifies via its archived provider directory data that Dr. Smith was listed as in-network on the same date. The MA organization then applies the protections, capping the enrollee's
(
printed page 66430)
cost sharing at the in-network rate, refunding any excess cost sharing the enrollee may have already paid, and counts the cost sharing toward the enrollee's in-network MOOP limit.
Notably, if Dr. Smith's office has no scheduling records available or an archive of the plan directory was unavailable, the MA organization would still be required to apply the protections in the enrollee's favor unless the MA organization was able to clearly demonstrate that the cost sharing protections do not apply, such as proof that the provider was never in the specified MA plan network.
These proposed requirements are designed to strengthen enrollee protections and reduce the risk of unexpected higher out-of-network costs resulting from inaccurate provider directory information. CMS believes these proposals align with the statutory goal of ensuring all enrollees have timely access to the new cost sharing protections and incentivizing MA organizations to maintain accurate and up-to-date directories on an ongoing basis. CMS proposes that the burden of proof for determining whether these protections apply rests with the MA organization, not the enrollee, and that MA organizations must make reasonable, good-faith efforts to gather all relevant documentation prior to rendering an eligibility determination from the provider consistent with the contract term requirements at § 422.124(d). The impact of the proposed policy changes is discussed in the Collection of Information Requirements and Regulatory Impact Analysis under sections III.A. through D. and IV.A. through K. of this proposed rule, respectively. CMS seeks comments on ways to improve enrollee access to the cost sharing protections, the operational feasibility of these requirements, including the processes MA organizations would use to verify whether an enrollee relied on directory information at the time an appointment was made, and whether additional documentation or verification standards are necessary to ensure the integrity and effective administration of these protections.
11. Provider Directory Disclosure Requirements (§§ 422.111(b)(3)(i), (b)(12), and (k) and 422.120(b)(1))
The REAL Health Providers Act also affects CMS's current MA disclosure requirements. First, section 1852(c)(1)(C) of the Act requires MA organizations, for plan year 2028 and subsequent plan years, in the case of a specified MA plan, to disclose to enrollees the information described in paragraph (c)(3)(B) (that is, provider directory information). 12. Conclusion
As discussed in section II.B. of this proposed rule, CMS believes that the accuracy scoring and verification framework required under the REAL Health Providers Act will serve to strengthen the integrity of the underlying provider data that both MPF and the NPD will likely come to depend upon, helping to ensure a consistent and reliable foundation for the larger health tech ecosystem. In addition, CMS recognizes that the data flow contemplated under this framework—in which MA organizations submit data to CMS, the NPD conceivably ingests that data and may enrich that data from additional sources, and MA organizations then publish NPD-informed directories—could raise questions about the appropriate scope of MA organization accountability for accuracy scores. CMS wishes to clarify that MA organization accountability under the REAL Health Providers Act as proposed herein attaches to the data the MA organization submits, verifies, and attests to, and to the rigor of the MA organization's own verification processes, rather than to data elements that may be added or modified by the NPD from sources outside the MA organization's control. MA organizations will retain an independent obligation under the REAL Health Providers Act to verify their provider directory information on the prescribed cycle as defined under § 422.123(b), if finalized. In addition, as CMS's various provider directory initiatives mature, CMS anticipates a process that will allow MA organizations to reconcile any discrepancies between NPD-returned data and their own verified records prior to publication if such discrepancies are identified. CMS will provide further guidance on the delineation of accountability between MA organization-originated and NPD-enriched data elements as the NPD infrastructure continues to be developed, implemented, and operationalized. This delineation of accountability approach could possibly include a safe-harbor component, as NPD infrastructure matures to be able to accept validated data programmatically from health care providers and organizations.
CMS seeks comments on whether this proposed approach effectively integrates the REAL Health Providers Act requirements with the existing § 422.111(m) framework and the developing NPD initiative in a way that is practical and achieves the statute's goals. CMS is particularly interested in
(
printed page 66432)
whether any conflicts or gaps exist among these three frameworks that this proposed implementation does not adequately address, and whether additional guidance is needed prior to the contract year 2028 effective date of the REAL Health Providers Act mandates. More broadly, CMS welcomes input on any aspects of provider directory accuracy, verification burden, data standardization, or beneficiary transparency that interested parties believe CMS has not fully considered, including potential specific mechanisms for an effective technology-based safe harbor that allows for the NPD to mediate accountability.
C. Modernizing and Ensuring PBM Accountability (Section 6224 of the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2026)
1. Background
Section 6224 of CAA (
Pub. L. 119-75
, enacted February 3, 2026) added sections 1860D-12(h) and 1857(f)(3) of the Act, which establish new and enhanced requirements under the Medicare Part D program that address, among other issues, compensation and data transparency for pharmacy benefit managers (PBMs). CMS is proposing to implement these requirements through this rulemaking.
PBMs provide services such as drug price negotiation, prescription claims adjudication, formulary development, and pharmacy network contracting for insurance plans, including Part D plan sponsors that manage the Part D prescription drug benefit. Federal agencies, academics, and others have raised concerns that PBM business practices and corporate structure have contributed to the high cost of prescription drugs in the United States.
[
1
]
In 2022, the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) issued special orders pursuant to section 6(b) of the Federal Trade Commission Act to the six largest PBMs to gather information about their business practices. After studying the information received, the FTC released two reports: a 2024 report titled “Pharmacy Benefit Managers: The Powerful Middlemen Inflating Drug Costs and Squeezing Main Street Pharmacies” and a 2025 report titled “Specialty Generic Drugs: A Growing Profit Center for Vertically Integrated Pharmacy Benefit Managers.”
10
These reports discussed several concerning aspects of the PBM industry, including a market featuring a high degree of concentration and vertical integration (with the three largest PBMs, which are integrated with both pharmacies and health plans, processing about 80 percent of prescription drug claims in the United States), higher payment rates for pharmacies that are affiliated with PBMs (especially specialty pharmacies) compared to unaffiliated pharmacies, opaque contract terms that disadvantage smaller and independent pharmacies, formulary placement decisions that favor higher-cost branded drugs over generics in exchange for higher rebates, and significant spread pricing in which PBMs retain a portion of the amount that a health plan pays the PBM for a drug rather than passing on the full amount to the pharmacy for specialty generics.
The FTC reports also expressed concern with PBM-affiliated rebate aggregators, also referred to as PBM group purchasing organizations (PBM GPOs), which do not function as traditional GPOs but rather as spin-off entities to which PBMs have shifted the function of rebate negotiation with pharmaceutical manufacturers. There are three PBM GPOs in this category, affiliated with the three largest PBMs in the United States. The first FTC report
11
referenced previously discussed the recent formation of these entities—which the FTC noted likely occurred in an attempt to take advantage of the antikickback safe harbor for GPOs. The FTC issued supplemental orders to collect information from those three PBM GPOs in 2023 but noted in its second report that the PBM GPOs had provided only a partial response to these orders.
[
12
]
While PBM GPOs themselves are relatively new, they are representative of a consistent pattern of utilization of complex affiliate structures and vertical and horizontal integration in the PBM industry and demonstrate PBMs' ability to adapt in the face of changing legislative and regulatory dynamics.
Academics have similarly raised concerns with PBMs' impact on the price of drugs. Revenue retained by PBMs at several points in the pharmaceutical supply chain—including pharmacy spread pricing, retention of a portion of the rebate negotiated with the pharmaceutical manufacturer, and increasing ownership of 340B contract pharmacies—is often not transparent to health plans and may contribute to high drug prices.
[
13
]
Because PBM compensation is often linked to the price of the drug, there are perverse incentives for PBMs to favor higher cost drugs;
[
14
]
one recent article estimated that if compensation for wholesalers, pharmacies, and PBMs were delinked from list prices, net drug spending could be reduced by approximately 15 percent.
[
15
]
As similarly noted by the FTC, the PBM market is also highly concentrated and vertically integrated; almost all major PBMs operate their own mail order or specialty pharmacies (and some retail pharmacies), and the largest health insurers in the country either own PBMs or share a common ownership structure with PBMs.
[
16
]
In addition to the reports that the FTC has issued following its issuance of 6(b) orders, the FTC has also filed lawsuits against the three largest PBMs and their affiliated PBM GPOs in September 2024, alleging that their rebating practices for insulin products were anticompetitive, unfair, and artificially inflated list prices. Specifically, the FTC claimed that PBMs gave insulin products with higher list prices favorable formulary placement due to the potential to extract and retain higher rebates and price-linked fees associated with such products, which caused pharmaceutical manufacturers to artificially inflate list prices and prevented patients from accessing insulin products with lower list prices and lower cost-sharing. The FTC reached settlements with two of the PBMs—Express Scripts, Inc. (ESI), announced in February 2026,
[
17
]
and Caremark, announced in July 2026.
[
18
]
The proposed ESI consent order include requirements to prohibit formulary placement on the basis of wholesale acquisition cost (WAC) (also known as list price), to pass through rebates at the point of sale so that they will be incorporated into patient cost-sharing, to provide a standard offering to plan sponsors allowing them to transition away from rebate guarantees and spread pricing, to delink fees paid from
(
printed page 66433)
pharmaceutical manufacturers to PBM GPOs from drug prices, and to maintain PBM GPO activities in the United States (two of the three major PBM GPOs had been established off shore), among other requirements.
[
19
]
CMS has already made some efforts to address PBM practices in Medicare. In the May 9, 2022,
Federal Register
(
87 FR 27704
), we addressed opaque performance-based penalties and price concessions from pharmacies that PBMs sometimes applied after the point of sale, preventing pharmacies from having access to predictable, transparent payment structures. CMS analysis showed that pharmacy price concessions grew more than 107,400 percent between 2010 and 2020. These practices rendered prescription drug prices less transparent and less representative of the actual amount the plan sponsor paid to the pharmacy for the drug dispensed. The new requirements, finalized in the final rule, “
Medicare Program; Contract Year 2023 Policy and Technical Changes to the Medicare Advantage and Medicare Prescription Drug Benefit Programs
,” restructured the financial relationship between plan sponsors, PBMs, and pharmacies by mandating transparency for all pharmacy price concessions at the point of sale.
The new requirements changed the definition of the negotiated price for a covered Part D drug at
42 CFR 423.100
to include all pharmacy price concessions at the point of sale, and not just those that could be reasonably determined at the point of sale. Beginning in 2024, a patient's cost share is based on the lowest possible reimbursement that a pharmacy could receive for that drug. CMS has noted a significant decrease in plan-reported pharmacy price concessions. Pharmacy direct and indirect remuneration (DIR) changed from a positive amount in CY 2023 (meaning Part D plan sponsors and PBMs recouped more from pharmacies in price concessions than they paid to pharmacies in bonus payments) to a negative amount in CY 2024 (meaning Part D plan sponsors and PBMs recouped less from pharmacies in price concessions than they paid to pharmacies in bonus payments).
[
20
]
Pharmacy payment for covered Part D drugs is now more transparent and predictable for pharmacies.
Section 6224 of the CAA builds on prior efforts to address PBM practices. The law introduces enhanced requirements for remuneration that PBMs may receive for services in connection with the utilization of covered Part D drugs. Generally, section 6224 of the CAA requires that such remuneration be restricted to bona fide service fees that may not be tied to the price of a drug or the rebates, discounts, or other price concessions negotiated. The law also introduces requirements for increased transparency, such as a new requirement for PBMs to report certain information such as drug prices and utilization, DIR, formulary placement of branded and generic drugs, information about payment rates at affiliated and unaffiliated pharmacies, and information on affiliates and brokers, to both Part D plan sponsors and the Secretary of Health and Human Services (HHS) annually. These requirements are to be effectuated through written agreements between Part D plan sponsors—inclusive of both sponsors offering standalone Part D prescription drug plans (PDPs) and sponsors offering Medicare Advantage prescription drug (MA-PD) plans that combine Medicare Advantage and Part D prescription drug benefits—and PBMs beginning with contract year 2028.
An overview of the new requirements included in section 6224 of the CAA related to Part D plan sponsor contract requirements and federal oversight and enforcement mechanisms is provided later in this section, as well as a summary of the proposed policies that are required to implement this law. a. Overview of Part D Plan Sponsor Contract Requirements for Written Agreements With PBMs
Section 6224 of the CAA amended section 1860D-12 of the Act by adding a new subsection (h)(1), which specifies that beginning with contract year 2028, any Part D plan sponsor with a contract under section 1860D-12 of the Act to offer a prescription drug plan must have a written agreement, containing certain requirements, with any PBM acting on its behalf. The requirements that must be in the written agreement with the PBM address remuneration derived by PBMs and their affiliates in connection with the utilization of Part D drugs, transparency regarding guarantees and cost performance evaluations, reporting of information by PBMs to Part D plan sponsors and the Secretary, and enforcement mechanisms provided to the Part D plan sponsor. We briefly describe each of the topics that the written agreement between the Part D plan sponsor and the PBM must address; each topic is addressed in greater detail in subsequent sections of this rule.
(1) Remuneration
Section 1860D-12(h)(1)(A)(i) of the Act, as added by the CAA, generally requires that PBMs and any affiliates of such PBMs not derive any remuneration with respect to any services provided on behalf of any entity or individual, in connection with the utilization of covered Part D drugs, other than bona fide service fees. Included in the definition of bona fide service fees is that such fees must be flat dollar amounts, reflective of fair market value (as specified by the Secretary through notice and comment rulemaking), for an itemized service, and that they may not be contingent on the amount of rebates, discounts, fees, or other direct or indirect remuneration; drug price; coverage or formulary placement; and any other amounts or methodologies prohibited by the Secretary.
There are certain exceptions to the requirement that PBMs and their affiliates only receive remuneration in the form of bona fide service fees. First, section 1860D-12(h)(1)(A)(ii) of the Act allows PBMs or their affiliates to receive incentive payments paid by a Part D plan sponsor if they meet certain requirements. Second, section 1860D-12(h)(1)(A)(iii) of the Act provides that rebates, discounts, or other price concessions received by a PBM or an affiliate of a PBM from manufacturers are not considered a violation of the bona fide service fee requirement if they are fully passed through to a Part D plan
(
printed page 66434)
sponsor and are compliant with all regulatory and sub-regulatory requirements related to DIR for manufacturer rebates, discounts, and other price concessions. Third, these remuneration requirements do not prohibit flat dispensing fees or reimbursement or payment for ingredient costs to PBMs or affiliates of PBMs that acquire or dispense prescription drugs, nor do they modify regulatory requirements or sub-regulatory program instruction or guidance related to pharmacy payment, reimbursement, or dispensing fees, in accordance with the rule of construction at section 1860D-12(h)(4) of the Act.
Section 1860D-12(h)(1)(A)(iv) of the Act requires that components of subsets of remuneration agreements between PBMs or their affiliates and other entities involved in the dispensing or utilization of covered Part D drugs be subject to review by the Secretary, in consultation with the Office of the Inspector General of the Department of Health and Human Services, as determined appropriate by the Secretary, for consistency with fair market value. It also requires that the PBM disgorge any remuneration received by the PBM or its affiliate that is in violation of the requirements added by the CAA to the Part D plan sponsor.
(2) Transparency
The CAA also introduces new requirements regarding transparency that must be reflected in the written agreements between Part D plan sponsors and PBMs. Part D plan sponsors must include in their written agreements with PBMs a requirement that PBMs “define, interpret, and apply” terms in a fully transparent and consistent manner for purposes of evaluating PBM performance against pricing guarantees or similar cost performance measurements. Pricing guarantees are agreements under which PBMs guarantee Part D plan sponsors a certain price for drugs—often represented as a percent off list price for specific categories of drugs, such as brand, generic, or specialty drugs—and either retain or reimburse the Part D plan sponsor for the difference between that price and the actual price negotiated with a pharmacy. As discussed later in this rule, PBMs' interpretation of certain terms such as `generic' or `specialty' can significantly impact their ability to retain revenue through price guarantees.
Section 1860D-12(h)(1)(C) of the Act, as added by the CAA, requires that PBMs annually submit a report to the Part D plan sponsor and the Secretary of HHS beginning no later than July 1 of 2028. This report is to include information on dispensed drugs covered by the plan, information about affiliate pharmacies, information on cost-sharing and formulary placement for reference listed drugs and reference products compared to their generic or biosimilar biological products, plan spending, PBM remuneration, benefit design parameters, information on brokers and consultants, and a list of affiliates.
Finally, PBMs must also provide a written explanation of certain information to Part D plan sponsors within 30 days of finalization of a contract or agreement between the PBM or an affiliate of the PBM and a manufacturer that makes rebates, discounts, payments, or other financial incentives related to one or more covered Part D drugs or other prescription drugs, as applicable, directly or indirectly contingent upon coverage, formulary placement, or utilization management conditions on any other covered Part D drugs or other prescription drugs.
(3) Enforcement by the Part D Plan Sponsor
In addition to the previous requirements, the CAA also requires that the written agreement between the Part D plan sponsor and PBM include certain mechanisms that the Part D plan sponsor may use to enforce the new requirements. Section 1860D-12(h)(1)(D) of the Act, as added by the CAA, requires that not less than once a year, at the request of the Part D plan sponsor, the PBM allow for an audit of the PBM to ensure compliance with all terms and conditions of the written agreement. Additionally, sections 1860D-12(h)(2)(A)(ii) and (iii) of the Act provide that the written agreement between the Part D plan sponsor and the PBM must require that the PBM or any affiliate of such PBM reimburse the Part D plan sponsor for any civil money penalty imposed on the Part D plan sponsor as a result of the failure of the PBM or affiliate to meet the requirements of section 1860D-12(h)(1) of the Act that are applicable to the PBM or affiliate, and must require in a written agreement with the PBM that the PBM or its affiliate be subject to punitive remedies for breach of contract for failure to comply with the requirements under section 1860D-12(h)(1) of the Act.
b. Overview of Federal Enforcement and Compliance Mechanisms
Sections 1860D-12(h)(2) and (3) of the Act, as added by the CAA, introduce certain enforcement and compliance mechanisms related to section 1860D-12(h) of the Act. Section 1860D-12(h)(2)(A)(i) of the Act requires that each Part D plan sponsor shall disgorge to the Secretary any amounts disgorged to the Part D plan sponsor by a PBM due to violations of the remuneration requirements under section 1860D-12(h)(1)(A) of the Act. Additionally, section 1860D-12(h)(2)(B) of the Act specifies that the Secretary shall make available and maintain a mechanism for manufacturers, Part D plan sponsors, pharmacies, and other entities that have contractual relationships with PBMs or their affiliates to report, on a confidential basis, alleged violations of section 1860D-12(h)(1)(A) or (C) of the Act to the Secretary. Section 1860D-12(h)(2)(C) of the Act requires that a Part D plan sponsor shall not retaliate against an individual or entity for such reporting of an alleged violation, nor coerce, intimidate, threaten, or interfere with the ability of an individual or entity to report any such alleged violations. In addition, section 1860D-12(h)(3) of the Act requires that each Part D plan sponsor furnish to the Secretary an annual certification of compliance with section 1860D-12(h) of the Act, as well as information the Secretary determines necessary to carry out section 1860D-12(h) of the Act; the Secretary may implement this requirement by program instruction.
