3. Pharmacy Benefit Manager (PBM)
Section 1860D-12(h)(7)(C) of the Act defines a PBM as “any person or entity that, either directly or through an intermediary, acts as a price negotiator or group purchaser on behalf of a PDP sponsor or prescription drug plan, or manages the prescription drug benefits provided by such sponsor or plan, including the processing and payment of claims for prescription drugs, the performance of drug utilization review, the processing of drug prior authorization requests, the adjudication of appeals or grievances related to the prescription drug benefit, contracting with network pharmacies, controlling the cost of covered Part D drugs, or the provision of related services. Such term includes any person or entity that carries out one or more of the activities described in the preceding sentence, irrespective of whether such person or entity calls itself a 'pharmacy benefit manager.' ”
This definition is functional in nature. An entity may qualify as a PBM based on the activities it performs, regardless of how it describes itself. The Act identifies the functions of a PBM as including the processing and payment of prescription drug claims, drug utilization review, processing of prior authorization requests, adjudication of appeals or grievances related to the prescription drug benefit, contracting with network pharmacies, controlling the cost of covered Part D drugs, and the provision of related services, but does not limit the scope of the PBM definition to the persons and entities that engage in those activities. In addition, a person or entity may qualify as a PBM even if it carries out these functions indirectly through an intermediary.
Determining whether a particular entity is: (1) a PBM; (2) an affiliate as defined in section 1860D-12(h)(7)(A) of the Act and discussed in section II.C.4. of this proposed rule; or (3) neither is necessary to establish the entity's obligations under section 1860D-12(h) of the Act.
Specifically, a PBM—but not an affiliate—must have a written agreement with the Part D plan sponsor under which the PBM and its affiliates agree to satisfy certain requirements as specified in section 1860D-12(h) of the Act. The PBM—but not its affiliates—also bears responsibility, under its statutorily required contractual arrangement with the Part D plan sponsor, for submitting an annual report to the Part D plan sponsor and the Secretary under section 1860D-12(h)(1)(C)(i) of the Act, as discussed in section II.C.8. of this proposed rule Although an affiliate may hold information that must be reported, the affiliate is not responsible for submitting that information directly to the Part D plan sponsor or the Secretary.
The PBM also has audit-related obligations under its contractual arrangement with the Part D plan sponsor, as required by section 1860D-12(h)(1)(D) of the Act. The PBM must allow an annual audit at the request of the Part D plan sponsor and must provide relevant records, data, contracts, and other information requested by the Part D plan sponsor. Although an affiliate's records may be produced during an audit, the PBM is responsible for providing information held by its affiliates to the Part D plan sponsor.
Under the contractual requirements mandated by section 1860D-12(h)(1)(B)(i) through (iii) of the Act, a PBM is further responsible for defining, interpreting, and applying pricing guarantee and cost-performance terms transparently and consistently; identifying exclusions; and providing WAC-based equivalents when required. These responsibilities are not imposed directly on affiliates.
Finally, pursuant to the contractual requirements mandated by section 1860D-12(h)(1)(A)(vi)(I) of the Act, a PBM must enter into written agreements with its affiliates requiring them to identify and disgorge impermissible remuneration and must attest that it has entered into those agreements.
(i) Contract Requirement
As a threshold matter, an entity qualifies as a PBM under section 1860D-12(h)(7)(C) of the Act if it: (1) directly, or through an intermediary, performs at least one PBM function; and (2) performs that function on behalf of a Part D plan sponsor or prescription drug plan. Separately, section 1860D-12(h)(7)(A) of the Act defines an “affiliate”—with respect to any PBM or Part D plan sponsor—to include any entity that, directly or indirectly, acts as a contractor, principal, or agent to such PBM or Part D plan sponsor insofar as it performs any of the functions described in 1860D-12(h)(7)(C) of the Act.
These two definitions create a potential overlap. Absent clarification, a contractor or agent of a PBM that performs one or more PBM functions could simultaneously be considered to: (1) qualify as a PBM in its own right under subparagraph (C) because it performs PBM functions and the definition captures entities performing even a single such function regardless of
(
printed page 66436)
self-identification; and (2) qualify as an affiliate of the contracting PBM under subparagraph (A)(ii) because it is acting as a contractor performing those same functions. For example, based solely on the requirements related to the performance of PBM functions, a third-party claims processor retained by a PBM to process Part D prescription drug claims for a Part D plan sponsor could qualify as a PBM under subparagraph (C) because it performs a PBM function on behalf of a Part D plan sponsor, while also qualifying as an affiliate under subparagraph (A)(ii) because it performs that function as the PBM's contractor.
Section 1860D-12(h)(1) of the Act also establishes a general rule that any contract entered into with a Part D plan sponsor under this part with respect to a prescription drug plan offered by such sponsor must provide that any PBM acting on behalf of such sponsor has a written agreement with the Part D plan sponsor under which the PBM agrees to certain requirements as specified in section 1860D-12(h) of the Act.
Based on this statutory structure, we propose to clarify that an entity qualifies as a PBM only if it holds a written agreement with a Part D plan sponsor, either directly or through a parent organization of such Part D plan sponsor. We believe this clarification resolves the definitional overlap between PBMs and their affiliates and is consistent with the Act's requirement of a contractual relationship between a PBM and a Part D plan sponsor. We intend that this proposed requirement for a written agreement between a PBM and the Part D plan sponsor can be met by an agreement between the PBM and the parent organization of the Part D plan sponsor to account for instances in which the parent organization possesses delegated contracting authority for subsidiary Part D plan sponsors. We note that our proposal to allow for a Part D plan sponsor to meet its obligation to have a written agreement under section 1860D-12(h)(1) of the Act through its parent organization is consistent with the implementation of section 1860D-12(b)(1) of the Act, under which a Part D plan sponsor may also meet its contract requirements through a written agreement by its parent organization when the parent organization has a legally enforceable delegation of Part D plan sponsor's contracting authority (see, for example,
42 CFR 423.503(a)(3)
and
423.504(b)(8)
).
Accordingly, we propose to establish at
42 CFR 423.2804(a)
a general rule for PBM status. An entity would qualify as a PBM, regardless of how it describes itself, if: (1) the entity has a written contract with the Part D plan sponsor, either directly or through a parent organization of such Part D plan sponsor; and (2) the entity, directly or through an intermediary, performs at least one PBM function on behalf of a Part D plan sponsor or prescription drug plan with which it has such written contract.
We solicit comment on this proposal.
(ii) Related Services and PBM Functions
As described earlier in this section, a PBM is any person or entity that acts as a price negotiator or group purchaser on behalf of a Part D plan sponsor or prescription drug plan, or that manages the prescription drug benefits provided by such a sponsor or plan. Section 1860D-12(h)(7)(C) of the Act identifies the functions of a PBM as including the processing and payment of prescription drug claims, drug utilization review, processing of prior authorization requests, adjudication of appeals or grievances related to the prescription drug benefit, contracting with network pharmacies, controlling the cost of covered Part D drugs, and the provision of related services. Because the Act introduces this list with the word “including” and separately references “the provision of related services,” these enumerated functions are illustrative rather than exhaustive.
To give effect to the “related services” language, CMS considered identifying specific additional functions to treat as PBM functions beyond the six functions enumerated in the statute. That approach would provide certainty, but we believe it could improperly narrow the definition to a fixed list, which would be inconsistent with the statute's broad language. A fixed list could suggest that unlisted functions are excluded, even when they are closely related to the enumerated ones. The Act's use of “including” and its separate reference to “related services” signal that the enumerated functions are illustrative examples. Accordingly, codifying a fixed list of additional functions, however carefully constructed, could be contrary to the statute's open-ended language.
At the same time, we believe “related services” should be defined with sufficient precision to give PBMs and their affiliates compliance parameters given that performing a PBM function on behalf of a Part D plan sponsor or prescription drug plan carries significant regulatory obligations. We believe the best approach is to treat “related services” as services that have a
direct nexus
to the functions enumerated in the statute. This approach would treat the statutory list as illustrative while still requiring a meaningful connection to those functions.
To provide compliance parameters, we have sought to draw on concepts that are commonly understood to anchor the proposed direct-nexus standard.
42 CFR part 423
does not currently define “price negotiator,” “group purchaser,” “drug benefit management,” “prescription drug benefit management,” or “pharmacy benefit management services” as standalone terms, so no existing overarching definitions are available in the context of the Part D program. However, we propose to use three commonly understood concepts to give the directnexus standard an appropriate level of specificity.
First, an “integral part” concept could provide an administrable test for determining when a service is sufficiently connected to an enumerated PBM function to be classified as having a direct nexus to that function—specifically, by asking whether the service is an essential component (that is, “integral part”) of that function's performance. For example, in the context of PBM functions, an entity that performs only one step in adjudicating appeals or grievances may be considered to have not performed “the adjudication of appeals or grievances” as defined in section 1860D-12(h)(7)(C) of the Act. However, that entity may have performed a function that is an “integral part” of appeals or grievance adjudication. However, relying exclusively on this concept would likely be too narrow.
Second a “necessity” standard offers an additional element for operationalizing the direct-nexus approach—capturing not only functions that are components of an enumerated activity but also functions without which an enumerated activity could not reasonably be performed. In the context of PBM functions, this could include, for example, maintaining and operating the data-exchange infrastructure used to transmit claims data for payment processing, prior authorization review, or other purposes. Although maintenance of data-exchange infrastructure is not itself an integral component of the functions enumerated in statute, this maintenance activity could nonetheless be considered necessary to carry out such functions to the extent that payment processing and prior authorization review could not be reliably performed without it.
Third, we believe there is value in including a “support” concept in the definition of direct nexus. Many PBM activities are highly complex and PBMs
(
printed page 66437)
sometimes rely on other organizations to perform key elements of those activities to support them. This “support” concept provides a third basis for defining “related services” under the direct-nexus standard—one that extends beyond functions that are a component of, or necessary to, the performance of an enumerated activity to encompass functions that, while not strictly necessary, contribute to the actual operation of those activities. For example, data analysis services—such as producing dashboards, utilization reports, and trend analyses related to cost control, formulary management, or drug utilization review—could be viewed as distinct from the underlying PBM function of controlling the cost of covered Part D drugs in the sense that they are not integral to, or necessary for, carrying out that function. But data analysis may nonetheless support the execution of this function.
Together, we believe these three concepts give the direct-nexus standard the precision and administrability necessary for effective compliance. Accordingly, we propose to define “related service” at
42 CFR 423.2802
as any activity, service, or function that is performed on behalf of a Part D plan sponsor or prescription drug plan and has a direct nexus to the activities that are enumerated in the definition of PBM function and propose that the requisite direct nexus to the enumerated activities will exist if the activity is: (1) integral to such enumerated activity; (2) necessary to carry out such enumerated activity; or (3) performed in support of such enumerated activity. We also propose to define “PBM function” at § 423.2802 to include any activity described in section 1860D-12(h)(7)(C) of the Act inclusive of any related service as we propose to define that term at § 423.2802.
CMS considered including a limiting clause to exclude activities incidentally related to PBM functions but concluded that such a clause would raise concerns similar to those posed by a fixed enumerated list. Moreover, we believe the “related service” definition as proposed would not include activities incidentally related to PBM functions such that a limiting clause would be necessary. Notably, the term “related services” at section 1860D-12(h)(7)(C) of the Act is listed with the enumerated PBM services rather than activities that a PBM or Part D plan sponsor would need to conduct under the ordinary course of business as a company (such as accounting or paying taxes). For example, our proposed definition of “related service” would not include the provision of professional services that, while necessary to the operations of a PBM, Part D plan sponsor, or prescription drug plan, do not have a direct nexus to the activities that are enumerated in the definition of PBM function. Accounting, auditing, legal, information technology and other professional services that are commonly performed on behalf of any company in the health care industry, but are not related to the enumerated PBM functions, do not become a “related service” that is a PBM function under the proposed definition simply because that service is performed for a PBM, Part D plan sponsor or prescription drug plan. Likewise, we believe the proposed definition of “related service” would not include services by commercial entities that offer information, datasets, technology platforms, or similar products on standardized or generally applicable commercial terms. For example, while information regarding WAC may be necessary to controlling the cost of covered Part D drugs, the sale of data from a drug pricing compendium does not become a “related service” under the proposed definition simply because the purchaser of that data of general applicability is a PBM, Part D plan sponsor or prescription drug plan. If the drug pricing compendium did not perform that data provision service on behalf of a Part D plan sponsor, but rather provided widely commercially available data of general applicability to a variety of customers, the provision of such data would not be considered a “related service” under the proposed definition.
Finally, we note that proposed definition of “related service” describes those services performed on behalf of a Part D plan sponsor or prescription drug plan. Accordingly, provision of information to a PBM, Part D plan sponsor or prescription drug plan by or on behalf of a provider or pharmacy in connection with claims processing, drug utilization review, prior authorization requests or other PBM functions is not itself a PBM function under the proposed definition of “related service.” For instance, a pharmacy services administrative organization (PSAO) performing claims submission on behalf of its client pharmacies would not be performing a PBM function under the proposed definition of related service because the PSAO would be providing the service on behalf of client pharmacies, not the Part D plan sponsor or prescription drug plan.
We solicit comment on this proposal. Specifically, we solicit comment on whether any categories of activities should be explicitly excluded from the definition of “PBM function” or “related service.”
The definitions of “PBM function” and “related service” at proposed § 423.2802 are intended to ensure that the range of activities that could lead an entity or individual to become a PBM or affiliate for purposes of this rule is clear and comprehensive. We believe the direct-nexus standard in our proposed definition of related service is appropriate to avoid parties understating or circumventing reporting obligations related to
bona fide
PBM functions. As an alternative to the direct-nexus standard in our proposed definition of “related service,” we considered adopting a substantial-similarity standard under which the definition of “related service” would serve as a less prescriptive catch-all to include functions that are different in name but similar in character to the PBM functions provided by a Part D plan sponsor or prescription drug plan that are expressly listed in section 1860D-12(h)(7)(C) of the Act. Specifically, an alternative definition of “related service” could be “an activity, service or function that is substantially similar to a function listed in section 1860D-12(h)(7)(C) of the Act and any successor function to any listed function.” We believe this alternative definition could provide clarity by emphasizing that the scope of a “related service” is coextensive with the activities on behalf of a Part D plan sponsor or prescription drug plan that are acting as a price negotiator or group purchaser on behalf of such sponsor or plan or involve the management of the prescription drug benefits provided by such sponsor or plan. However, we have concern such definition may be underinclusive or insufficiently precise to be administrable. We solicit comment on this alternative definition and whether the direct-nexus standard in our proposal or this substantially similar alternative would define “related service” in a manner that better enables consistent and complete identification of PBM functions for purposes of the reporting obligations under this proposed rule.
(iii) Minimum Threshold for Performance of a PBM Function
As discussed earlier in this section, the PBM definition is functional in nature. An entity may qualify as a PBM based on the activities it performs, regardless of how it describes itself. To determine when PBM status applies based on the performance of a particular PBM function, we must establish whether a minimum level of performance is required—in other
(
printed page 66438)
words, whether a single instance of performing a PBM function renders an entity a PBM.
We considered a de minimis or safe harbor approach under which CMS would establish numeric thresholds—such as minimum claims volume or dollar value of transactions—below which an entity's performance of a listed function would not trigger PBM status. However, calibrating appropriate thresholds across the full range of PBM functions would be analytically complex and potentially subject to gaming. Moreover, the statute does not specify any minimum frequency, volume, or materiality threshold for PBM function performance. An explicit threshold-based de minimis standard would therefore be in tension with the statutory language, which does not contemplate such a carve out.
We also considered a contractual standard, under which PBM status would be determined based on the terms of a written agreement to perform services on behalf of a Part D plan sponsor or prescription drug plan. Under this approach, an entity that has contracted to perform certain functions would be presumed to perform those functions during the contract term. However, actual performance cannot always be derived from contractual terms. A contractual standard therefore risks being simultaneously overinclusive—capturing entities that contracted to perform certain functions but do not actually do so—and underinclusive—failing to capture entities that do perform certain functions not expressly required under a contract.
Instead, we propose to adopt an “any performance standard,” under which PBM status attaches the moment an entity performs even a single instance of any listed PBM function, regardless of frequency, volume, or materiality. We believe this approach is most consistent with the statutory structure, which does not explicitly contemplate limitations on the minimum level of performance required to confer PBM status.
Accordingly, at
42 CFR 423.2804(b)
, we propose to clarify that an entity satisfies the performance element of the PBM definition upon performing one or more PBM functions during a calendar year, regardless of the frequency, volume, regularity, or materiality of such performance.
We recognize that application of an “any performance standard” could, in some circumstances, be overinclusive. However, we believe that the additional statutory constraints that a PBM function be an act as a price negotiator or group purchaser on behalf of a Part D plan sponsor or to manage the benefits provided by such sponsor or plan substantially limit the potential for over-inclusiveness. Certain functions that are included in the statutory definition of PBM are routinely performed by entities for purposes unrelated to pharmacy benefit management. For example, pharmacies process prescription drug claims as part of their own operational workflows (for example, when submitting claims to Part D plan sponsors seeking payment), which are independent of any functions they may also carry out on behalf of the Part D plan sponsor. Likewise, pharmacies and pharmacists regularly provide certain clinical services to their patients, such as drug utilization review and medication adherence monitoring, in accordance with applicable state pharmacy practice or professional conduct requirements, respectively, without regard to whether the drug is dispensed to an enrollee of a Part D plan for which the Part D plan sponsor has engaged any person or entity to act as a price negotiator or group purchaser on its behalf or to manage its prescription drug benefit. Accordingly, we believe that the statutory text establishing that an entity performs a PBM function when it acts as a price negotiator or group purchaser
on behalf of
a Part D plan sponsor or prescription drug plan or to manage the benefits
of such sponsor or plan
should substantially limit the potential for over-inclusiveness in understanding which pharmacy and wholesaler activities are PBM functions. Nevertheless, we request comment on whether circumstances exist in which this standard could still be overinclusive, and whether CMS should consider additional limitations.
We request comment on this proposal.
(iv) Intermediaries
The statute includes within the definition of PBM entities that act “through an intermediary” but does not define the term “intermediary,” raising two questions: what constitutes an intermediary, and when does an entity that performs PBM functions through an intermediary qualify as a PBM?
Part D regulations already employ a conceptually similar framework through the “first tier, downstream, and related entity” categories. Under
42 CFR 423.501
:
A first tier entity is “any party that enters into a written arrangement, acceptable to CMS, with a Part D plan sponsor or applicant to provide administrative services or health care services for a Medicare eligible individual under Part D.”
A downstream entity is a “party that enters into a written arrangement, acceptable to CMS, below the level of the arrangement between a Part D plan sponsor (or applicant) and a first-tier entity,” continuing down to the level of the ultimate provider of health and administrative services.
A related entity is an entity that is “related to the PDP sponsor by common ownership or control and (1) performs some of the Part D plan sponsor's management functions under contract or delegation; (2) furnishes services to Medicare enrollees under an oral or written agreement; or (3) leases real property or sells materials to the Part D plan sponsor at a cost of more than $2,500 during a contract period.”
Under
42 CFR 423.505(i)
, Part D plan sponsors may delegate functions to these entities. Contracts with such entities must preserve audit and record-access rights for HHS, the Comptroller General, and their designees.
[
22
]
These entity types are further incorporated into compliance program, prescription drug event (PDE) submission, claims-data certification, and Medicare Transaction Facilitator Data Module requirements.
[
23
]
There are meaningful similarities between first tier, downstream, and related entities and intermediaries. Both concepts are function-based: first tier, downstream, and related entities are identified, in part, by their performance of administrative or health care services under Part D, while the PBM and intermediary concepts under section 1860D-12(h) of the Act similarly depend on an entity's performance of PBM functions. Both are chain-of-delegation concepts that reach below a direct contractor to downstream entities, and both preserve accountability for compliance obligations notwithstanding outsourcing. The first tier, downstream, and related entity framework preserves sponsor responsibility despite delegation to another entity, which is similar to how the Act imposes PBM status, and associated accountability for compliance with certain requirements as specified in section 1860D-12(h) of the Act, on an entity regardless of whether it uses intermediaries to perform PBM functions.
However, the two concepts are not exact analogs. First tier, downstream, and related entity status is triggered by a written arrangement to provide administrative or health care services under Part D and applies broadly to Part D contractors regardless of whether they
(
printed page 66439)
perform PBM functions. By contrast, intermediary status is not expressly dependent on a written agreement, applies more narrowly within the context of PBM functions, and does not extend to entities performing exclusively non-PBM functions. Therefore, we believe it is appropriate to establish a definition of “intermediary” for purposes of section 1860D-12(h) of the Act that accounts for differences from the standard used to determine first tier, downstream and related entity status.
Given the complexity of modern pharmacy benefit arrangements, which commonly involve multi-layered contractual chains, we believe the definition of “intermediary” and the statutory phrase “through an intermediary” should be interpreted broadly to give appropriate effect to the statute.
[
24
]
Accordingly, at proposed § 423.2802, we propose to define “intermediary” to mean any person or entity in a chain of contractual or delegated relationships, of any length, through which one or more PBM functions are performed on behalf of a Part D plan sponsor or prescription drug plan during a calendar year. At proposed § 423.2804(c), we would specify that any entity that causes, arranges, procures, or relies on an intermediary to perform a PBM function must be deemed to have performed that function for all purposes of section 1860D-12(h) of the Act.
Under this approach, an entity would qualify as a PBM acting through an intermediary if—
The entity holds a written contract with the Part D plan sponsor, either directly or through a parent organization of such Part D plan sponsor, to provide or arrange PBM functions;
The entity causes, arranges, procures, or relies on another entity to perform one or more listed PBM functions on behalf of the Part D plan sponsor or prescription drug plan as described in such written contract; and
That intermediary performs such function on behalf of such Part D plan sponsor or prescription drug plan.
We considered limiting intermediary status to entities within a set number of links in a contractual chain. However, that approach would allow entities to shield PBM activities from section 1860D-12(h) of the Act by positioning the function-performing entity far enough from the Part D plan sponsor to fall outside the intermediary definition.
We also considered a control-based approach, under which a PBM acting through an intermediary would be required to direct or control how the function-performing entity performs the PBM function. For example, a PBM could be said to direct or control a function-performing entity when the PBM contracts with a rebate aggregator to negotiate manufacturer rebates on behalf of a Part D plan sponsor, and the PBM sets the negotiation parameters, approves or rejects rebate offers, specifies which manufacturers or drugs the aggregator must prioritize, or requires the aggregator to follow PBM-established formulary or contracting terms. However, that approach would be highly fact-specific and could create significant uncertainty about when PBM status attaches to an entity acting through an intermediary.
We request comment on this proposal and on potential alternative approaches.
(v) Performance of PBM Functions by Part D Plan Sponsors
Section 1860D-12(h)(7)(C) of the Act defines a PBM in part as “any person or entity that . . . acts as a price negotiator or group purchaser on behalf of a prescription drug plan sponsor or prescription drug plan, or manages the prescription drug benefits provided by such sponsor or plan.” Additionally, section 1860D-12(h)(1)(A)(iii) of the Act addresses the application of requirements for agreements with PBMs “in cases where a PDP sponsor is acting as a pharmacy benefit manager on behalf of a prescription drug plan offered by such PDP sponsor.”
Taken together, these provisions could be read to suggest that the requirements of section 1860D-12(h) of the Act apply to all Part D plan sponsors that engage in any activity which we propose to include within the definition of PBM functions under proposed § 423.2802. However, most of the statutory requirements in section 1860D-12(h) of the Act contemplate a two-party relationship between a Part D plan sponsor and a PBM. This raises the question of whether—and under what circumstances—a Part D plan sponsor that performs the activities described in the proposed definition of PBM functions is subject to the requirements of section 1860D-12(h) of the Act.
Under existing Part D statutory and regulatory requirements, a Part D plan sponsor's contract with CMS must require the sponsor to, among other things: provide qualified prescription drug coverage; comply with quality assurance and cost and utilization management requirements; support e-prescribing; comply with coverage determination, grievance, appeal, and formulary exception requirements; submit claims and other information to CMS; provide information CMS determines necessary to carry out the applicable payment provisions; and operate systems that adjudicate drug claims at the point of sale.
[
25
]
The activities described in these requirements for Part D plan sponsors overlap significantly with the activities that are characterized as PBM functions under proposed § 423.2802.
Nevertheless, the overall structure of section 1860D-12(h) of the Act largely assumes that a Part D plan sponsor and a PBM are separate entities and seeks to hold the PBM accountable to the Part D plan sponsor for the PBM's activities on behalf of the sponsor. For example, section 1860D-12(h)(1)(C)(i) of the Act requires the PBM to submit an annual report to both the Part D plan sponsor and the Secretary. Section 1860D-12(h)(1)(D) of the Act provides a Part D plan sponsor with audit rights over the PBM to ensure the PBM's compliance with the written agreement and the accuracy of information reported under section 1860D-12(h)(1)(C) of the Act. Likewise, section 1860D-12(h)(2)(A)(ii) of the Act requires that, in order to enforce the requirements related to PBMs, each Part D plan sponsor is required to have a written agreement with any PBM—or an affiliate of such PBM—acting on behalf of such sponsor that requires the PBM or affiliate to reimburse the sponsor for any civil money penalty imposed on the sponsor as a result of the PBM's or affiliate's failure to meet applicable requirements. This consistent structural distinction between a PBM and a Part D plan sponsor suggests that a Part D plan sponsor is not a PBM for purposes of section 1860D-12(h) of the Act solely by virtue of its functions as a Part D plan sponsor—even though Part D plan sponsors engage in activities that overlap with the activities in the PBM definition. At the same time, the statute does not categorically exclude Part D plan sponsors from ever qualifying for PBM status. Rather, the overall structure of section 1860D-12(h) of the Act affirms that a Part D plan sponsor is a PBM when it is performing PBM functions on behalf of a distinct entity (that is, when such activities performed
(
printed page 66440)
by the Part D plan sponsor are not performed under the sponsor's own contract for the operation of the Part D plan sponsor's own prescription drug plan).
Therefore, we propose to clarify a limitation on how the performance standard to have PBM status as described in proposed § 423.2804(a) applies to the activities of a Part D plan sponsor. Specifically, we propose to establish in proposed § 423.2804(d) that a Part D plan sponsor would not meet the performance standard in paragraph (a)(2) based solely on the sponsor performing activities under such sponsor's contract for the operation of its own prescription drug plan.
We considered supplementing this proposal with regulatory text to identify criteria under which a Part D plan sponsor would meet the performance standard for PBM status as described in proposed § 423.2804. For example, we considered whether to affirm in regulatory text that a Part D sponsor would meet the standard for PBM status in proposed § 423.2804 if the sponsor performs one or more functions described at proposed paragraph § 423.2802 with respect to a prescription drug plan for which it does not have a contract with CMS or if the sponsor or any affiliate of such Part D plan sponsor derives any remuneration from any entity in connection with the sponsor's performance of PBM functions on behalf of a separate Part D plan sponsor. We also considered whether to introduce regulatory text to clarify how the performance standards would apply to a Part D plan sponsor in the context of a vertically integrated entity. However, we concluded that regulatory text to this effect would be superfluous and could inadvertently understate the standards for PBM status as applied to Part D plan sponsors.
Under proposed § 423.2804(d), a Part D plan sponsor would not meet the standards for PBM status based solely on the sponsor performing activities under such sponsor's contract for the operation of its own prescription drug plan; however, this proposal does not limit the circumstances in which a Part D plan sponsor may meet the standards for PBM status based on the sponsor performing activities on behalf of other prescription drug plans. As noted previously, section 1860D-12(h)(1)(A)(iii) of the Act permits manufacturer price concessions, including concessions that are calculated as a percentage of a drug's price, provided they are fully passed through to the Part D plan sponsor and comply with all regulatory and subregulatory requirements related to DIR, for manufacturer rebates, discounts, and other price concessions. This exception to the otherwise applicable remuneration restrictions on PBMs and their affiliates in section 1860D-12(h)(1)(A) of the Act explicitly encompasses scenarios where a Part D plan sponsor acts as a PBM on behalf of a prescription drug plan it offers. Accordingly, we propose to clarify how this exception applies in the context of a Part D plan sponsor that does not fall within the specific limitation on PBM status described at proposed § 423.2804(d). Specifically, we propose that when assessing whether a price concession complies with the requirements in section 1860D-12(h)(1)(A)(iii) of the Act as described in proposed § 423.2810(d), in cases where the Part D plan sponsor meets the standards for PBM status described at proposed § 423.2804(a)(2) and acts as a PBM on behalf of its own prescription drug plan, a price concession to such sponsor for such plan would be deemed to satisfy the passed through condition in paragraph (d)(2)(i) of this section, provided that such Part D plan sponsor receives 100 percent of the gross economic value of the price concession. This clarification ensures a price concession can meet the requirement that it be fully passed through to the Part D sponsor even in those cases where the price concession is paid to a sponsor acting as a PBM on behalf of its own prescription drug plan. We believe this interpretation best resolves the statutory tensions discussed above by preserving the structural distinction between a PBM and a Part D plan sponsor inherent across the various requirements of section 1860D-12(h) of the Act, while also giving full force to the statute's express directive that rebates, discounts, and other price concessions from manufacturers be fully passed through to the Part D plan sponsor including in cases where the sponsor is acting as a PBM on behalf of its own prescription drug plan.
We request comment on these proposals, including whether this proposed approach to applying PBM status to Part D plan sponsors achieves the appropriate application of transparency and remuneration requirements.
4. Affiliate
Section 1860D-12(h)(7)(A) of the Act defines an affiliate, “with respect to any pharmacy benefit manager or PDP sponsor,” as “any entity that, directly or indirectly—(i) owns or is owned by, controls or is controlled by, or is otherwise related in any ownership structure to such pharmacy benefit manager or PDP sponsor; or (ii) acts as a contractor, principal, or agent to such pharmacy benefit manager or PDP sponsor, insofar as such contractor, principal, or agent performs any of the functions described under subparagraph (C).”
This definition has two independent prongs: an ownership or control prong, set out in clause (i), and a functional and contractual prong, set out in clause (ii). As the statute sets these prongs out as alternatives, an entity that satisfies either prong qualifies as an affiliate, regardless of whether it satisfies the other.
Determining whether a particular entity is an affiliate is necessary to establish the entity's obligations under section 1860D-12(h) of the Act. As discussed in section II.C.1. of this proposed rule, the PBM industry is characterized by complex affiliate structures and substantial vertical and horizontal integration. In addition, PBMs have demonstrated an ability to adapt to changing legislative and regulatory dynamics. Together, these factors underscore the importance of determining affiliate status for the effective administration of section 1860D-12(h) of the Act.
Although affiliates have fewer obligations under the Act than PBMs, they remain subject to significant requirements. Specifically, affiliates are subject to the same bona fide service fee restrictions as PBMs under section 1860D-12(h)(1)(A) of the Act. Affiliates must also identify and disgorge impermissible remuneration to the PBM under the required PBM-affiliate agreement described in section 1860D-12(h)(1)(A)(vi)(I) of the Act.
In addition, information concerning affiliates is required to be included in the PBM's annual report. This includes information regarding an affiliate's retained revenue, pharmacy activity, acquisition costs, 340B arrangements, compensation paid to consultants or brokers, and identity as an affiliate under sections 1860D-12(h)(1)(C)(i)(I)(kk), (II), (VI), (VIII), (IX), and (X) of the Act.
Information owned or held by an affiliate may also be subject to audit. Under section 1860D-12(h)(1)(D)(v) of the Act, such information must be produced by the PBM if it is required for reporting or audit verification.
Furthermore, manufacturer contracts entered into by affiliates may trigger disclosure obligations. A manufacturer agreement entered into by an affiliate can trigger the written-explanation requirement under section 1860D-12(h)(1)(C)(ii)(I) of the Act if the agreement involves rebates, discounts,
(
printed page 66441)
payments, or other financial incentives contingent on coverage, formulary placement, or utilization-management conditions. Under section 1860D-12(h)(1)(C)(ii)(II)(bb) of the Act, an affiliate's Chief Executive Officer, Chief Financial Officer, or General Counsel or individual delegated the authority to sign on behalf of one of these officers may also be required to certify the explanation when the affiliate is the relevant contracting entity.
Affiliates may also be required to reimburse Part D plan sponsors for certain penalties. Under section 1860D-12(h)(2)(A)(ii) of the Act, a Part D plan sponsor must require an affiliate to reimburse the sponsor for civil money penalties imposed on the sponsor as a result of the affiliate's failure to meet applicable requirements.
Additionally, affiliates must be subject to punitive contractual remedies. Under section 1860D-12(h)(2)(A)(iii) of the Act, a Part D plan sponsor must require an affiliate to be subject to punitive remedies for breach of contract if the affiliate fails to comply with applicable requirements under the Act.
The affiliate designation is also central to the implementation of the essential retail pharmacies requirements at section 1860D-42(e) of the Act, as added by section 6223(b) of the CAA. Among other requirements, section 1860D-42(e) of the Act directs CMS to publish an annual list of essential retail pharmacies and requires Part D plan sponsors to submit to CMS a list of retail pharmacies that are affiliates of such sponsor or are affiliates of a PBM acting on behalf of such sponsor. Section 1860D-42(e)(4) of the Act provides that the definitions for PBM and affiliate in the provisions implementing section 6224 of the CAA apply to implementation of the essential retail pharmacies requirements under section 1860D-42(e) of the Act. Accordingly, Part D plan sponsors will be using the regulatory standard finalized through this rulemaking when making their annual report of affiliated retail pharmacies, as required by section 1860D-42(e)(3)(B) of the Act. Moreover, because the definition of essential retail pharmacy at section 1860D-42(e)(2)(A) of the Act excludes affiliates, every pharmacy that is an affiliate under proposed § 423.2802 must be excluded from the list of essential retail pharmacies published under 1860D-42(e)(3)(A) of the Act. Acknowledging that this rulemaking does not otherwise address the essential retail pharmacies provisions, we solicit comment on how the affiliate standard being proposed here, if finalized, would impact the implementation of these essential retail pharmacies provisions, including how sponsors would implement this standard for purposes of their reporting obligations under section 1860D-42(e)(3)(B) of the Act.
Section 1860D-12(h)(7)(A)(i) of the Act defines “affiliate” through three independent clauses: “owns or is owned by,” “controls or is controlled by,” and “otherwise related in any ownership structure.” Each clause is independently sufficient to establish affiliate status, and CMS intends to propose regulations giving effect to each. Given the breadth of this prong, CMS also intends to build on existing concepts of ownership, control, attribution, and aggregation to specify a workable framework to the greatest extent possible.
Several Part D regulatory provisions already establish ownership and control concepts with respect to Part D plan sponsors. We discuss several different Part D regulatory provisions including first tier, downstream and related entities; parent organizations; and Part D party in interest rules. We also discuss ownership and control concepts from other Federal provisions and agencies, including definitions used in the Internal Revenue Code (IRC) controlled group rules, Employee Retirement Income Security Act of 1974 (ERISA) party in interest rules, and Security and Exchange Commission (SEC) beneficial ownership rules.
First tier, downstream, and related entities.
As discussed in section II.C.2.a. of this proposed rule, Part D regulations regularly refer to “first tier, downstream, or related entities” together. Under
42 CFR 423.4
:
A first tier entity is “any party that enters into a written arrangement, acceptable to CMS, with a Part D plan sponsor or applicant to provide administrative services or health care services for a Medicare eligible individual under Part D.”
A downstream entity is “any party that enters into a written arrangement, acceptable to CMS, with persons or entities involved with the Part D benefit, below the level of the arrangement between a Part D plan sponsor (or applicant) and a first tier entity,” continuing down to the ultimate provider of health and administrative services.
A related entity includes an entity “related to the Part D sponsor by common ownership or control” that either (1) performs some of the Part D plan sponsor's management functions under contract or delegation, (2) furnishes services to Medicare enrollees under an oral or written agreement, or (3) leases real property or sells materials to the Part D plan sponsor at a cost of more than $2,500 during a contract period.
There are meaningful similarities between the requirements applicable to affiliates under section 1860D-12(h) of the Act and those applicable to first tier, downstream, and related entities under Part D regulations. Under
42 CFR 423.505(i)
, Part D plan sponsors may delegate functions to such entities. Under
42 CFR 423.505(i)(2)
through
(4)
, contracts with those entities must preserve audit and record-access rights for HHS, the Comptroller General, and their designees. First tier, downstream, and related entities are also incorporated into compliance program, PDE submission, claims-data certification, and Medicare Transaction Facilitator Data Module requirements.

However, these existing concepts are not perfect analogs for affiliates under the ownership and control prong. A first-tier entity must have a direct written arrangement with a Part D plan sponsor; downstream entities sit below that relationship; and related entities are linked to the Part D plan sponsor through common ownership or control and certain service, property, or management relationships. The ownership and control prong of section 1860D-12(h)(7)(A)(i) of the Act, by contrast, captures entities that own or are owned by the PBM or Part D plan sponsor without regard to the entity's position in the Part D contract chain. The existing `related entity' definition does capture entities connected to a Part D plan sponsor by common ownership or control. However, it also imposes additional functional requirements—namely that the entity perform management functions or furnish services to enrollees—that are not present in the affiliate definition's ownership and control prong.
Parent organizations.
Under
42 CFR 423.4
, a “parent organization” is the legal entity that exercises a controlling interest through share ownership, the power to appoint voting board members, or other means, directly or through subsidiaries. “Parent organization” is used in various contexts to determine when legally separate entities or contracts should be treated as related for Part D regulatory purposes. For example, the term is used to determine when contracts or plans are sufficiently related to permit consolidation, crosswalks between plan benefit packages (PBPs), or transfers between wholly owned subsidiaries of the same parent organization. Section 423.182(a)
(

defines consolidation by reference to contracts under the same parent organization. Sections 423.530(a)(2)(i) and 423.530(c)(2)(i) address crosswalks involving contracts or plans under the same parent organization. Section 423.551(g)(1) recognizes certain transfers between wholly owned subsidiaries of the same parent organization.
The definition shares important features with the ownership and control prong—both contemplate multi-tier ownership chains and non-ownership-based arrangements that confer control. However, under the existing parent organization definition, ownership and control are intertwined, whereas the affiliate definition treats ownership and control as distinct and independently sufficient bases for affiliate status. Under the parent organization definition, shared ownership may establish a “controlling interest.” In that context, ownership can be the mechanism by which control is established. By contrast, the affiliate definition treats ownership and control as distinct, alternative bases for affiliate status. An entity may qualify as an affiliate if it “owns or is owned by” another entity, “controls or is controlled by” another entity, or is otherwise related through an ownership structure.
Part D Party in Interest Rules.
Under
42 CFR 423.501
, a “party in interest” includes, among other categories, any person who is directly or indirectly the beneficial owner of more than 5 percent of the organization's equity, or the beneficial owner of a mortgage, deed of trust, note, or other interest secured by and valuing more than 5 percent of the organization. The definition therefore includes a clear ownership-based threshold, but it is not limited to ownership interests. It also includes certain management or administrative personnel, nonprofit incorporators or members, related entities, persons or entities under common control with the Part D plan sponsor, and certain family members.
The Part D requirements applicable to parties in interest are more limited than the requirements applicable to affiliates. Under
42 CFR 423.514(b)(1)
, a Part D plan sponsor must annually report to CMS significant business transactions with parties in interest and must either indicate that the transaction costs do not exceed the costs that would have been incurred in comparable transactions with persons who are not parties in interest or justify any higher costs as consistent with prudent management and fiscal soundness requirements. Under
42 CFR 423.514(b)(2)

Under
42 CFR 423.514(c)
, the combined financial statements must separately present the financial information for the sponsor and each party in interest, eliminate inter-entity transactions in the consolidated column, and be examined by an independent auditor in accordance with generally accepted accounting principles, with appropriate opinions and notes.
Affiliates, on the other hand, are subject to broad remuneration restrictions and reporting requirements. Accordingly, we believe the 5-percent beneficial ownership threshold used to identify certain parties in interest is not appropriate for identifying affiliates, as it would impose significant compliance obligations on a broad swath of entities which may have limited relationships with Part D plan sponsors and PBMs.
Beyond CMS's own precedents, several other federal regulatory and statutory frameworks address concepts of ownership and control.
IRC controlled group rules.
The IRC's controlled group rules represent a well-developed framework for determining when separate entities are treated as a single economic unit. Section 1563 of the IRC defines “controlled group of corporations” and identifies three types:
A parent-subsidiary group, consisting of one or more chains of corporations connected through stock ownership of a common parent. That is, to have a parent-subsidiary group, a common parent must own at least 80 percent of the voting power or value of at least one subsidiary member, and 80 percent of the voting power or value of every other subsidiary member is owned by another subsidiary member of the group (§ 1563(a)(1));
A brother-sister group, consisting of two or more corporations in which five or fewer individuals, estates, or trusts own at least 80 percent of each corporation and share more than 50 percent identical ownership of each corporation (§ 1563(a)(2) and (f)(5)); and
A combined group consisting of three or more corporations that, together, form a hybrid of the parent-subsidiary and brother-sister structures, with one of the corporations being both the common parent of a parent-subsidiary group and a member of a brother-sister group (§ 1563(a)(3) of the IRC).
Section 1563 of the IRC also provides detailed constructive ownership rules—including family and entity attribution under section 1563(d) through (e) of the IRC—ensuring that control is measured based on both direct and indirect interests, as well as through options.
The IRC also contains related aggregation provisions that identify controlled groups or commonly controlled trades or businesses for different regulatory purposes. Section 414(b) and (c) of the IRC treat employees of controlled groups of corporations and trades or businesses under common control as employed by a single employer for specified employee benefit plan provisions of the Code, using the section 1563(a) of the IRC definitions and 80-percent controlled group standard with modifications for corporate controlled groups and parallel regulatory rules for trades or businesses under common control. ERISA Title IV separately uses section 414 of the IRC concepts in Pension Benefit Guaranty Corporation regulations.

Section 52 of the IRC likewise aggregates employees of controlled groups of corporations and trades or businesses under common control for purposes of the work opportunity credit and expressly substitutes “more than 50 percent” for “at least 80 percent” in section 1563(a)(1). As a result, § 52 may aggregate a broader set of entities than the baseline section 1563(a) of the IRC 80-percent controlled group standard used in Section 414(b) through (c) of the
IRC. Section 52
of the IRC is also incorporated into Medicare Part D through section 1860D-14C(g)(4) of the Act, which treats all persons treated as a single employer under section 52(a) or (b) of the IRC as one manufacturer for purposes of the “specified manufacturer” and “specified small manufacturer” phase-in rules.
The IRC controlled group frameworks align with the affiliate definition in several respects. They directly address direct ownership, indirect ownership through attribution, and control via equity interests—all concepts that map closely to the statutory language “directly or indirectly owns or is owned by, controls or is controlled by.” They incorporate constructive ownership, including family attribution and ownership through entities which supports the statutory requirement to capture indirect ownership relationships.

Principles Derived from Existing Frameworks.
Several common principles emerge from the foregoing analysis and inform the proposed regulatory framework:
Entity-form neutrality. The regulatory framework should account for corporations, partnerships, limited liability companies, trusts, and other organizational forms so that ownership and control are evaluated consistently across entity types.
Attribution rules. Ownership and control should be attributed to entities that exercise ownership or control through intermediary entities, consistent with frameworks that recognize indirect ownership, constructive ownership, and beneficial ownership.
Governance-based control independent of equity. Governance rights, including board appointment rights, management rights, consent rights, or veto rights over material decisions, may confer control even without majority equity. Exclusive dealing arrangements or economic dependence may also be relevant where they give one entity practical authority over another entity's material business decisions.
Purpose-or-effect analysis. For arrangements below any bright-line ownership threshold, CMS could consider whether the arrangement has the purpose or effect of giving one entity the ability to influence material business decisions of another entity.
Accordingly, at
42 CFR 423.2806(a)(1)
we propose to establish a general rule that an entity is an affiliate if it satisfies one or more of the following paragraphs.
At proposed paragraph (2), we propose to define an ownership relationship for purposes of section 1860D-12(h) of the Act as one where an entity has an ownership relationship with a PBM or Part D plan sponsor if the entity and the PBM or Part D plan sponsor would be treated as members of a parent-subsidiary controlled group under section 1563(a)(1) of the IRC, as modified by section 52(a), of the IRC, as applicable, including the modifications and attribution rules incorporated or applied under those provisions. We believe these parent-subsidiary controlled group rules provide an appropriate basis for determining majority ownership. Section 52 of the IRC is already incorporated into Part D to aggregate entities when determining manufacturer status, and it captures both direct majority ownership and indirect ownership through chains of entities.
At proposed paragraph (3), we propose to define a control relationship between an entity and a PBM or Part D plan sponsor as one where either the entity or the PBM or Part D plan sponsor has the power to materially determine or direct the material actions, policies, or decisions of the other entity, regardless of ownership percentage, through any of the following: (i) the power to appoint, elect, or remove a majority of the other's governing body; (ii) contractual veto, consent, or supermajority rights over material business decisions of the other; (iii) contractual rights to appoint, direct, or remove senior officers or to direct day-to-day operations through a
(
printed page 66444)
management or administrative services agreement; or (iv) exclusive dealing, requirements contracts, or similar arrangements that, alone or together with other contractual or economic arrangements, give one entity practical authority to direct or materially constrain the other entity's material business decisions related to the Part D program. We also propose that control include indirect control exercised through one or more intermediary entities, assessed link by link through the chain of relationships.
We believe this proposed definition is consistent with existing Part D precedent. Under
42 CFR 423.4
, “parent organization” is already defined to mean the legal entity that exercises “a controlling interest, through . . . the power to appoint voting board members, or other means,” expressly recognizing governance-based control, independent of equity ownership, as sufficient to establish a control relationship. It is also consistent with the SEC's beneficial ownership framework at
17 CFR 240.13d-3(a)
, which grounds ownership and control in the practical ability to vote, direct the voting of, or dispose of securities.
At proposed paragraph (a)(4), we propose to define an entity as being otherwise related in an ownership structure to a PBM or Part D plan sponsor if it does not meet the requirements of paragraphs (2) or (3), but the relationship between the entity and a PBM or Part D plan sponsor meets any of the requirements (i) through (iii) described later in this section and the relationship confers meaningful influence either to the entity or to the PBM or Part D plan sponsor: (i) the entities are in a brother-sister controlled group under section 1563(a)(2) of the IRC, as modified by section 52(a) of the IRC; (ii) one entity holds a 10 percent or greater capital or profits interest in a joint venture, limited partnership, limited liability company, or comparable arrangement in which the other participates; or (iii) the totality of the structural features of the relationship confers meaningful influence by one entity over the other, notwithstanding the failure to satisfy the thresholds in paragraphs (a)(4)(i) through (ii). In determining whether the relationship between the entity and the PBM or Part D plan sponsor confers meaningful influence by one entity over the other under paragraph (a)(4), consideration should be given to the purpose or effect of the relationship; financial interdependence; common personnel exercising authority over business decisions; and structural features indicating evasion of applicable thresholds.
We believe this approach is consistent with existing frameworks for identifying non-majority ownership relationships. For example, section 3(14)(I) of ERISA expressly designates as a “party in interest” any 10 percent or more partner or joint venturer of a person described in other party-in-interest categories, providing precedent for addressing joint venture relationships. In addition, the SEC's Regulation 13D-G distinguishes passive investment from control-seeking investment based on whether the holding was acquired or is held “with the purpose or effect of changing or influencing the control of the issuer,” providing precedent for a facts-and- circumstances residual test. Finally, at proposed paragraph (a)(5), we propose that the following principles apply to paragraphs (a)(2) through (4): (i) Entity-form neutrality. “Interest” would be measured by voting power or equity value for corporations; capital or profits interest for partnerships and LLCs; and beneficial interest for trusts and unincorporated enterprises. (ii) Right-to-acquire rules. The right to acquire an ownership interest exercisable within 60 days—through option, warrant, conversion, or revocable proxy—would be treated as a present holding of that interest.
We intend that in the context of vertically integrated structures, the potential affiliation of an entity under this proposal would be assessed based on that particular entity's relationship to the PBM or Part D plan sponsor. If an entity is part of the same vertically integrated structure as a PBM or Part D plan sponsor, then we intend for that entity to be an affiliate of that PBM or Part D plan sponsor as described at § 423.2806(a)(2). If an entity is not part of the same vertically integrated structure as a PBM or Part D plan sponsor, then we intend that the entity would not be an affiliate of the PBM or Part D plan sponsor in the vertically integrated structure unless that entity has a direct relationship with that PBM or Part D plan sponsor and meets the affiliate criteria as described at § 423.2806(a)(3) and (4). We do not intend that affiliation with an entity that is in a vertically integrated structure with a PBM or Part D plan sponsor would confer affiliation with such PBM or Part D plan sponsor, absent a direct relationship with that PBM or Part D plan sponsor that meets the affiliation criteria described at § 423.2806.
We solicit comment on these proposals.
(ii) Functional and Contractual Prong
The functional and contractual prong, set out in the second clause of the affiliate definition, encompasses any entity that acts as a contractor, principal, or agent to a PBM or Part D plan sponsor, “insofar as” that contractor, principal, or agent performs any PBM function.
Unlike the ownership or control prong, which applies categorically to any entity meeting certain relational requirements, the functional and contractual prong conditions affiliate status on an entity's actual performance of PBM functions. The PBM definition is similarly functional, conditioning PBM status on the performance of PBM functions. However, affiliate status under the functional and contractual prong attaches when an entity “acts as a contractor, principal, or agent to such PBM or PDP sponsor,
insofar as
such contractor, principal, or agent performs any of the functions described under subparagraph (C)” (emphasis added).
To determine when affiliate status attaches under the functional and contractual prong, we propose to clarify the effect of the “insofar as” language. We considered several interpretive approaches.
First, we considered a purposive approach under which affiliate status would attach only when performing one or more PBM functions constitutes the primary role under the relevant contract. However, this approach, risks excluding entities retained for multiple purposes where PBM functions represent a substantial—though not primary—component of the contractual relationship. Therefore, we believe this approach would be underinclusive.
Second, we considered establishing quantitative thresholds—such as minimum claims volume or dollar value of transactions—below which an entity's performance of a listed function would not trigger affiliate status. However, calibrating appropriate thresholds across the full range of PBM functions would be analytically complex, and this approach would be susceptible to manipulation through contractual arrangements deliberately structured to fall below any imposed threshold.
Third, we considered applying the same “any performance standard” we are proposing for PBM status. However, this approach, would fail to give effect to the “insofar as” language in the functional and contractual prong, which has no equivalent in the PBM definition. We also believe this approach could be overinclusive, categorizing entities as
(
printed page 66445)
affiliates even when they perform PBM functions solely on an incidental basis.
Finally, we considered and elected to propose to codify at proposed § 423.2806(b) that affiliate status attaches under the functional and contractual prong where a contractor, principal, or agent performs one or more PBM functions as a material part of its contractual services. We believe this standard appropriately captures entities for which PBM functions constitute a significant portion of their contractual obligations, without sweeping in entities that perform such functions only incidentally or excluding entities for which such functions are a major—but not primary—part of their contractual obligations.
We solicit comment on this proposal.
