6. Remuneration Requirements
a. Bona Fide Service Fees
Section 1860D-12(h)(1)(A)(i) of the Act, as added by the CAA, requires that PBMs and any affiliates of such PBMs shall not derive any remuneration with respect to any services provided on behalf of any entity or individual, in connection with the utilization of covered Part D drugs, from any such entity or individual other than bona fide service fees, defined in added section 1860D-12(h)(7)(B) of the Act, subject to clauses in section 1860D-12(h)(1)(A)(ii) and(iii) of the Act. This requirement to limit remuneration to bona fide service fees addresses concerns that PBM practices such as spread pricing or rebate retention may contribute to higher drug costs
[
39
]
by prohibiting income other than flat dollar amounts for specific, itemized services. Additionally, this requirement addresses concerns that even administrative fee structures (as opposed to spread pricing or rebate retention) create incentives for PBMs to favor higher cost drugs when the administrative fees are based on a percent of the cost of the drug
[
40
]
by prohibiting bona fide service fees from being directly or indirectly based on, or contingent on, drug price.
We are proposing to codify at § 423.2810(b) the statutory requirement that a bona fide service fee be defined as a fee that is reflective of the fair market value (defined at § 423.2802(c)) for a bona fide, itemized service actually performed on behalf of an entity, that the entity would otherwise perform (or contract for) in the absence of the service arrangement and that is not passed on in whole or in part to a client or customer, whether or not the entity takes title to the drug. Such fee must be a flat dollar amount and shall not be directly or indirectly based on or contingent upon—drug price (such as wholesale acquisition cost) or drug benchmark price (such as average wholesale price); the amount of discounts, rebates, fees, or other direct or indirect remuneration with respect to covered Part D drugs dispensed to enrollees in a prescription drug plan, except as permitted under the definition of incentive payments at proposed § 423.2802; coverage or formulary placement decisions or the volume or value of any referrals or business generated between the parties to the arrangement; or the amounts or methodologies prohibited at proposed § 423.2810(b)(3).
(1) Remuneration
Section 1860D-12(h)(1)(A)(i) of the Act sets out a general rule that a PBM and any affiliate of a PBM “shall not derive any remuneration with respect to any services provided on behalf of any entity or individual, in connection with the utilization of covered Part D drugs, from any such entity or individual other than bona fide service fees. . . .”
This statutory provision has two operative components. First, “remuneration” determines which payment streams are subject to the prohibition. Second, “in connection with covered Part D drug utilization” determines when the restriction applies. Together, these components define the universe of PBM and affiliate remuneration subject to the bona fide service fee restrictions under 1860D-12(h) of the Act.
To determine which payment streams are subject to the general prohibition, we must first understand the meaning of “remuneration” in the context of section 1860D-12(h) of the Act. The statutory structure provides several contextual clues.
First, section 1860D-12(h)(1)(A)(i) of the Act uses the phrase “any remuneration” rather than a narrower term such as “fees,” “payments,” or “compensation.”
Second, section 1860D-12(h)(1)(A)(iii) of the Act creates a specific exception to the prohibition for manufacturer rebates, discounts, and other price concessions under certain conditions. That exception would be unnecessary if such payments were not otherwise encompassed within the general category of remuneration.
Third, section 1860D-12(h)(4) of the Act sets out a rule of construction providing that nothing in section 1860D-12(h) of the Act shall be construed as: (A) prohibiting flat dispensing fees or reimbursement or payment for ingredient costs—including customary, industry-standard discounts directly related to drug acquisition that are retained by pharmacies or wholesalers—to entities that acquire or dispense prescription drugs; or (B) modifying regulatory requirements or subregulatory program instructions or guidance related to pharmacy payment, reimbursement, or dispensing fees. This rule of construction would similarly be unnecessary if such payments did not otherwise fall within the general category of remuneration.
Given this statutory structure, we believe “remuneration” must be understood broadly for purposes of section 1860D-12(h) of the Act. Several Part D regulatory provisions, as well as related statutory and regulatory frameworks, already establish concepts of remuneration with respect to services provided in connection with the utilization of Part D drugs, and these provide valuable precedent for specifying the scope of remuneration in this context.
The new statutory provisions cite some of these concepts. For example, the exception for manufacturer rebates,
(
printed page 66446)
discounts, and other price concessions at section 1860D-12(h)(1)(A)(iii) of the Act imposes two conditions: (1) the rebates, discounts, and other price concessions must be fully passed through to the Part D plan sponsor, and (2) they must comply with all regulatory and subregulatory requirements related to DIR for manufacturer rebates, discounts, and other price concessions.
CMS has defined several concepts related to remuneration in the context of DIR that are relevant here; the exception for price concessions depends in part on compliance with these existing DIR-related regulatory requirements.
Under
42 CFR 423.308
, costs are “actually paid” only if they are actually incurred by the Part D plan sponsor and are net of any DIR—including “discounts, chargebacks or rebates, cash discounts, free goods contingent on a purchase agreement, up-front payments, coupons, goods in kind, free or reduced-price services, grants, or other price concessions or similar benefits”—from manufacturers, pharmacies, enrollees, or any other person that would serve to decrease costs incurred under the Part D plan. Under this provision, remuneration may be direct or indirect, encompass both cash and non-cash value, and include rebates, discounts, price concessions, chargebacks, coupons, grants, and similar benefits.
The definition of “price concession” at
42 CFR 423.100
further supports a broad interpretation of the concept of remuneration. That provision defines a price concession as any form of discount, direct or indirect subsidy, or rebate received by the Part D plan sponsor or its intermediary contracting organization from any source that serves to decrease costs incurred under the Part D plan. It includes discounts, chargebacks, rebates, cash discounts, free goods contingent on purchase agreements, coupons, free or reduced-price services, goods in kind, and other similar benefits—as well as credits, offsets, non-cash benefits, in-kind benefits, and similar direct or indirect financial advantages. Under the statutory structure of section 1860D-12(h) of the Act, such payments would constitute remuneration if the requirements of section 1860D-12(h)(1)(A)(iii) of the Act are not satisfied.
While the provisions discussed previously illustrate the breadth of payments encompassed by “remuneration” for purposes of section 1860D-12(h) of the Act, other statutory frameworks governing remuneration in connection with Part D drug utilization offer precedent for the outer limits of the term.
Specifically, under section 1128B(b) of the Act, the Anti-Kickback Statute (AKS) prohibits knowingly and willfully soliciting, receiving, offering, or paying “any remuneration”—including any kickback, bribe, or rebate—directly or indirectly, overtly or covertly, in cash or in kind, in return for or to induce referrals, purchases, leases, orders, or recommendations involving items or services payable by a Federal health care program. The OIG has consistently interpreted “any remuneration” in the AKS context to mean “anything of value.”
Although the regulatory contexts of the AKS and section 1860D-12(h) of the Act differ, both statutes use the same phrase—“any remuneration”—to describe the payments subject to their respective restrictions. Accordingly, we believe it is reasonable to define the outer boundaries of “remuneration” for purposes of section 1860D-12(h) of the Act consistently with the AKS.
Therefore, we propose to define “remuneration” at
42 CFR 423.2802
to mean anything of value, whether provided directly or indirectly, overtly or covertly, in cash or in kind, including, but not limited to, monetary payments, non-cash consideration, administrative fees, data fees, service fees, spread pricing, retained margins, rebates, discounts, chargebacks, price concessions, credits, offsets, up-front payments, coupons, free or reduced-price goods or services, goods in kind, grants, in-kind benefits, guarantee reconciliation amounts, interest payments, financing benefits, and any other direct or indirect financial advantage.
(2) A Service That the Entity “Would Otherwise Perform, or Contract For”
Section 1860D-12(h)(7)(B) of the Act states that a bona fide service fee must be “for a bona fide, itemized service actually performed on behalf of an entity, that the entity would otherwise perform (or contract for) in the absence of the service arrangement.” As discussed in section II.C.6.a. of this proposed rule, we are proposing to define a bona fide service fee as a fee for a bona fide, itemized service actually performed on behalf of an entity, that the entity would otherwise perform, or contract for, in the absence of the service arrangement.
This proposed definition would establish that a fee paid to a PBM will not qualify as a bona fide service fee unless certain conditions are met. To qualify as a bona fide service fee, the underlying service must be one that the entity on whose behalf the service is performed would itself perform, or procure through a third-party contract, absent the service arrangement. The “would otherwise perform, or contract for” requirement helps to distinguish legitimate service fees from fees that have no meaningful connection to the purchaser's actual operational needs (such as a data portal fee). To ensure that bona fide service fees reflect genuine value exchanged for real services tied to the entity's operational needs, we are proposing to establish a regulatory standard for determining when a service qualifies as a “service that the entity would otherwise perform, or contract for.” Absent such a standard, the bona fide service fee framework could potentially be circumvented through arrangements in which fees are nominally labeled as service fees but are for activities that the entity would not otherwise perform.
To define what constitutes a service that an entity would otherwise perform or contract for, and to establish how we would evaluate whether a particular service meets that standard, we considered definitions previously contemplated in rulemaking, including the Medicare Program; Revisions to Payment Policies, Five-Year Review of Work Relative Value Units, Changes to the Practice Expense Methodology Under the Physician Fee Schedule, and Other Changes to Payment Under Part B; Revisions to the Payment Policies of Ambulance Services Under the Fee Schedule for Ambulance Services; and Ambulance Inflation Factor Update for CY 2007 (“CY 2007 PFS”). The CY 2007 PFS final rule established that, beginning with average sales price (ASP) reporting for sales during the first quarter of CY 2007, bona fide service fees that are paid by a manufacturer to an entity, whether or not the entity takes title to the drug, are not considered price concessions under § 414.804(a)(2) insofar as, and to the extent that, they satisfy the definition of a bona fide service fee described at § 414.802: “fees paid by a manufacturer to an entity, that represent fair market value for a bona fide, itemized service actually performed on behalf of the manufacturer that the manufacturer would otherwise perform (or contract for) in the absence of the service arrangement [. . .].”
The CY 2007 PFS explained that these elements of the definition of bona fide service fees established at § 414.802 “encompass any reasonably necessary or useful services of value to the manufacturer that are associated with the efficient distribution of drugs.” While this existing definition addresses the concept from the manufacturer's perspective, the concept that a qualifying service must reflect a
(
printed page 66447)
reasonably necessary or useful service of value associated with the efficient distribution of drugs to the entity on whose behalf it is performed is equally appropriate in the context of services performed by a PBM (or other entity) on behalf of Part D plan sponsors. Therefore, we are proposing a definition of “a service that the entity would otherwise perform, or contract for” that largely aligns with the definition and interpretation of this concept in the CY 2007 PFS final rule, with some additional specifications.
Importantly, there is a distinction between the PBM function performance standard proposed at section 423.2804(b) and the “would otherwise perform, or contract for” requirement. As discussed in section II.C.3. of this proposed rule, under the Act, a PBM is any person or entity that (1) acts as a price negotiator or group purchaser on behalf of a Part D plan sponsor or prescription drug plan; or (2) manages the prescription drug benefits provided by such a sponsor or plan. The Act states that management of prescription drug benefits includes the processing and payment of prescription drug claims, drug utilization review, processing of prior authorization requests, adjudication of appeals or grievances related to the prescription drug benefit, contracting with network pharmacies, controlling the cost of covered Part D drugs, and the provision of related services, but does not limit prescription drug benefit management to these activities.
This illustrative list of PBM functions enumerated in the statute is relevant to, but not determinative of, whether a particular service for which the entity is paying remuneration to the PBM is one that an entity would otherwise perform or contract for in the absence of a service arrangement with a PBM. Although there will often be substantial overlap between PBM functions and services that an entity would otherwise perform or contract for, the two concepts are distinct, and satisfying one does not necessarily satisfy the other. The fact that a service may be one an entity would otherwise perform or contract for does not itself determine PBM status, which is dependent on the performance of specific PBM functions, as proposed at § 423.2804(b).
To further clarify this distinction between the PBM function performance standard proposed at section 423.2804(b) and the “would otherwise perform, or contract for” requirement of the proposed bona fide service fees definition proposed here, the PBM function performance standard is a threshold that identifies when a person or entity is performing a PBM function, as defined at proposed § 423.2802 and as discussed in section II.C.3. of this proposed rule. By contrast, the “would otherwise perform, or contract for” requirement proposed here is a separate payment-eligibility standard within the proposed bona fide service fee definition. Relevant to this standard is whether the service for which the fee is paid is a service of operational, administrative, clinical, financial, compliance, or programmatic value to the entity on whose behalf the service is performed, such that the entity would reasonably perform the service itself or procure it from another party in the absence of the service arrangement.
We propose to establish at § 423.2810(b)(2) that a service qualifies as “a service that the entity would otherwise perform, or contract for” if the service is a necessary or useful service of operational, administrative, clinical, financial, compliance, or programmatic value to the entity on whose behalf the service is performed, such that the entity would perform the service itself or procure it from another party in the absence of the service arrangement. We seek comment on this proposed definition and whether additional guidance or examples would be useful to illustrate the application of this payment-eligibility standard within the bona-fide service fee definition to specific types of services commonly encountered in the Part D marketplace.
(3) Definition of “In Connection With the Utilization of Part D Drugs”
Section 1860D-12(h)(1)(A)(i) of the Act prohibits PBMs and their affiliates from deriving any remuneration other than bona fide service fees for any services in connection with the utilization of covered Part D drugs, from any entity or individual. Determining whether a payment arrangement is “in connection with the utilization of covered Part D drugs” establishes whether the prohibition in section 1860D-12(h)(1)(A)(i) of the Act applies. If a payment to a PBM is unrelated to the utilization of Part D drugs (as defined at § 423.100), the payment is not covered by this prohibition. Clarity in this prong of the prohibition is therefore important to ensure an appropriate scope that neither allows entities to circumvent the statutory prohibition by labeling payments as unrelated to Part D drugs even when such a connection exists, nor applies to payments that truly have no connection to Part D drug utilization.
For this reason, we are proposing to define what it means for remuneration to be in connection with the utilization of Part D drugs. We also propose to clarify the treatment of remuneration arrangements that involve both Part D drugs and non-Part D drugs, because the prohibition applies specifically to remuneration received in connection with the utilization of Part D drugs, and not to remuneration received in connection with drugs dispensed under other benefit programs, such as Medicaid or commercial insurance.
We propose that remuneration is “in connection with the utilization of Part D drugs” if the remuneration relates to the prescribing, dispensing, furnishing, coverage, reimbursement, or management of Part D drugs, including activities that directly or indirectly influence or determine such utilization. For services supporting multiple lines of business, only the portion of remuneration allocable to the utilization of Part D drugs under a Part D plan would be considered to be in connection with such utilization.
This definition reflects two important principles. First, “in connection with utilization” is construed broadly to encompass the full range of activities that contribute to a Part D drug being prescribed, dispensed, furnished, covered, reimbursed, or managed on behalf of Part D enrollees. This includes not only the direct act of dispensing a drug but also upstream (for example, formulary placement, contracting with network pharmacies) and downstream (for example, processing and payment of prescription drug claims, adjudication of appeals or grievances related to the prescription drug benefit) activities that directly or indirectly influence or determine whether and how Part D drugs are utilized.
Second, we recognize that PBMs frequently administer benefits that span multiple lines of business, including Part D, Medicaid, and commercial insurance, and that a single service (and the remuneration associated with it) may not always be solely attributable to a single line of business. We propose a definition of “in connection with the utilization of Part D drugs” that is designed to reflect this reality by clarifying that “only the portion of remuneration allocable to the utilization of Part D drugs under a Part D plan is considered.” Therefire, we propose that, where a service performed by a PBM or its affiliate encompasses Part D drug utilization—even if it also encompasses non-Part D activity—only the portion of remuneration allocable to the utilization of Part D drugs under a Part D plan is subject to the bona fide service fee requirement.
This allocability standard would operate as follows. Where a PBM
(
printed page 66448)
performs a service that covers both Part D and non-Part D drug utilization, the total remuneration received for that service is not excluded from the prohibition simply because the service also encompasses activity that does not involve a Part D drug. Rather, the PBM must allocate the total remuneration between the portion that is in connection with the utilization of Part D drugs and portion that is not connection with the utilization of Part D drugs when reporting on remuneration to a Part D plan sponsor, following the standards at proposed § 423.2810(e)(1)(ii)(B). That portion allocated to the utilization of Part D drugs is the amount subject to the bona fide service fee requirement.
We propose to codify this definition at 423.2810(h). We seek comment on the proposal and whether the allocability standard described previously provides sufficient clarity and flexibility for PBMs and Part D plan sponsors to identify and allocate remuneration under mixed arrangements. We also seek comment on whether additional guidance or specific examples would be useful to address particular types of services or remuneration structures commonly encountered in the Part D marketplace.
(4) Fair Market Value for Bona Fide Service Fees
In accordance with section 1860D-12(h)(7)(B) of the Act, bona fide service fees must be “reflective of the fair market value (as specified by the Secretary, through notice and comment rulemaking)”. In specifying the meaning of fair market value for bona fide service fees, we considered definitions previously contemplated in federal rulemaking, including the
Medicare Program; Revisions to Payment Policies, Five-Year Review of Work Relative Value Units, Changes to the Practice Expense Methodology Under the Physician Fee Schedule, and Other Changes to Payment Under Part B; Revisions to the Payment Policies of Ambulance Services Under the Fee Schedule for Ambulance Services; and Ambulance Inflation Factor Update for CY 2007
(“CY 2007 PFS”) and the
Medicare and Medicaid Programs; CY 2026 Payment Policies Under the Physician Fee Schedule and Other Changes to Part B Payment and Coverage Policies; Medicare Shared Savings Program Requirements; and Medicare Prescription Drug Inflation Rebate Program
(“CY 2026 PFS”).
The CY 2007 PFS final rule established that, beginning with average sales price (ASP) reporting for sales during the first quarter of CY 2007, bona fide service fees that are paid by a manufacturer to an entity, whether or not the entity takes title to the drug, are not considered price concessions under § 414.804(a)(2) insofar as, and to the extent that, they satisfy the definition of a bona fide service fee described at § 414.802: “fees paid by a manufacturer to an entity, that represent fair market value for a bona fide, itemized service actually performed on behalf of the manufacturer that the manufacturer would otherwise perform (or contract for) in the absence of the service arrangement, and that are not passed on in whole or in part to a client or customer of an entity, whether or not the entity takes title to the drug.” The CY 2007 PFS final rule did not provide guidance on specific methodologies that manufacturers must use to determine fair market value.
The CY 2026 PFS proposed rule elaborated on the approach to fair market value, as applied to the definition of bona fide service fees that are not considered price concessions under § 414.804(a)(2). CMS proposed additional requirements for the standards and methodology that should be used to determine fair market value, specifically: for fees paid by a manufacturer to an entity that do not vary directly with the amount of drug sold or price of a manufacturer's drug, the fair market value must be determined either based on comparable market transactions that generally reflect current market conditions or the cost of the service plus a reasonable markup to the total cost, and for fees paid by a manufacturer to an entity that vary directly with the amount of drug sold or price of a manufacturer's drug, the fair market value must be determined by using the cost of the service and adding a reasonable markup to the total cost. CMS further proposed that for fees paid by a manufacturer to an entity that vary directly with the amount of drug sold or price of a manufacturer's drug, if any material portion of cost data is not available, manufacturers should follow a market-based approach based on verifiable market data until such time as sufficient cost data becomes available. CMS additionally proposed that under such circumstances, the fair market value assessment must be conducted by an independent, third-party valuator that does not have any financial relationship (other than the arrangement to conduct fair market value analyses) with either party to the arrangement and no stake in the outcome of the valuation, and the assessment must be documented with a clear explanation, including a description of the methodology used. Finally, CMS proposed to require that manufacturers update fair market analyses no less frequently than the renewal period of the agreement for the service arrangement between the manufacturer and the other entity and that they include documentation of the update in the reasonable assumptions documentation corresponding with the quarter when the update was made. CMS did not finalize these proposals, which were regulatory actions and not statutorily required, in the CY 2026 PFS final rule.
We believe that, of the previously approaches to fair market value previously contemplated by CMS, the approach proposed in the CY 2026 PFS proposed rule for purposes of average sales price reporting provides the most appropriate foundation for specifying the meaning of fair market value under Section 1860-D(h)(7)(B) of the Act, since it includes the most detail and was informed by market dynamics that CMS had observed since the earlier CY 2007 PFS rule. We are proposing a definition of fair market value that largely aligns with the approach in the CY 2026 PFS proposed rule, with some changes due to the differences between the programs and the introduction of additional requirements by the CAA. For example, because section 1860-D(h)(7)(B) of the Act specifies that bona fide service fees “shall not be directly or indirectly based on, or contingent upon” drug price, we are not proposing a separate fair market value standard for fees that vary with the manufacturer's price of a drug. Additionally, our proposed definition would apply to a broader set of fees than those paid by a pharmaceutical manufacturer, since it would apply to any remuneration received by a PBM or any affiliates of such PBM from any individual or entity in connection with the utilization of Part D drugs. Finally, whereas the purpose of the CY 2026 proposed rule was to define bona fide service fees to inform average sales price reporting, the purpose of this rule is to define bona fide service fees in the broader context of the statutory requirement that generally prohibits PBMs and their affiliates from receiving remuneration other than bona fide service fees with respect to services provided on behalf of any entity or individual in connection with the utilization of Part D drugs.
We are proposing at § 423.2810(e)(1) that fair market value be defined as the cost of the itemized service plus a reasonable markup to the total cost, for all bona fide service fees. This single definition of fair market value for bona fide service fees differs from the
(
printed page 66449)
definition in the CY 2026 PFS proposed rule—which contemplated different standards for fees that do and do not vary directly with the amount of drug sold or price of a manufacturer's drug—because section 1860D-12(7)(B) provides that bona fide service fees may not be directly or indirectly based on or contingent upon drug price. Commenters did raise concerns with the cost-based definition of fair market value in response to the CY 2026 PFS proposed rule. Specifically, commenters argued that CMS should allow multiple valuation approaches (cost-, market-, income-based, or hybrid) to reflect market realities, that the existing average sales price framework for fair market value (which does not specify a particular valuation methodology) is adequate, and that fees based on a percentage of drug cost are not inherently improper. However, we believe those comments and concerns are not relevant to this proposal for several reasons. First, the context in which we are undertaking this rulemaking is different than the context in which the CY 2026 PFS was developed due to the unique requirements of section 1860D-12(h) of the Act, as added by the CAA. The CAA enumerated requirements for bona fide service fees and expressly instructed the Secretary to specify the meaning of fair market value, delegating authority to the Secretary to consider definitions of fair market value beyond the PFS framework, as well as imparting a statutory imperative to address fair market value (whereas the proposed definition of fair market value in the CY 2026 PFS rule was a regulatory action). Second, the CAA explicitly prohibits bona fide service fees from being tied to the price of a drug, so comments in response to the CY 2026 PFS proposed rule defending fees that are a percentage of drug cost are not relevant in the context of the CAA. Third, the comments in response to the CY 2026 PFS proposed rule contemplated the definition of fair market value specifically in the context of bona fide service fees that may be retained in the determination of average sales price reported to CMS by the manufacturer, rather than in the context of bona fide service fees received by any PBM or affiliate of such PBM in connection with the utilization of Part D drugs. We do not assume that the public comments submitted in response to the CY 2026 PFS proposed rule provide a comprehensive picture of sentiment regarding a cost-based definition of fair market value outside of the context of average sales price reporting, and we are soliciting public comment on our proposed definition of fair market value for application in the context of regulations implementing section 1860D-12(h) of the Act.
If observed data on any material portion of the cost of the service are not available—for example, if the PBM or affiliate of such PBM begins providing a new service for the first time—we propose at § 423.2810(e)(1)(i) that the fair market value for the bona fide service fee be defined as an estimate of the expected cost of the itemized service plus a reasonable markup to the total cost, until such time as sufficient observed cost data are available. Sufficient observed cost data would be considered available no later than 1 year after the bona fide service fee based on estimated costs is in effect. In addition, we propose that the estimated cost be consistent with, if available, the cost to the PBM or affiliate of such PBM of providing other itemized services, with reasonable adjustments as necessary to account for bona fide differences between the resources needed to perform each itemized service. For example, a PBM or affiliate would use the actual labor costs associated with employees with similar credentials and job requirements who perform other itemized services on behalf of the PBM or affiliate when estimating the labor costs of providing a new itemized service for which any material portion of cost data is not available to the PBM or affiliate. We propose using an estimate of expected costs—rather than a market-based approach based on verifiable market data until such time as sufficient cost data becomes available as proposed in the CY 2026 PFS proposed rule—for several reasons. CMS received many comments in response to the CY 2026 proposed rule arguing that the proposed requirement for use of an independent, third-party valuator that does not have any financial relationship (other than the arrangement to conduct fair market value analyses) with either party to the arrangement and no stake in the outcome of the valuation would disrupt the market and add significant burden since there are few valuators that currently meet that requirement. We also believe that PBMs and their affiliates typically have either sufficient data on their own internal costs or a sufficient ability to estimate their own expected costs, such that a cost-based approach to fair market value is appropriate for any services provided by PBMs or their affiliates in connection with the utilization of Part D drugs.
To clarify what expenses should be considered costs, we examined existing federal regulations that address cost-based compensation structures. Federal Acquisition Regulation (FAR) 31.201-1 describes the composition of total costs for federal acquisition as: “The total cost, including standard costs properly adjusted for applicable variances, of a contract is the sum of the direct and indirect costs allocable to the contract, incurred or to be incurred, plus any allocable cost of money pursuant to 31.205-10, less any allocable credits. The FAR further defines reasonableness and allocability at FAR 31.201-3 and FAR 31.201-4 and discusses the treatment of credits in FAR 31.201-5.

2 CFR 200.403

200.405

We considered a single quantitative percent ceiling on reasonable markup but did not propose this option due to the diversity of entities that may fit the definition of PBM or affiliate of such PBM and the wide variation in the types of services they provide. We also considered not defining “reasonable” with respect to markup and instead requiring that the PBM or affiliate of such PBM disclose the percent of the markup to the entity paying the bona fide service fee. We solicit comment on the previous proposals, including whether there are circumstances for which we should allow an alternative definition of fair market value for bona fide service fees, including but not limited to circumstances in which fair market value could be determined based on comparable market transactions. We also solicit comment on whether there are any requirements that should be placed on alternative mechanisms for defining fair market value, such as requiring use of an independent, third-party valuator without any financial relationship (other than the arrangement to conduct fair market value analyses) with either party to the arrangement and no stake in the outcome of the valuation.
Section 1860D-12(h)(7)(B) of the Act provides that bona fide service fees shall not be directly or indirectly based on, or contingent upon—(i) drug price, such as wholesale acquisition cost or drug benchmark price (such as average wholesale price); (ii) the amount of discounts, rebates, fees, or other direct or indirect remuneration with respect to Part D drugs dispensed to enrollees in a prescription drug plan, except as permitted pursuant to paragraph (1)(A)(ii); (iii) coverage or formulary placement decisions or the volume or value of any referrals or business generated between the parties to the arrangement; or (iv) any other amounts or methodologies prohibited by the Secretary. We are proposing to prohibit two specific additional types of methodologies for calculating bona fide service fees at § 423.2810(b)(3).
First, we are proposing at § 423.2810(b)(3)(i) to prohibit a methodology that requires the entity paying the bona fide service fee to the PBM or affiliate of such PBM for an itemized service to pay any additional fee, including any additional fee that otherwise would meet the requirements of a bona fide service fee, in order to access the primary benefit of such itemized service or have access to sufficient information to provide oversight of such itemized service. For example, if a Part D plan sponsor contracts with a PBM to negotiate rebates with a pharmaceutical manufacturer and pays a bona fide service fee for that itemized service, the PBM or its affiliate may not require that the Part D plan sponsor pay a separate data access fee in order to obtain basic information about the negotiated rebate (because such information is necessary to provide oversight of the itemized service of rebate negotiation). We solicit comment on the proposal to prohibit this methodology, including whether any modifications are warranted to account for differences in services offered by different types of PBM affiliates.
Second, we are proposing at § 423.2810(b)(3)(ii) that a PBM or its affiliate may not make the availability of an itemized service contingent on an agreement that the entity or individual with which the PBM or its affiliate is contracting for such itemized service provide remuneration to the PBM or affiliate of such PBM for a separate service. We are proposing to define a separate service as an itemized service that is not necessary for the PBM or affiliate of such PBM to perform in order for the PBM or affiliate of such PBM to provide the itemized service under contract. Reasons a separate service may not be necessary include that the contracting entity does not require that service or that the contracting entity is able to fulfill the service without use of the PBM or its affiliate, either independently or through a different contract. For example, if a Part D plan sponsor establishes a remuneration agreement with a PBM to adjudicate claims on the Part D plan sponsor's behalf, the PBM may not require that the agreement include the additional service of formulary development, because it is possible for the Part D plan sponsor to develop the formulary itself or contract with another entity to develop the formulary. This proposal would not prohibit the Part D plan sponsor in this scenario from voluntarily choosing to contract with the PBM for the additional service of formulary development. We solicit comment on the proposal to prohibit this methodology, including on whether any modifications are warranted to account for differences in services offered by different types of PBM affiliates.
These proposed prohibitions anticipate and attempt to prevent a potential adverse effect of requiring a remuneration structure that is entirely fee-based: the proliferation of individual fees which may not deliver benefit to the paying individual or entity. There is some evidence of the market moving in this direction already, such as the consolidation of rebate negotiation with PBM GPOs that retain revenue by charging multiple flat fees.

b. Incentive Payments
In addition to bona fide service fees, the CAA also provides for certain limited incentive payments to PBMs. Section 1860D-12(h)(1)(A)(2) of the Act, as added by the CAA, states that an incentive payment (as determined by the Secretary) paid by a Part D plan sponsor to a PBM or an affiliate of a PBM that is performing services on behalf of such sponsor shall be deemed a `bona fide service fee' (even if such payment does not otherwise meet the definition of such term under paragraph (7)(B)) if such payment is a flat dollar amount, is consistent with fair market value (as specified by the Secretary), is related to services actually performed by the PBM or affiliate of such PBM, on behalf of the Part D plan sponsor making such payment, in connection with the utilization of Part D drugs, and meets additional requirements, if any, as determined appropriate by the Secretary. We propose to codify these requirements at § 423.2810(c). An incentive payment would be a reasonable form of remuneration in targeted circumstances under which the Part D plan sponsor is incentivizing or rewarding measurable performance by a PBM or an affiliate of such PBM. It should not be treated as an alternative payment structure to bona fide service fees that serves to enhance overall compensation rather than rewarding higher levels of performance.
We believe that fair market value should be defined differently for incentive payments than for bona fide service fees. While a cost-based
(
printed page 66452)
definition is appropriate for determining the fair market value for bona fide service fees (proposed at § 423.2810(e)(1)), it may not necessarily be appropriate for incentive payments given that the cost to provide an itemized service may not differ meaningfully based on the quality of performance. Therefore, we believe it is appropriate to define fair market value for incentive payments on the basis of something other than cost. The definition of fair market value proposed in the CY 2026 PFS proposed rule included the concept of comparable market transactions, which we believe to be an appropriate basis for incentive payments since such an approach would allow Part D plan sponsors to offer meaningful incentives based on performance (rather than cost) while preventing remuneration structures that are untethered from actual market conditions. We propose at § 423.2810(e)(2) that fair market value for incentive payments be defined as an amount reflective of comparable market transactions that generally reflect current market conditions.
We solicit comment on this proposal, including whether it allows Part D plan sponsors to provide meaningful performance incentives to PBMs and affiliates of PBMs without creating an alternative remuneration structure that serves to enhance overall compensation rather than rewarding higher levels of performance. We specifically solicit comment on whether the proposals provide sufficient clarity regarding the circumstances under which incentive payments are a reasonable alternative to bona fide service fees.
c. Exception for Manufacturer Rebates, Discounts, and Price Concessions.
Section 1860D-12(h)(1)(A)(i) of the Act establishes a general rule prohibiting a PBM and its affiliates from deriving “any remuneration with respect to any services provided on behalf of any entity or individual, in connection with the utilization of covered Part D drugs” other than bona fide service fees. Section 1860D-12(h)(1)(A)(iii) of the Act creates an exception to that general rule for certain manufacturer rebates, discounts, and other price concessions.
That exception provides: “Rebates, discounts, and other price concessions received by a PBM or an affiliate of a PBM from manufacturers, even if such price concessions are calculated as a percentage of a drug's price, shall not be considered a violation of the requirements of clause (i) if they are fully passed through to a PDP sponsor and are compliant with all regulatory and subregulatory requirements related to direct and indirect remuneration for manufacturer rebates, discounts, and other price concessions under this part, including in cases where a PDP sponsor is acting as a pharmacy benefit manager on behalf of a prescription drug plan offered by such PDP sponsor.”
For a rebate, discount, or other price concession to qualify for this exception, two conditions must be satisfied: (1) the price concession must be fully passed through to the Part D plan sponsor; and (2) the price concession must comply with all regulatory and subregulatory requirements related to DIR under Part D.
The statute also expressly permits price concessions calculated as a percentage of a drug's price, extends the exception to both PBMs and their affiliates, and explicitly covers scenarios in which a Part D plan sponsor acts as its own PBM.
To establish the parameters of this exception, CMS proposes to specify: (1) when a price concession has been fully passed through to the Part D plan sponsor; (2) what process must be followed for price concessions received by affiliates; and (3) how compliance with DIR requirements will be determined.
As a threshold matter, the standard Part D benefit and Part D payment framework require plan costs to be determined based on costs actually incurred.
[
42

CMS has long implemented that requirement through regulations providing that Part D costs be reported net of applicable DIR. Notably, consistent with that statutory foundation,
42 CFR 423.308
defines amounts “actually paid” to mean costs that are actually incurred by the Part D plan sponsor and are net of any DIR. DIR is further defined to include all “price concessions or similar benefits from manufacturers, pharmacies, or similar entities obtained by an intermediary contracting organization with which the Part D plan sponsor has contracted, regardless of whether the intermediary contracting organization retains all or a portion of the DIR or passes the entire DIR to the Part D plan sponsor.”
42 CFR 423.100

Although section 1860D-12(h)(1)(A)(iii) of the Act refers to “rebates, discounts, and other price concessions,” we believe it is reasonable to interpret those terms by reference to the existing Part D definitions of “price concession” at
42 CFR 423.100

42 CFR 423.308

Therefore, we propose, at

Under that interpretation, the exception applies only to the subset of price concessions and DIR that are: (1) received by a PBM or PBM affiliate from a manufacturer; (2) attributable to covered Part D drug utilization; (3) fully passed through to the Part D plan sponsor; and (4) compliant with applicable regulatory and subregulatory DIR requirements under Part D. Remuneration from non-manufacturer entities would not qualify for this exception as proposed.
In determining when a payment is “fully passed through,” an important principle can be derived from the existing Part D framework. Under
42 CFR 423.308

d. Rule of Construction
As discussed earlier in section 6 of this proposed rule, section 1860D-12(h)(1)(A)(i) of the Act establishes the general remuneration restriction for PBMs and PBM affiliates. Under that provision, a PBM or PBM affiliate may not derive remuneration in connection with services provided on behalf of an entity or individual and related to the utilization of Part D drugs, unless the remuneration is a bona fide service fee, subject to section 1860D-12(h)(1)(A)(ii) or (iii) of the Act.
Section 1860D-12(h)(4) of the Act includes a rule of construction addressing certain pharmacy and wholesaler payment arrangements. Specifically, section 1860D-12(h)(4)(A) of the Act provides that nothing in subsection (h) of the Act shall be construed as prohibiting flat dispensing fees or reimbursement or payment for ingredient costs, including customary, industry-standard discounts directly related to drug acquisition that are retained by pharmacies or wholesalers, to entities that acquire or dispense prescription drugs. Section 1860D-12(h)(4)(B) of the Act further provides that nothing in subsection (h) of the Act shall be construed as modifying regulatory requirements or subregulatory program instruction or guidance related to pharmacy payment, reimbursement, or dispensing fees.
We propose to codify the statute's rule of construction at proposed § 423.2810(i). Specifically, we propose to codify at proposed § 423.2810(i)(1) that the requirements for remuneration to PBMs and their affiliates to be codified at proposed § 423.2810 would not prohibit flat dispensing fees, or reimbursement or payment for ingredient costs, including customary, industry-standard discounts directly related to drug acquisition that are retained by pharmacies or wholesalers, to entities that acquire or dispense prescription drugs. Additionally, we propose to codify at proposed § 423.2810(i)(2) that the requirements for PBM remuneration codified at proposed § 423.2810 do not modify regulatory requirements or sub-regulatory program instructions or guidance related to pharmacy payment, reimbursement, or dispensing fees.
As discussed previously, PBMs may operate as part of vertically integrated entities or other ownership and control relationships with retail pharmacies, mail order pharmacies, specialty pharmacies, long-term care pharmacies, or wholesalers as described in proposed § 423.2806(a). PBMs may also have functional relationships under which a pharmacy or wholesaler may be an affiliate of the PBM as described in proposed § 423.2806(b). While the rule of construction excludes specific pharmacy and wholesaler payments from the requirements of subsection (h) of the Act, the rule of construction does not create a blanket exemption whereby all payments to pharmacies or wholesalers that are affiliated with a PBM are automatically exempted from the PBM and affiliate remuneration requirements of section 1860D-12(h) of the Act. Rather, the rule of construction is a constraint on the application of the requirements of section 1860D-12(h) of the Act in the specific circumstances identified by statute.
Accordingly, the rule of construction being codified at proposed § 423.2810(i)(1) would limit the application of the remuneration restrictions at section 1860D-12(h)(1)(A) of the Act to a wholesaler or pharmacy that is an affiliate of a PBM in those particular circumstances in which the application of the remuneration restrictions would prohibit dispensing fees, reimbursement, or payments directly protected by statute. Likewise, the rule of construction being codified at proposed § 423.2810(i)(2) would limit the application of the remuneration restrictions at section 1860D-12(h)(1)(A) of the Act in those particular circumstances in which the application of the remuneration restrictions would not be consistent with an applicable regulation, program instruction or guidance that establishes requirements for pharmacy payment, reimbursement or dispensing fees without modification to such regulation, program instruction or guidance. We believe this approach will appropriately restrict remuneration to PBMs and their affiliates, while continuing to allow pharmacies, including pharmacies affiliated with a PBM, to receive and retain without modification those particular payments, reimbursement and dispensing fees where such remuneration is expressly permitted under applicable regulation, program instruction or guidance. We offer two examples of specific circumstances where the rule of construction is implicated.
First, a pharmacy, including a pharmacy affiliated with a PBM, may receive and retain reimbursement from a Part D plan sponsor for dispensing a covered Part D drug when the reimbursement reflects a negotiated price equal to a pricing standard such as average wholesale price, plus a flat dispensing fee. Reimbursement for dispensing a covered Part D drug is a payment that would fall within the rule of construction in section 1860D-12(h)(4)(A) of the Act to be codified at proposed § 423.2810(i)(1) and would not be constrained under the proposed restrictions on remuneration described in proposed § 423.2810(a) through (d) even if the remuneration is paid to a pharmacy that is affiliated with a PBM.
Second, the CMS program instructions to implement the Medicare Drug Price Negotiation Program establish specific parameters under which a Primary Manufacturer may make a retrospective MFP refund to a pharmacy or other dispensing entity to provide access to the MFP for a selected drug.

e. Disgorgement of Remuneration to the Part D Plan Sponsor
Section 1860D-12(h)(1)(A)(v) of the Act, as added by the CAA, provides that the written agreement between the Part D plan sponsor and PBM require that the PBM shall disgorge to the Part D plan sponsor any remuneration paid to such PBM or an affiliate of such PBM in violation of the requirements described at section 1860D-12(h)(1)(A) of the Act. We interpret this requirement to mean that if remuneration received by a PBM or affiliate of such PBM is in violation of the requirements described at section 1860D-12(h)(1)(A) of the Act, the total amount of such remuneration should be disgorged to the PDP sponsor. For example, if a PBM were to receive a manufacturer rebate in connection with a covered Part D drug and did not fully pass through the rebate to the Part D plan sponsor in accordance with section 1860D-12(h)(1)(A)(iii), the rebate, inclusive of both the portion already passed through to the Part D plan sponsor and the portion that was retained by the PBM, would be considered remuneration in violation of such requirements and must be disgorged by the PBM to the Part D plan sponsor, which in turn must disgorge the same amount to CMS as discussed at proposed § 423.2920(a). As another example, if an audit by a Part D plan sponsor were to identify that remuneration paid by an entity to a PBM was not in compliance with bona fide service fee requirements because it was not reflective of fair market value, all such remuneration must be disgorged to the Part D plan sponsor. We propose to codify this requirement at § 423.2810(g).
We considered an alternative interpretation through which only the amount of remuneration in excess of what the remuneration would have been had it been compliant with the requirements described at section 1860D-12(h)(1)(A) of the Act would be required to be disgorged to the Part D plan sponsor. Under this alternative, the PBM or affiliate of such PBM would have identified the counterfactual remuneration that would have been compliant with the requirements described at section 1860D-12(h)(1)(A) of the Act, and CMS could request documentation of the assumptions and methodology used to determine the amount of remuneration that was in violation and require modifications as determined necessary by CMS. For example, under this alternative, if remuneration received by a PBM did not meet the bona fide service fee requirements because it was not reflective of fair market value, the PBM would determine what amount the remuneration would have been had it been reflective of fair market value and would disgorge the difference between that counterfactual amount and the actual amount of remuneration to the PDP sponsor. We did not propose this interpretation for several reasons. First, section 1860D-12(h)(1)(A)(v) of the Act applies the disgorgement requirement to “any remuneration paid to such pharmacy benefit manager or an affiliate of such pharmacy benefit manager in violation of this subparagraph”, not the difference between the violative amount and a counterfactually non-violative amount. Additionally, determining a methodology to calculate the counterfactually non-violative amount could be complex, for example if the remuneration violated the requirements at section 1860D-12(h)(1)(A) of the Act in multiple ways. Finally, remuneration is typically negotiated between parties to a contract, and it may be difficult to determine a counterfactual amount outside of that negotiation process.
We solicit comment on our interpretation of this requirement at section 1860D-12(h)(1)(A)(v) of the Act.
Section 1860D-12(h)(1)(A)(vi) of the Act requires that the PBM enter into an agreement with any affiliate of such PBM, under which the affiliate must identify and disgorge any remuneration paid to the affiliate in violation of the requirements described at section 1860D-12(h)(1)(A) of the Act to the PBM. We propose to codify this requirement at § 423.2810(g)(3). The same section also requires that the PBM attest, subject to any requirements determined appropriate by the Secretary, that the PBM has entered into such a written agreement with any affiliate of such PBM. We propose to require that the written agreement between the Part D plan sponsor and the PBM include this attestation at § 423.2810(g)(3)(i).

f. Evaluation of Remuneration Agreements
Section 1860D-12(h)(1)(A)(iv) of the Act, as added by section 6224 of the CAA, provides that components of subsets of remuneration arrangements, such as fees or other forms of compensation paid to or retained by the PBM or affiliate of the PBM, between PBMs or PBM affiliates and other entities involved in the dispensing or utilization of covered Part D drugs shall be subject to review by the Secretary, in consultation with the Office of Inspector General of the Department of Health and Human Services (OIG), as determined appropriate by the Secretary. Section 1860D-12(h)(1)(A)(iv) of the Act further provides that the Secretary, in consultation with OIG, shall review whether remuneration under such arrangements is consistent with fair market value, as specified by the Secretary.
As discussed in section II.C.3. of this proposed rule, we propose at § 423.2810(e)(1) to define fair market value for bona fide service fees based on the cost of the itemized service plus a reasonable markup to total cost. We also propose that, if observed cost data are not available, the fair market value for bona fide service fees may be based on expected cost plus a reasonable markup until sufficient observed cost data become available.
We propose to establish a two-part process for CMS to collect the information necessary to review whether remuneration arrangements involving PBMs and PBM affiliates are consistent with fair market value, as described at proposed § 423.2810(e), and otherwise comply with section 1860D-12(h) of the Act. This process would take place following the submission of the annual PBM reports, as proposed at § 423.2814.
In the first part of the process, CMS would identify a subset of PBMs for which components of a subset of their remuneration arrangements will be reviewed using a two-pronged sampling approach. First, CMS would review the annual PBM report, as proposed at § 423.2814, and any other available information to identify PBMs whose reported data warrant additional review. Second, to promote review of a broad range of PBM remuneration arrangements over time, CMS would also select a random sample of PBMs. For each PBM selected under either prong, CMS would select a sample of Part D plan sponsors with which the selected PBM has a written agreement to act on behalf of the Part D plan sponsor. All remuneration agreements held by the selected PBM, as well as those held by a sample of any affiliates of such PBM (selected by CMS from the list of affiliates reported by the PBM under the annual report described at § 423.2814), with any individual or entity, under which the PBM or affiliate of such PBM receives remuneration for services in connection with Part D drug benefits of the plan of that Part D plan sponsor would be subject to review. We propose at § 423.2810(f)(8) and § 423.2810(f)(9) this process for selecting PBMs and subsets of the remuneration arrangements of such PBMs and their affiliates for submission and review.
CMS would notify each selected PBM and, as described in proposed § 423.2810(f)(4), each selected PBM would be required to include in the summary of components of subsets of remuneration arrangements required to be submitted in the form and manner, and by the deadline, specified by CMS, all components of remuneration arrangements described in proposed § 423.2810(f)(9), that is, all remuneration arrangements between itself or any of its selected affiliates and any other individual or entity under which the PBM or affiliate of such PBM receives remuneration for services in connection with the utilization of Part D drugs by enrollees in a prescription drug plan offered by such Part D plan sponsor. As described in proposed § 423.2810(f)(4)(ii), the summary of components of subsets of remuneration arrangements must identify each remuneration arrangement at the level needed to identify and classify each distinct remuneration structure and classify amounts received or retained by the selected PBM or its selected affiliates. Proposed § 423.2810(f)(4)(iii) would establish specific information that the PBM must include in its summary, for each remuneration arrangement and payment stream. We propose the PBM's summary must include the following information: the payer of the remuneration; the recipient of the remuneration; the affiliate status of the payer and recipient in relation to the PBM; the applicable Part D plan sponsor, contract, and plan; the service or payment category for the remuneration; a brief description of the remuneration arrangement or payment stream; the total amount of remuneration paid, received, and retained by the recipient; the amount of remuneration attributable to the utilization of covered Part D drugs; and the unit of payment or fee methodology used by the payer to determine the amount of remuneration. We propose the PBM's summary must also address: whether the arrangement or payment stream covers multiple services, entities, functions, or both Part D and non-Part D lines of business and whether the arrangement or payment stream is bundled, and, if applicable, must provide information regarding these aspects of the arrangement or payment. We propose the PBM's summary must classify remuneration under each arrangement or payment as a bona fide service fee, incentive payment, fully passed-through rebate, discount or other price concession, protected amount as described in the rule of construction at § 423.2810(i), or other remuneration. In addition, as described at proposed § 423.2810(f)(4)(iv), the PBM's summary would also be required to provide a crosswalk sufficient for CMS to identify the location in the remuneration agreement where each of those elements may be found.

7. Transparency Regarding Guarantees and Cost Performance Evaluations
Section 1860D-12(h)(1)(B) of the Act, as added by the CAA, requires that for plan years beginning on or after January 1, 2028, each contract entered into with a Part D plan sponsor under section 1860D-12 with respect to a prescription drug plan offered by such sponsor shall provide that any PBM acting on behalf of such sponsor has a written agreement with the Part D plan sponsor under which the PBM agrees to define, interpret, and apply terms in a fully transparent and consistent manner, for purposes of calculating or otherwise evaluating PBM performance against pricing guarantees or similar cost performance measurements.
Pricing guarantees are a common feature of agreements between Part D plan sponsors and PBMs in which PBMs guarantee an effective rate, often expressed in terms of a percent off a reported price, paid by the Part D plan sponsor across a category of drugs, such as generic, brand, or specialty drugs.
[
44
]
For example, PBMs may guarantee to Part D plan sponsors an effective rate of 25percent off average wholesale price for all brand drugs; the PBM would reconcile actual payments for ingredient cost of such drugs against the guaranteed price across the entire category of drugs by reimbursing the Part D plan sponsor for any excess payment or retaining the difference between the guarantee and the lower amount paid to the PBM. However, imprecise or non-standardized definitions of terms such as “brand”, “generic”, or “specialty” may allow PBMs to categorize drug products in ways that maximize their ability to retain revenue via effective rate guarantees.
[
45
]
For example, if a PBM were to guarantee 60 percent off average wholesale price for generic drugs but only 20 percent off average wholesale price for specialty drugs, assuming that the PBM paid pharmacies less than the guaranteed rate for a given drug, the PBM could retain more of the difference between the guaranteed rate and the amount paid to the pharmacy if it were to categorize the drug as a specialty drug rather than a generic drug.
PBM revenue retained via pricing guarantees as described previously would not meet the requirements of bona fide service fees introduced by section 1860D-12(h)(1)(A) of the Act, since such revenue would be contingent upon both the price of the drug and DIR. However, section 1860D-12(h)(1)(A)(ii) of the Act provides that an incentive payment paid by a Part D plan sponsor to a PBM or an affiliate of such PBM that is performing services on behalf of such sponsor may be deemed a `bona fide service fee' if it meets certain

We are also proposing at § 423.2812(b) that definitions of such terms be included in the written agreement between Part D plan sponsors and PBMs and that PBMs provide a list of drugs, including the NDC-11 or NDC-12 identifier of each drug, included in each category including “generic drug”, “brand name drug”, “specialty drug”, or any other categories of drugs for which PBM performance against pricing guarantees or similar cost performance metrics is measured to Part D plan sponsors, upon request of the Part D plan sponsor, not less than annually.

We propose at § 423.2812(c) to require that the PBM provide such a list of drugs, claims, or price concessions to Part D plan sponsors with sufficient information for the Part D plan sponsor to clearly identify such drugs, claims, or price concessions—including NDC-11 or NDC-12 identifiers for such drugs, identifying information about such claims such as date of service and beneficiary identifier, and information about such price concessions such as the amount of the price concession and the drug(s) to which it applies—upon request of the Part D plan sponsor, not less than annually.
Section 1860D-12(h)(1)(B)(iii) of the Act requires that where a pricing guarantee or other cost performance measure is based on a pricing benchmark other than the wholesale acquisition cost (as defined in section 1847A(c)(6)(B) of the Act) of a drug, the PBM calculate and provide a wholesale acquisition cost-based equivalent to the pricing guarantee or other cost performance measure. 9. Written Explanation of Contracts or Agreements With Manufacturers
Section 1860D-12(h)(1)(C)(iii) of the Act, as added by the CAA, provides that not later than 30 days after the finalization of any contract or agreement between a PBM or an affiliate of such PBM and a manufacturer (or subsidiary, agent, or entity affiliated with such manufacturer) that makes rebates, discounts, payments, or other financial incentives related to one or more covered Part D drugs or other prescription drugs, as applicable, of the manufacturer directly or indirectly contingent upon coverage, formulary placement, or utilization management conditions on any other covered Part D drugs or other prescription drugs, as applicable, such PBM shall submit to the Part D plan sponsor a written explanation of such contract or agreement. It further specifies that such written explanation shall include the manufacturer subject to the contract or agreement, all covered Part D drugs and other prescription drugs, as applicable, subject to the contract or agreement and the manufacturers of such drugs, and a high-level description of the terms of such contract or agreement and how such terms apply to such drugs. We propose to adopt these requirements at § 423.2816(a).
Further, we propose at § 423.2816(c) that the high-level description of the terms of such contract or agreement describe the methodology by which the rebates, discounts, payments, or other financial incentives related to one or more Part D drugs or other prescription drugs is directly or indirectly contingent on coverage, formulary placement, or utilization management conditions on any other Part D drugs or other prescription drugs. 10. Audit Rights
Section 1860D-12(h)(1)(D) of the Act provides that not less than annually, at the request of the Part D plan sponsor, the PBM allow for an audit of the PBM to ensure compliance with all terms and conditions of the written agreement required by section 1860D-12(h)(1) of the Act and the accuracy of data reported under section 1860D-12(h)(1)(C) of the Act. It further provides that the Part D plan sponsor shall have the right to select an auditor and that the PBM shall not impose any limitations on the selection of such auditor. It additionally provides that the PBM shall make available to such auditor all records, data, contracts, and other information necessary to confirm the accuracy of information reported under section 1860D-12(h)(1)(C) of the Act, subject to reasonable restrictions on how such information must be reported to prevent redisclosure of such information. We propose to adopt these requirements at § 423.2818.
We note that while section 1860D-12(h)(1)(D)(i) of the Act describes the audit as encompassing both compliance with all terms and conditions of the written agreement required by section 1860D-12(h)(1) of the Act and the accuracy of data reported under section 1860D-12(h)(1)(C) of the Act, section 1860D-12(h)(1)(D)(iii) of the Act, which describes the information to be provided, only addresses records, data, contracts, and other information necessary to confirm the accuracy of information reported under section 1860D-12(h)(1)(C) of the Act. We do not interpret section 1860D-12(h)(1)(D)(iii) of the Act to mean that PBMs are not required to provide information related to compliance with all terms and conditions of the written agreement required by section 1860D-12(h)(1) of the Act as requested by the auditor. Rather, we interpret it to mean that a PBM may not refuse to provide records, data, contracts, and other information necessary to confirm the accuracy of information reported under section 1860D-12(h)(1)(C) of the Act under the logic that such PBM has already reported data to the Part D plan sponsor as required under section 1860D-12(h)(1)(C) of the Act. In other words, the reporting of data under section 1860D-12(h)(1)(C) of the Act is not equivalent to reporting sufficient information to support an audit. However, we do not believe that this clarification suggests that PBMs are not required to provide information related to compliance with all terms and conditions of the written agreement required by section 1860D-12(h)(1) of the Act as requested by the auditor.
Further, we propose at § 423.2818(c)(2) that such reasonable restrictions may address the types of records, data, contracts, and other information to be reported; the manner of reporting such information; and the use, disclosure, and dispensing of such information by the auditor and the Part D plan sponsor. They may not include requirements that wholly prevent the auditor from accessing records, data, contracts, and other information that are necessary to confirm the accuracy of information reported under section 1860D-12(h)(1)(C) of the Act.
Section 1860D-12(h)(1)(D)(iv) of the Act provides that the PBM must provide such information and other information, data, and records relevant to the audit to such auditor within 6 months of the initiation of the audit and respond to requests for additional information from such auditor within 30 days after the request for additional information. We propose to adopt this requirement at § 423.2818(d).
Finally, section 1860D-12(h)(1)(D)(v) of the Act provides that the PBM shall be responsible for providing to such auditor information required to be reported under proposed § 423.2814 or under § 423.2818(c) that is owned or held by an affiliate of such PBM. We propose to adopt this requirement at § 423.2818(e).

13. Severability
The Modernizing and Ensuring Pharmacy Benefit Manager Accountability provisions proposed herein at § 423.2800 through § 423.2822 are separate and severable from one another. If any of these provisions, once finalized, is held to be invalid or unenforceable by its terms, or as applied to any person or circumstance, or stayed pending further agency action, it is our intention that such provision would be severable from this rule and not affect the remainder thereof, or the application of such provision to other persons not similarly stated or to other, dissimilar circumstances. For example, if finalized, should the requirements for the timing of the disgorgement of fees proposed herein be deemed invalid or unenforceable, the underlying obligation under current statute would continue.
