B. Proposed Information Collection Requirements (ICRs)
The following ICRs are listed in the order of appearance within this proposed rule.
1. ICRs Regarding REAL Health Providers Act (Section 6220 of the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2026) (§§ 422.2, 422.111, 422.123, and 422.124)
The following proposed changes will be submitted to OMB under control number 0938-10981 (CMS-TBD) At this time the OMB control number has not been determined, but it will be assigned by OMB upon their clearance of our proposed collection of information request. The control number's expiration date will be issued by OMB upon their approval of our final rule's collection of information request.
We are proposing several requirements related to the REAL Health Providers Act, which is part of section 6220 of the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2026, effective for contract year 2028. Topics in this proposal include provider directory verification, updating, accuracy analysis, accuracy scoring, reporting, public transparency, enrollee cost sharing protections, and disclosure. Through these proposed codifications implementing the REAL Health Providers Act, CMS seeks to promote provider directory accuracy and accountability among MA organizations to ensure that beneficiaries are provided with clear, accurate information on the network of providers available to meet their health care needs.
a. ICRs Regarding Provider Directory Verification, Updating, and Disclosure (§§ 422.2, 422.123(b) Through (c) and 422.111(b)(12) and (k)(6))
CMS's proposed provider directory verification requirements (§ 422.123(b)) would require MA organizations to verify the provider directory information of each provider listed in a specified MA plan's provider directory at least every 90 days, or every 12 months for specified hospitals and facilities, using one or more CMS-specified verification methods. Provider directory information that cannot be verified would be identified in the provider directory as potentially out of date. Proposed § 422.123(b)(4) would also require MA organizations to include a new contract term obligating contracted providers to maintain current and accurate provider directory information. CMS's proposed provider directory updating requirements at § 422.123(c) would retain the existing 30-day update standard, require a quarterly addendum containing updates for all enrollees who requested physical hardcopy directories, require a disclaimer on physical hardcopy provider directories directing beneficiaries to the online provider directory or the MA organization for the latest updates, and require removal of non-contracted providers within 5 business days. Proposed disclosure requirements at §§ 422.111(b)(12) and (k)(6) would require provider directory disclosures regarding cost sharing protections and the accuracy score, as well as a cost sharing protection notice in the first EOB of each plan year.
For most of the proposed provider directory changes, CMS expects that MA organizations would build upon existing provider directory processes rather than develop entirely new processes. Existing § 422.111(b)(3)(i) requires MA organizations to disclose the number, mix, and distribution of providers from whom enrollees may reasonably be expected to obtain services and each provider's cultural and linguistic capabilities. Existing § 422.111(m), finalized in the September 2025 final rule (
90 FR 45140
), further requires MA organizations to make the information described in § 422.111(b)(3)(i) available to CMS/HHS for publication in MPF, update that information within 30 days after becoming aware of a change, and attest to its accuracy at least annually. The information collection for these MPF submission, formatting, and attestation requirements is approved under OMB control number 0938-1491 (CMS-10906).
As CMS explained in the September 2025 final rule, CMS's operational guide would specify how MA organizations must format and submit provider directory data, and the current Technical Implementation Guide identifies data points used for MPF, including provider or facility NPI and name, specialty or facility type, MA plan identifier, address, telephone number, practitioner languages, and whether a practitioner is accepting new patients. Existing provider directory content is also specified in the Medicare Advantage and Section 1876 Cost Plan Provider Directory Model and Instructions. For example, the model requires provider name, specialty, address, telephone number, cultural and linguistic capabilities, and information identifying whether providers are accepting new patients or directing beneficiaries to contact the provider. The model also addresses accessibility restrictions and telehealth capabilities. Therefore, the proposed definition of “provider directory information” at § 422.2 largely consolidates and standardizes information already addressed through existing provider directory requirements and guidance, including provider name, specialty, contact information, address, accepting new patients status, accommodations for people with disabilities, cultural and linguistic capabilities, and telehealth capabilities.
We are also proposing to add “common ownership or control disclosure” as a provider directory information element at § 422.2. Because this information is not part of the existing MPF provider directory data submission, CMS preliminarily estimates that it would take an MA organization 1.5 hours at $90.36/hr for a business operations specialist to identify applicable ownership or common-control relationships. With 708 contracts, CMS estimates an annual burden of 1,062 hours (708 MA organization contracts × 1.5 hr/response) at a cost of $95,962 (1,062 hr × $90.36/hr). CMS assumes MA organizations would use ownership and affiliation information they already maintain. If they need to confirm this information with a provider, that time would be included in the verification burden discussed later in this section. CMS seeks comments on these assumptions, including the time needed to identify, maintain, verify, and disclose ownership/affiliation information and whether MA organizations or providers would incur additional burden.
(
printed page 66464)
CMS believes that some routine administrative activities associated with maintaining provider directory information may qualify as usual and customary business practices under
5 CFR 1320.3(b)(2)
and, therefore, may be exempt from review by OMB under the authority of the PRA of 1995 (
44 U.S.C. 3501
et seq.
). However, CMS would assess any additional burden resulting from proposed requirements that go beyond existing practices. Although the data elements contained within the proposed definition of “provider directory information” at § 422.2 largely overlap with existing provider directory requirements and guidance, CMS would consider burden associated with any expansion in the information required and, in particular, changes to the frequency and manner of verification, updating, disclosure, or submission.
The proposed verification requirements may also impose burden on contracted providers. Proposed § 422.123(b)(4) would require MA organizations to include a new contract term obligating contracted providers to maintain current and accurate provider directory information. Because this is a new contractual requirement, CMS does not consider the burden associated with modifying existing provider contracts to be covered by the usual and customary business practice exemption. CMS estimates a one-time burden of 3 hours per MA organization contract to add the new proposed contract term. Across 708 contracts, this results in a one-time burden of 2,124 hours (708 contracts × 3 hr) at a cost of $191,925 (2,124 hr × $90.36/hr).
The proposed provider directory verification activities of MA organizations under § 422.123(b)(2) may also require providers to review, confirm, correct, or attest to provider directory information. To estimate the additional burden from recurring verification, CMS assumes each direct verification contact would take about 15 minutes for the provider and 15 minutes for the MA organization. This would result in up to 1 hour annually for providers verified every 90 days and 15 minutes annually for specified hospitals and facilities verified every 12 months. These estimates exclude verification using existing plan information or CMS-maintained data sources. We seek comments on these assumptions, including the frequency of direct provider contacts, time required, verification methods used, and the extent to which these activities exceed current practices.
Proposed § 422.123(c)(4)(i) would also require MA organizations to remove a provider from the provider directory no later than 5 business days after determining that the provider is no longer participating in the specified MA plan's network, rather than under the existing 30-day update standard. CMS estimates that meeting the shorter timeframe would add about 15 minutes of administrative work for each provider removal. CMS cannot estimate the total burden because it does not know how many providers are removed each year or how many MA organizations already meet the 5-business day timeframe. We seek comments on these assumptions, including the number of removals, current practices, and the time and cost needed to meet the proposed requirement.
b. ICRs Regarding Provider Directory Accuracy Analysis and Accuracy Score (§ 422.123(d)(1) Through (4))
At § 422.123(d)(1) through (4), CMS is proposing new requirements for MA organizations offering specified MA plans to conduct an annual provider directory accuracy analysis for each specified MA plan using a random sample of provider directory listings, including providers with provider specialty types with high provider directory inaccuracy rates, and to estimate an annual provider directory accuracy score based on such analysis. Although the proposed requirements would add some new burden for MA organizations, the requirements are designed to build upon the existing provider directory framework.
For each specified MA plan, MA organizations would use a random sample consisting of 65 percent of records in the provider directory, excluding records for providers with provider specialty types with high provider directory inaccuracy rates, and 35 percent of records for providers with provider specialty types with high provider directory inaccuracy rates, using the sampling methodology specified by CMS.
MA organizations would verify provider directory data elements for sampled providers using CMS's specified verification methods, subject to any applicable limitations on the methods that may be used to verify each provider directory element for purposes of calculating the accuracy score. Following verification, for each specified MA plan, MA organizations would calculate the accuracy percentage for each scored provider directory element, apply the applicable provider directory element weight, combine the weighted results to calculate the final composite score, and round the result to the nearest whole number to determine the final provider directory accuracy
(
printed page 66465)
score, in accordance with the scoring methodology specified by CMS.
CMS estimates the burden for the annual provider directory accuracy analysis and accuracy score based on the number of specified MA plans offered under an MA parent organization. CMS used available 2026 data to estimate the number of specified MA plans and the number of MA parent organizations in each grouping. For MA parent organizations with 10 or fewer specified MA plans, CMS estimates 13 hours per response at $90.36/hr for a business operations specialist. With 113 respondents, CMS estimates an annual burden of 1,469 hours (113 respondents × 13 hr/response) at a cost of $132,739 (1,469 hr × $90.36/hr).
For contracts with 11 to 50 specified MA plans, CMS estimates 20 hours per response. With 38 respondents, CMS estimates an annual burden of 760 hours (38 respondents × 20 hr/response) at a cost of $68,674 (760 hr × $90.36/hr).
For contracts with 51 or more specified MA plans, CMS estimates 30 hours per response. With 12 respondents, CMS estimates an annual burden of 360 hours (12 respondents × 30 hr/response) at a cost of $32,530 (360 hr × $90.36/hr).
The estimated hours reflect that MA parent organizations with more specified MA plans would have an increasing amount of effort, including developing plan-level samples, calculating plan-level scores, and performing quality assurance. CMS assumes that all MA parent organizations would consolidate samples across the organization and would not need to repeat verification when the same record appears in multiple plan samples, which would lower the burden for the MA parent organization as they would only need to verify the record once and could count that verification in the calculation of each of the plan accuracy scores where the record appears. As the number of specified MA plans that an MA parent organization has increases, CMS assumes that MA parent organizations would develop efficiencies related to developing plan-level samples and calculating plan-level accuracy scores, limiting the overall burden associated with these activities for each additional plan. We seek comments on these burden estimates and assumptions used, including the time required to develop the plan-level sample, conduct the accuracy analysis, and calculate plan-level accuracy scores. CMS also seeks comments on the groupings based on the number of plans an MA parent organization has and whether the cut points for the groupings represent reasonable burden estimates for each grouping.
Because certain sampling, verification, and scoring requirements remain subject to comment and finalization, the burden estimate may change. Final decisions on sample size and timing, verification requirements, and the scoring methodology could affect the amount and complexity of work required to complete the provider directory accuracy analysis. We may revise the burden estimate based on comments received and the finalized
(
printed page 66466)
requirements. The burden estimate may also need to account for finalized requirements concerning provider non-response, use of additional permitted verification methods, replacement records, minimum response rates, and sample size parameters.
c. ICRs Regarding Provider Directory Accuracy Report (§ 422.123(d)(5))
At § 422.123(d)(5), CMS is proposing that MA organizations offering specified MA plans must submit to CMS an annual provider directory accuracy report containing the results of the accuracy analysis and the provider directory accuracy score for each specified MA plan. CMS is proposing that the report must be submitted not later than the first Monday in April of the year following the contract year being measured, in a form and manner specified by CMS. CMS seeks comments on these burden

d. ICRs Regarding Enrollee Cost Sharing Protections When Provider Directories Are Inaccurate (§ 422.124)
CMS is proposing to codify the new requirements at § 422.124 such that beginning with contract year 2028, MA organizations offering specified MA plans will be required to: (1) include a term in each provider contract obligating the provider to supply documentation of the earliest date on which the enrollee's appointment was made; (2) maintain a daily archive of provider directory data for not less than 10 years and make such records available to CMS upon request within 5 business days; (3) process enrollee requests for cost sharing protections as organization determinations or reconsideration requests; and (4) issue refunds to enrollees when cost sharing is collected in excess of the permitted amount.
Section 422.124(d) would require MA organizations offering specified MA plans to include a term in each provider contract for a specified MA plan obligating the provider to supply documentation of the earliest date on which the enrollee's appointment was scheduled, regardless of any rescheduling. MA organizations would then be required to obtain the scheduling documentation from the provider to determine whether the cost sharing protection applies. To comply with this requirement, each MA organization will need to review its existing provider contracts to incorporate the new contractual language. We estimate that adding the contract provision to each specified MA plan would require 3 hours at $90.36/hr for a business operations specialist. We estimate a one-time burden of 2,124 hours (708 MA organization contracts × 3 hr) at a cost of $191,925 (2,124 hr × $90.36/hr).
Section 422.124(e) would require MA organizations offering specified MA plans to confirm whether the enrollee is eligible for the provider directory cost sharing protection by maintaining and referencing a daily archive of the provider directory sufficient to identify whether a provider was listed in the directory at any time on a given date for not less than 10 years. Additionally, MA organizations would be required to make provider directory records available to CMS upon request within 5 business days. CMS estimates that establishing and maintaining a daily automated archive of provider directory data would require an initial one-time system build and an ongoing annual maintenance burden. MA organizations would need to develop or modify existing IT infrastructure to capture and store a daily snapshot of specified MA plan provider directories in a format sufficient to identify whether a provider was listed on any given date. CMS believes most MA organizations have existing data warehousing capabilities that could be adapted for this purpose, given other record retention obligations of MA organizations required by CMS.
The one-time system development burden is estimated to take approximately 40 hours at $142.40/hr for a software developer. CMS estimates a one-time burden of 28,320 hours (708 MA organization contracts × 40 hr) and $4,032,768 (28,320 hr × $142.40/hr).
Ongoing maintenance including storage management, quality checks, and responding to CMS records requests is estimated to take 10 hours at $142.40/hr for a software developer. CMS estimates an annual burden of 7,080 hours (708 MA organization contracts × 10 hr) at a cost of $1,008,192 (7,080 hr × $142.40/hr). CMS seeks comments on whether these estimates accurately reflect the operational burden of daily archiving, particularly for smaller MA organizations.

IV. Regulatory Impact Analysis
A. Statement of Need
This proposed rule addresses several critical needs in the Medicare Advantage (Part C) and Medicare Prescription Drug Benefit (Part D)
(
printed page 66470)
programs that require regulatory action to ensure program integrity, beneficiary protection, and statutory compliance. Specifically, this rule consists of proposals intended to codify and implement certain statutory requirements of the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2026 (CAA).
Proposed changes implementing section 6219 of the CAA (Adjustments to Medicare Part D Cost-Sharing Reductions for Low-Income Individuals) would reduce the generic drug copayment from for full-benefit dual eligible individuals. This rulemaking would reduce the generic drug copayment from $1 to $0 for full-benefit dual eligible individuals at or below 100 percent of the Federal Poverty Level, effective for plan years starting January 1, 2028.
Proposed changes implementing section 6220 of the CAA (Requiring Enhanced and Accurate Lists of (REAL) Health Providers Act) would establish new provider directory accuracy and accountability requirements for MA organizations beginning in contract year 2028. Without regulatory implementation of these statutory requirements, CMS cannot ensure that MA organizations meet their obligations under Federal law to maintain accurate provider directories, nor can CMS provide the beneficiary cost sharing protections and public transparency mechanisms Congress enacted into law. Specifically, the REAL Health Providers Act requires CMS to establish provider directory verification and updating standards, annual accuracy analyses and scoring, submission of accuracy reports to CMS for public posting, and beneficiary notification and cost sharing protections for enrollees who rely on inaccurate directory information.
Proposed changes implementing section 6224 of the CAA (Modernizing and Ensuring Pharmacy Benefit Manager Accountability) would establish new and enhanced requirements governing PBM remuneration, data reporting, pricing transparency, and disclosure of manufacturer agreements within Medicare Part D, along with definitions of key terms and compliance and enforcement mechanisms, including disgorgement of funds to CMS for violations.
The absence of regulatory action would result in statutory non-compliance regarding CAA implementation, ongoing operational inefficiencies, and missed opportunities for program improvement and innovation. Therefore, this rulemaking is necessary to ensure the Medicare program operates effectively, efficiently, and in compliance with Federal law while serving the best interests of Medicare beneficiaries.

1. Adjustments to Medicare Part D Cost-Sharing Reductions for Low-Income Individuals (Section 6219 of the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2026)
This section provides the impact associated with the proposed provision to eliminate the copayment on non-multi-source generic drugs for the $1/$3 low-income subsidy (LIS) beneficiary group. The affected entities include Medicare Part D beneficiaries (specifically full-benefit dual-eligible individuals with incomes at or below 100 percent of the Federal Poverty Level) and the Medicare program. Impacts are quantified using 2025 Prescription Drug Event (PDE) data. We seek public comment on the assumptions and methodologies described below, particularly where data limitations exist.
The potential benefits of this proposed provision include improved medication access and adherence for low-income Medicare Part D beneficiaries, reduced financial burden for vulnerable populations, and potential long-term health outcome improvements associated with increased use of clinically appropriate generic medications. To the extent that the proposal induces switching from brand-name drugs to lower-cost generics, this effect is a transfer—a redistribution of drug spending among the Medicare program and beneficiaries, rather than a net benefit or cost of the provision.

Table IV.2 summarizes the estimated benefit, premium, and net Federal cost impacts of the proposed provision over the 2028-2037 period (in millions of dollars).
The net Federal cost of the proposed provision is estimated at approximately $1.337 billion over the 2028-2037 period, reflecting the direct copay elimination cost net of premium offsets. The benefit impact of $1.461 billion reflects the total increase in Medicare program spending attributable to the three modeled effects. The premium impact of $124 million reflects the partial offset from increased Part D plan premiums resulting from higher program costs.
The elimination of the copayment on non-multi-source generic drugs is a transfer, not a cost of the proposed provision. Beneficiaries in the $1/$3 LIS group who previously paid the copay will no longer bear that cost; the Medicare program will absorb it instead. Consistent with OMB Circular A-4's treatment of subsidies as transfer payments, this direct copay elimination effect redirects existing resources from the Medicare program's financing base to the affected beneficiary population; it does not consume real resources.
To the extent that the proposal induces brand-to-generic switching, there may be a partial offsetting transfer in the form of reduced drug spending—from brand manufacturers to the Medicare program and beneficiaries—as lower-cost generics replace higher-cost brand drugs. This transfer represents a redistribution of drug spending rather than a change in the total resources consumed. This switching effect is assumed to be limited given the relatively modest actual copay differential between brand and generic drugs under the current $1/$3 LIS structure.

3. Modernizing and Ensuring Pharmacy Benefit Manager Accountability (Section 6224 of the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2026)
Section 6224 of the CAA requires that, beginning in plan year 2028, remuneration to PBMs and affiliates of PBMs in connection with the utilization of Part D drugs be limited to bona fide service fees reflecting fair market value, as defined by the Secretary, subject to certain exceptions. The Congressional Budget Office has estimated that this provision would reduce federal direct spending by approximately $444 million over the 2026-2035 period. Contract arrangements between PBMs, Part D plan sponsors, pharmacies, and pharmaceutical manufacturers are complex. The contracts between PBMs and Part D plan sponsors vary widely by the size of the sponsor and vertical integration of some PBM functions has increased in recent years. While it is possible that the fair market value definition proposed in this rule will result in lower service fees, we do not have sufficient data on the difference between the proposed fair market value definition and current fee structures or the range of potential PBM responses to form a reasonable analysis of the overall impact to the Part D program. For PBMs and Part D plan sponsors with common corporate ownership, any changes to the PBM fee structure may be offset by changes to the Part D bid to achieve the same overall target revenue of the parent organization. For PBMs without such a related party arrangement, they may adjust other terms of their agreements with Part D plan sponsors or pharmacies to the extent allowable under current laws and regulations. Alternatively, PBMs could balance lower fees under Medicare with higher fees on other lines of business. Without a more comprehensive understanding of how the fair market value definition relates to current contracting levels and what flexibility the PBMs will have to adjust other contract terms, the impact of this proposed rule is uncertain. We welcome comments regarding the quantification of the impact of these provisions.
D. Alternatives Considered for REAL Health Providers Act (Section 6220 of the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2026)

1. Alternatives Considered for Provider Directory Verification Requirements (§ 422.123(b))
Under proposed § 422.123(b), MA organizations would verify provider directory information using CMS-specified verification methods. CMS considered limiting which verification methods could be used for particular provider directory elements during the routine 90-day and 12-month verification cycles but did not propose these limitations because they could increase administrative burden. CMS proposes limitations for verification conducted for purposes of calculating the accuracy score and may revisit these approaches as provider data sources and the NPD develop. The proposed 12-month verification cycle for specified hospitals and facilities is intended to limit verification burden on both MA organizations and providers. CMS also recognizes that MA organizations may need to use more than one verification method to verify all required provider directory elements, and that direct provider verification may increase burden depending on the method and frequency of contact.
2. Alternatives Considered for Provider Directory Accuracy Analysis and Sampling Methodology (§ 422.123(d)(1) and (2))
Consistent with section 1857(e)(6)(A) of the Act, proposed § 422.123(d)(1) and (2) would require an annual plan-level accuracy analysis using a random sample of providers. CMS considered alternative approaches for identifying high-inaccuracy provider specialty types, geographic stratification, sample size parameters, consolidation of overlapping provider samples, and timing of sample selection. In evaluating these approaches, CMS considered data availability, administrative burden, operational flexibility, comparability across plans, duplicative verification, and potential for gaming. CMS seeks comments on several of these considerations before finalizing the sampling requirements. In particular, CMS recognizes that larger samples could increase burden on MA organizations and providers and intends to consolidate overlapping plan-level samples across an MA organization to reduce duplicative provider contacts. CMS is also considering minimum and maximum sample parameters that balance meaningful accuracy results with administrative burden.
3. Alternatives Considered for Provider Directory Accuracy Score and Scoring Methodology (§ 422.123(d)(3) and (4))
Consistent with section 1857(e)(6)(B) of the Act, proposed § 422.123(d)(3) and (4) would establish verification and weighted scoring requirements for calculating provider directory accuracy scores. CMS considered incorporating results from the routine 90-day and 12-month verification cycles into the accuracy score, alternative approaches for weighting those results relative to the annual sample, and giving greater weight to high-inaccuracy specialty types. CMS did not propose these approaches because they could increase the complexity and burden of the scoring methodology but seeks comments on whether they should be considered. CMS did not propose more complex scoring alternatives that could increase burden on MA organizations and providers.
4. Alternatives Considered for Provider Directory Accuracy Reporting (§ 422.123(d)(5))
Consistent with section 1857(e)(6)(A)(ii) of the Act, proposed § 422.123(d)(5) would require MA organizations to submit an annual provider directory accuracy report to CMS. CMS considered requiring additional reporting elements, including specialty-level response and sampling data and administrative cost information, and whether the accuracy analysis and score should be independently reviewed and certified by a qualified third party. CMS also seeks comments on whether the proposed reporting deadline provides sufficient time for MA organizations to complete the report. Requiring additional reporting elements or independent third-party review and certification could increase reporting and compliance burden beyond the proposed annual report. CMS seeks comments on these considerations, including administrative costs to MA organizations and contracted providers.

G. Impact on Small Businesses—Regulatory Flexibility Act (RFA)
The RFA, as amended, requires agencies to analyze options for regulatory relief of small businesses if a rule has a significant impact on a substantial number of small entities. For purposes of the RFA, small entities include small businesses, nonprofit organizations, and small governmental jurisdictions.
We believe this proposed rule will have a direct economic impact on beneficiaries and health insurance plans. Based on the size standards set by the Small Business Administration (SBA) effective March 17, 2023, (for details, see the Small Business Administration's website at
https://www.sba.gov/​document/​support-table-size-standards
), Direct Health and Medical Insurance Carriers, classified using the NAICS code 524114, have a $47 million threshold for “small size.” Many Medicare Advantage organizations (about 30 to 40 percent) are not-for-profit,

which allows them to qualify as “small entities” so long as they are independently owned and operated and nondominant in their field. We believe all of the not-for-profit organizations qualify as small under the aforementioned criteria. Of the 1,071 businesses using this NAICS code, we believe 799 (or 74.6 percent) are small businesses.
Using CMS's own payment records, we have been able to make estimates as to the minimum size of the smallest Medicare Advantage and Part D insurance contracts. The vast majority of Part D contracts and MA organizations must meet minimum size and financial thresholds that ensures their resilience. Based on payments made for the current year, we estimated that the three smallest MA parent organizations, excluding new entities that are not yet required to fulfill CMS enrollment thresholds, are expected to average over $5 million in total receipts by the end of 2026.
The RFA does not define the terms “significant economic impact” or “substantial number.” The SBA advises that this absence of statutory specificity allows what is “significant” or “substantial” to vary, depending on the problem that is to be addressed in the rulemaking, the rule's requirements, and the preliminary assessment of the rule's impact. Nevertheless, HHS typically considers a “significant economic impact” to be 3 to 5 percent or more of the affected entity's costs or revenues, and a “substantial number” to mean 5 percent or more of affected small entities within a given industry.

1. Operational Aspects of the Medicare Program
To explain our position, we will first note certain operational aspects of the Medicare program. Each year, MA organizations submit a bid for each plan for furnishing Parts A and B benefits and the entire bid amount is paid to the plan by the government through the Medicare Trust Funds, if the plan's bid is below an administratively set benchmark. If the plan's bid exceeds that benchmark, the beneficiary pays the difference in the form of a basic premium (note that, historically, only 2 percent of plans bid above the benchmark, and they contain roughly 1 percent of all plan enrollees). Part D sponsors also submit a bid for each plan, and the payments made to stand-alone Part D plans (PDPs) are covered by the Supplementary Medical Insurance Medicare Trust Fund.
MA plans can also offer enhanced benefits—that is, benefits not covered under Original Medicare. These enhanced benefits are paid for through enrollee premiums, rebates or a combination. Under the statutory payment formula, if the plan bid submitted by an MA organization for furnishing Part A and B benefits is lower than the administratively set benchmark, the government pays a portion of the difference to the plan in the form of a rebate. The rebate must be used to provide supplemental benefits (that is, benefits not covered under Original Medicare) and/or to lower beneficiary cost sharing, Part B or Part D premiums. Some examples of these supplemental benefits include vision, dental, and hearing, fitness and worldwide coverage of emergency and urgently needed services.
Part D sponsors submit bids and plans are paid through a combination of Medicare funds and beneficiary premiums. In addition, for enrolled low-income beneficiaries, Part D plans receive special government payments to cover most of premium and cost sharing amounts those beneficiaries would otherwise pay.
Thus, the cost of providing services by these insurers is funded by the government and, in some cases, by enrollee premiums. As a result, MA plans, Part D plans, Prescription Drug Plans, and PACE organizations are not expected to incur burden or losses since the private companies' costs are being supported by the government and enrolled beneficiaries. This lack of expected burden applies to both large and small health plans.
In addition to the direct costs discussed earlier, there are certain indirect consequences of these provisions which also create impact. We have already explained that 98 percent of MA plans (including MA-PD plans) bid below the benchmark. Thus, their estimated costs for the coming year are fully paid by the Federal Government, given that as previously noted, under the statutory payment formula, if a bid submitted by a MA plan for furnishing Part A and B benefits is lower than the administratively set benchmark, the government pays a portion of the difference to the plan in the form of a beneficiary rebate, which must be used to provide supplemental benefits or lower beneficiary cost sharing or both, Part B or Part D premiums. If the plan's
(
printed page 66475)
bid exceeds the administratively set benchmark, the beneficiary pays the difference in the form of a basic premium. However, as also noted previously, the number of MA plans bidding above the benchmark to whom this burden applies does not meet the RFA criteria of a significant number of firms.
In addition, section 1102(b) of the Act requires us to prepare a regulatory impact analysis if a rule may have a significant impact on the operations of a substantial number of small rural hospitals. For purposes of section 1102(b) of the Act, we define a small rural hospital as a hospital that is located outside of a metropolitan statistical area and has fewer than 100 beds. This analysis must conform to the provisions of section 603 of the RFA. Therefore, the Secretary has certified that this proposed rule would not have a significant impact on the operations of a substantial number of small rural hospitals.
If the provisions of the rule were to cause bids to increase and if the benchmark remains unchanged or increases by less than the bid does, the result could be a reduced rebate. Plans have different ways to address this in the short-term, such as reducing administrative costs, modifying benefit structures, or adjusting profit margins. These decisions may be driven by market forces. Part of the challenge in pinpointing the indirect effects is that there are many other factors combining with the effects of the rule, making it effectively impossible to determine whether a particular policy had a long-term effect on bids, administrative costs, margins, or supplemental benefits.
2. Anticipated Costs and Savings
As indicated in Table IV.1, the proposals described in this rule are expected to result in de minimis costs amounting to approximately $6 million in 2028, with costs of approximately $1.6 million expected in subsequent years. MA organizations and Part D sponsors will be the entities most economically impacted by this rule.
The costs incurred by MA and Part D contracts fall below the HHS significance threshold. For an MA organization that incurred all anticipated costs stemming from the REAL Health Providers Act provisions of this rule, they may be expected to see $17,105 in new costs in 2028 and $10,867 a year thereafter. Measured against the average revenue of the smallest MA parent organizations as identified earlier in this section ($5 million), these new costs resulting from the REAL Health Providers Act provision are expected to reflect less than 3 percent of the affected entity's costs or revenues.
In summation, this proposed rule will not have a significant economic impact on a substantial number of small entities. The vast majority of MA organizations and Part D sponsors are expected to see de minimis costs as a result of this rule.

§ 422.124
Cost sharing protections for reliance on incorrect provider directory information.
(a)
Applicability.
This section applies to a specified MA plan as defined in § 422.2 for contract year 2028 and subsequent contract years.
(b)
General rule.
If an enrollee in a specified MA plan is furnished an item or service by a provider that is not participating in the plan's network but is listed in the plan's online provider directory as defined in § 422.2 on the date on which the appointment is made, and if such item or service would otherwise be covered under the plan if furnished by a provider that is participating in the plan network, the MA organization offering the plan must ensure the enrollee is only responsible for the lesser of—
(1) The amount of cost sharing that would apply if the provider had been participating in the plan network; or
(2) The amount of cost sharing that would otherwise apply.
(c)
Access to cost sharing protections.
The MA organization must apply the protections under paragraph (b) of this section without requiring that an enrollee makes a request when the MA organization knows or reasonably should know that the protections apply.
(1) An enrollee or the enrollee's authorized representative may also submit a request verbally or in writing to their MA organization.
(2) The enrollee request for the cost sharing protections must be treated by the MA organization as an organization determination or reconsideration request, as applicable, consistent with subpart M of this part.
(d)
Documentation for date appointment was made.
Beginning January 1, 2028, consistent with § 422.202(f), MA organizations must include a term in each provider contract for a specified MA plan obligating the provider to supply documentation of the earliest date on which the enrollee's appointment was made, regardless of any subsequent rescheduling.
(1) Acceptable documentation includes—
(i) A paper or electronic record from the provider's scheduling system; or
(ii) A written or electronic confirmation sent to the enrollee or their authorized representative by the provider.
(2) If the documentation described in paragraph (d)(1) of this section is not reasonably obtainable, a signed attestation from the provider accompanied by any available corroborating information, including but not limited to a calendar entry, a referral record, electronic communications, or a phone log, is sufficient to establish the date on which the appointment was made. The contract term required under this paragraph must survive the expiration or termination of the contract between the MA organization and the provider for not less than 10 years beginning on the date the contract expiration or termination becomes effective.
(e)
Provider directory archiving and verification.
The MA organization must verify whether the provider was listed as an in-network provider in the specified MA plan's online provider directory on the date the enrollee's appointment was made, by referencing archived electronic provider directory data maintained online by the MA organization. Archived provider directory data maintained under this paragraph must be—
(1) Sufficient to identify whether any provider was listed in the plan's online directory at any point on a given date;
(2) Retained for not less than 10 years, consistent with the record retention requirements at § 422.504(d); and
(3) Made available to CMS upon request within 5 business days.
(f)
Absence of documentation.
If the MA organization cannot obtain documentation demonstrating the date on which the appointment was made or cannot verify online provider directory data within the applicable standard or expedited organization determination timeframes under subpart M of this part, the provider directory cost sharing protections must be applied in favor of the enrollee. This default application may be reversed if the MA organization is able to clearly demonstrate that the cost sharing protections do not apply.
(g)
Application of cost sharing protections.
(1) If the MA organization collects cost sharing from an enrollee in excess of the amount permitted under the protections, the MA organization must refund the excess amount to the enrollee consistent with § 422.270(b).
(2) The MA organization must treat cost sharing applied under paragraph (b) of this section as in-network cost sharing for purposes of the maximum out-of-pocket limit consistent with § 422.100(f)(4).

Subpart BB—Modernizing and Ensuring Pharmacy Benefit Manager Accountability
§ 423.2800
Basis and scope.
(a)
Basis.
This subpart implements subsection 1860D-12(h) of the Act.
(b)
Scope.
This subpart sets forth the requirements of section 6224 of the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2026, which establishes requirements for prescription drug plans and pharmacy benefit managers in relation to services in connection with the utilization of Part D drugs.
§ 423.2802
Definitions.
As used in this subpart, the following definitions apply:
Affiliate
means, with respect to a pharmacy benefit manager or Part D plan sponsor, any entity that satisfies the ownership or control standard at § 423.2806(a) or the functional relationship standard at § 423.2806(b).
Bona fide service fee
means any payment that meets the requirements of § 423.2810(b).
Fair market value
has the meaning described at § 423.2810(e).
Fully passed through
means that the Part D plan sponsor receives 100 percent of the gross economic value of each manufacturer rebate, discount, or other price concession attributable to Part D drug utilization. A pharmacy benefit manager or affiliate of such pharmacy benefit manager may not reduce, offset, net, hold back, retain, reclassify, or otherwise diminish the
(
printed page 66480)
value passed through to the Part D plan sponsor, including through administrative fees, data fees, aggregation fees, reconciliation charges, or other deductions.
Incentive payment
means any payment that meets the requirements of § 423.2810(c).
Intermediary
means any person or entity in a chain of contractual or delegated relationships, of any length, through which one or more PBM functions are performed on behalf of a Part D plan sponsor or prescription drug plan.
Pharmacy benefit manager (PBM)
means any person or entity that satisfies the general rule in § 423.2804(a).
PBM function
means acting as a price negotiator or group purchaser or managing the prescription drug benefits provided by a Part D plan sponsor or plan, when performed by any person or entity, directly or through an intermediary, on behalf of a Part D plan sponsor or prescription drug plan, including any of the following activities:
(1) Processing and payment of claims for prescription drugs.
(2) Drug utilization review.
(3) Processing of drug prior authorization requests.
(4) Adjudication of appeals or grievances related to the prescription drug benefit.
(5) Contracting with network pharmacies.
(6) Controlling the cost of Part D drugs.
(7) Providing related services.
Related service
means an activity, service, or function that is performed on behalf of a Part D plan sponsor or prescription drug plan and has a direct nexus to the activities described in paragraphs (1) through (6) of the definition of PBM function. An activity, service, or function has a direct nexus to the activities described at (1) through (6) of the definition of PBM function if it is one of the following:
(1) Integral to such activity.
(2) Necessary to carry out such activity.
(3) Performed in support of such activity.
Remuneration
means anything of value, whether provided directly or indirectly, overtly or covertly, in cash or in kind, including but not limited to any of the following:
(1) Monetary payments.
(2) Non-cash consideration.
(3) Administrative fees, data fees, and service fees.
(4) Spread pricing and retained margins.
(5) Rebates, discounts, and chargebacks.
(6) Price concessions, credits, and offsets.
(7) Up-front payments and coupons.
(8) Free or reduced-price goods or services, and goods in kind.
(9) Grants and in-kind benefits.
(10) Guarantee reconciliation amounts.
(11) Interest payments and financing benefits.
(12) Any other direct or indirect financial advantage.
§ 423.2804
Pharmacy benefit manager status.
(a)
General rule.
A person or entity qualifies as a pharmacy benefit manager, regardless of how it describes itself, if it satisfies both of the following conditions:
(1) The person or entity has a written contract with a Part D plan sponsor, either directly or through a parent organization of such Part D plan sponsor.
(2) The person or entity, directly or through an intermediary, performs at least one PBM function, as defined at § 423.2802 on behalf of the Part D plan sponsor or prescription drug plan with which it has such written contract.
(b)
Performance standard.
A person or entity satisfies the performance element of paragraph (a)(2) and (c)(2) of this section upon performing one or more PBM functions on any occasion during a calendar year, regardless of the frequency, volume, regularity, or materiality of such performance.
(c)
Performance through an intermediary.
Any person or entity that causes, arranges, procures, or relies on an intermediary to perform a PBM function is deemed to have performed that function for purposes of this subpart. A person or entity qualifies as a pharmacy benefit manager acting through an intermediary if—
(1) The person or entity holds a written contract with the Part D plan sponsor, either directly or through a parent organization of such Part D plan sponsor, to provide or arrange PBM functions;
(2) The person or entity causes, arranges, procures, or relies on an intermediary to perform one or more PBM functions on behalf of the Part D plan sponsor or prescription drug plan as described in such written contract; and
(3) That intermediary performs such function on behalf of such Part D plan sponsor or prescription drug plan.
(d)
Performance by Part D plan sponsors.
A Part D plan sponsor does not meet the performance standard in paragraph (a)(2) of this section based solely on the sponsor performing activities under such sponsor's contract for the operation of its own prescription drug plan.
§ 423.2806
Affiliate status.
(a)
Ownership or control
—(1)
General rule.
An entity is an affiliate of a pharmacy benefit manager or Part D plan sponsor if it meets the requirements of any of paragraphs (a)(2) through (4) with respect to the pharmacy benefit manager or Part D plan sponsor.
(2)
Ownership relationship.
An entity has an ownership relationship with a pharmacy benefit manager or Part D plan sponsor if the entity and the pharmacy benefit manager or Part D plan sponsor are treated as members of a parent-subsidiary controlled group under subsection (a) or (b) of section 52 of the Internal Revenue Code of 1986.
(3)
Control relationship.
(i) An entity has a control relationship with a pharmacy benefit manager or Part D plan sponsor if either the entity or the pharmacy benefit manager or Part D plan sponsor has the power to materially determine or direct the material actions, policies, or decisions of the other entity, regardless of ownership percentage, through any of the following:
(A) The power to appoint, elect, or remove a majority of the other entity's governing body.
(B) Contractual veto, consent, or supermajority rights over material business decisions of the other entity.
(C) Contractual rights to appoint, direct, or remove senior officers of the other entity, or to direct the other entity's day-to-day operations through a management or administrative services agreement.
(D) Exclusive dealing, requirements contracts, or similar arrangements that, alone or together with other contractual or economic arrangements, give one entity practical authority to materially direct or constrain the other entity's material business decisions related to the Part D program.
(ii) Control includes indirect control exercised through one or more intermediary entities, assessed link by link through the chain of relationships.
(4)
Otherwise related in an ownership structure.
An entity is otherwise related in an ownership structure to a pharmacy benefit manager or Part D plan sponsor if it does not meet the requirements of paragraph (a)(2) or (3) of this section, but the relationship between the entity and a pharmacy benefit manager or Part D plan sponsor meets any of the following requirements in paragraphs (a)(4)(i) through (iv) of this section and
(
printed page 66481)
the relationship confers meaningful influence either to the entity or the pharmacy benefit manager or Part D plan sponsor.
(i) The entities are treated as members of a brother-sister controlled group under subsection (a) or (b) of section 52 of the Internal Revenue Code of 1986.
(ii) One entity holds a 10 percent or greater capital or profits interest in a joint venture, limited partnership, limited liability company, or comparable arrangement in which the other entity participates.
(iii) The totality of the structural features of the relationship confers meaningful influence by one entity over the other, notwithstanding the failure to satisfy the thresholds in paragraphs (a)(4)(i) through (ii) of this section.
(5)
General principles.
The following principles apply to paragraphs (a)(2) through (4) of this section:
(i)
Entity-form neutrality.
The term interest is measured by any of the following:
(A) Voting power or equity value for corporations.
(B) Capital or profits interest for partnerships and limited liability companies.
(C) Beneficial interest for trusts and unincorporated enterprises.
(ii)
Right-to-acquire rules.
The right to acquire an ownership interest that is exercisable within 60 days—through option, warrant, conversion right, or revocable proxy—is treated as a present holding of that interest.
(b)
Functional relationships.
An entity is an affiliate of a pharmacy benefit manager or Part D plan sponsor if it meets all of the following requirements with respect to the pharmacy benefit manager or Part D plan sponsor:
(1) Acts as a contractor, principal, or agent to such pharmacy benefit manager or Part D plan sponsor.
(2) Performs one or more PBM functions as a material part of its contractual services.
§ 423.2808
Part D plan sponsor contracts.
For plan years beginning on or after January 1, 2028, each contract entered into with a Part D plan sponsor under § 423.505 with respect to a prescription drug plan offered by such sponsor must provide that any pharmacy benefit manager acting on behalf of such sponsor has a written agreement with the Part D plan sponsor under which the pharmacy benefit manager, and any affiliates of such pharmacy benefit manager, as applicable, agree to the requirements described in §§ 423.2810, 423.2812, 423.2814, 423.2816, 423.2818, and 423.2820(b) and (c).
§ 423.2810
Pharmacy benefit manager and affiliate remuneration.
(a)
General.
Pharmacy benefit managers and any affiliates of such pharmacy benefit managers must not derive any remuneration with respect to any services provided on behalf of any entity or individual, in connection with the utilization of Part D drugs, from any such entity or individual, other than bona fide service fees, subject to paragraphs (b) through (d) of this section.
(b)
Bona fide service fees.
(1)
General rule.
A bona fide service fee is a flat dollar amount that meets all of the following:
(i) Reflects the fair market value, as defined in paragraph (e)(1) of this section, of a bona fide, itemized service actually performed on behalf of an entity.
(ii) Covers a service the entity would otherwise perform, or contract for, in the absence of the service arrangement, as described in paragraph (b)(2) of this section.
(iii) Is not passed on, in whole or in part, to a client or customer, regardless of whether the entity takes title to the drug.
(iv) Is not directly or indirectly based on, or contingent upon—
(A) Drug price, such as wholesale acquisition cost or a drug benchmark price (for example, average wholesale price);

(A) Access the primary benefit of the itemized service; or

(An incentive payment paid by a Part D plan sponsor to a pharmacy benefit manager or an affiliate of a pharmacy benefit manager that is performing services on behalf of such sponsor must be deemed a bona fide service fee (even if such payment does not otherwise meet the definition of bona fide service fee under § 423.2810(b)), if such payment meets all of the following criteria:

(2) Is consistent with fair market value as defined under § 423.2810(e)(2).

§ 423.2812

(a)
General.
(1) For purposes of calculating or otherwise evaluating pharmacy benefit manager performance against pricing guarantees or similar cost performance measurements related to rebates, discounts, price concessions, or net costs, the pharmacy benefit manager must define, interpret, and apply in a fully transparent and consistent manner any terms that are integral to the evaluation or calculation of cost performance under such agreement, including but not limited to `generic drug', `brand name drug', `specialty drug', `rebate', and `discount'. (2) The pharmacy benefit manager must identify any drugs, claims, or price concessions excluded from any pricing guarantee or other cost performance measure in a clear and consistent manner. Where a pricing guarantee or other cost performance measure is based on a pricing benchmark other than the wholesale acquisition cost (as defined in section 1847A(c)(6)(B) of the Act) of a drug, the pharmacy benefit manager must calculate and provide a wholesale acquisition cost-based equivalent to the pricing guarantee or other cost performance measure.

(a)
General.

(xi) Total manufacturer-derived revenue, inclusive of bona fide service fees, attributable to the drug and retained by the pharmacy benefit manager and any affiliate of such pharmacy benefit manager.
(2) In the case of a pharmacy benefit manager that has an affiliate that is a retail, mail order, or specialty pharmacy, with respect to drugs covered by such plan that were dispensed, the following information:
(i) The percentage of total prescriptions that were dispensed by pharmacies that are an affiliate of the pharmacy benefit manager for each drug.
(ii) The interquartile range of the total combined costs paid by the plan and plan enrollees, per dosage unit, per course of treatment, per 30-day supply, and per 90-day supply for each drug dispensed by pharmacies that are not an affiliate of the pharmacy benefit manager and that are included in the pharmacy network of such plan.
(iii) The interquartile range of the total combined costs paid by the plan and plan enrollees, per dosage unit, per course of treatment, per 30-day supply, and per 90-day supply for each drug dispensed by pharmacies that are an affiliate of the pharmacy benefit manager and that are included in the pharmacy network of such plan.
(iv) The lowest total combined cost paid by the plan and plan enrollees, per dosage unit, per course of treatment, per 30-day supply, and per 90-day supply, for each drug that is available from any pharmacy included in the pharmacy network of such plan.
(v) The difference between the average acquisition cost of the affiliate, such as a pharmacy or other entity that acquires prescription drugs, that initially acquires the drug and the amount reported under § 423.2814(d)(1)(x) for each drug.
(vi) A list inclusive of the brand name, generic or non-proprietary name, and National Drug Code of covered Part D drugs subject to an agreement with a covered entity under section 340B of the Public Health Service Act for which the pharmacy benefit manager or an affiliate of the pharmacy benefit manager had a contract or other arrangement with such a covered entity in the service area of such plan.
(3) Where a drug approved under section 505(c) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (referred to in this subclause as the listed drug) is covered by the plan, the following information:
(i) A list of currently marketed generic drugs approved under section 505(j) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act in accordance with an application that references such listed drug that are not covered by the plan, are covered on the same formulary tier or a formulary tier typically associated with higher cost-sharing than the listed drug, or are subject to utilization management that the listed drug is not subject to.
(ii) Whether each such generic drug is private label or not.
(iii) The estimated average beneficiary cost-sharing under the plan for a 30-day supply of the listed drug.
(iv) Where a currently marketed generic drug approved under section 505(j) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act in accordance with an application that references such listed drug is on a formulary tier typically associated with higher cost-sharing than the listed drug, the average beneficiary cost-sharing under the plan for a 30-day supply of each such generic drug.
(v) Where a generic drug listed under paragraph (d)(3)(i) of this section is on a formulary tier typically associated with higher cost-sharing than the listed drug, the estimated average cost-sharing that a beneficiary would have paid for a 30-day supply of each of the generic drugs described in paragraph (d)(3)(i) of this section, had the plan provided
(
printed page 66487)
coverage for such drugs on the same formulary tier as the listed drug.
(vi) A written justification for providing more favorable coverage of the listed drug than the generic drugs described in paragraph (d)(3)(i) of this section.
(vii) The number of currently marketed generic drugs approved under section 505(j) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act in accordance with an application that references such listed drug.
(viii) Where the listed drug is subject to prior authorization under the plan, the average denial rate of prior authorizations submitted for the listed drug during the plan year.
(ix) Where a currently marketed generic drug approved under section 505(j) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act in accordance with an application that references such listed drug is subject to prior authorization under the plan, the average denial rate of prior authorizations submitted for each such generic drug during the plan year.
(x) Where the listed drug is subject to any utilization management tool other than prior authorization under the plan, a brief description of each such utilization management tool.
(xi) Where the listed drug is subject to any utilization management tool other than prior authorization, the average denial rate of each such utilization management tool during the plan year.
(xiii) Where a currently marketed generic drug approved under section 505(j) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act in accordance with an application that references such listed drug is subject to the same utilization management tool (other than prior authorization) as the listed drug, the average denial rate of each such utilization management tool during the plan year.
(4) Where a reference product (as defined in section 351(i) of the Public Health Service Act) is covered by the plan, the following information:
(i) A list of currently marketed biosimilar biological products licensed under section 351(k) of the Public Health Service Act in accordance with an application that refers to such reference product that are not covered by the plan, are covered on the same formulary tier or a formulary tier typically associated with higher cost-sharing than the reference product, or are subject to utilization management that the reference product is not subject to.
(ii) Whether each such biosimilar biological product is private label or not.
(iii) The estimated average beneficiary cost-sharing under the plan for a 30-day supply of the reference product.
(iv) Where a currently marketed biosimilar biological product licensed under section 351(k) of the Public Health Service Act in accordance with an application that refers to such reference product is on a formulary tier typically associated with higher cost-sharing than the reference product, the average beneficiary cost-sharing under the plan for a 30-day supply of each such biosimilar biological product.
(v) Where a biosimilar biological product listed under paragraph (d)(3)(i) of this section is on a formulary tier typically associated with higher cost-sharing than the reference product, the estimated average cost-sharing that a beneficiary would have paid for a 30-day supply of each of the biosimilar biological products described in paragraph (d)(3)(i) of this section, had the plan provided coverage for such products on the same formulary tier as the reference product.
(vi) A written justification for providing more favorable coverage of the reference product than the biosimilar biological products described in paragraph (d)(3)(i) of this section.
(vii) The number of currently marketed biosimilar biological products licensed under section 351(k) of the Public Health Service Act, in accordance with an application that refers to such reference product.
(viii) Where the reference product is subject to prior authorization under the plan, the average denial rate of prior authorizations submitted for the reference product during the plan year.
(ix) Where a currently marketed biosimilar biological product licensed under section 351(k) of the Public Health Service Act in accordance with an application that refers to such reference product is subject to prior authorization under the plan, the average denial rate of prior authorizations submitted for each such biosimilar biological product during the plan year.
(x) Where the reference product is subject to any utilization management tool other than prior authorization under the plan, a brief description of each such utilization management tool.
(xi) Where the reference product is subject to any utilization management tool other than prior authorization, the average denial rate of each such utilization management tool for the reference product during the plan year.
(xii)Where a currently marketed biosimilar biological product licensed under section 351(k) of the Public Health Service Act in accordance with an application that refers to such reference product is subject to the same utilization management tool (other than prior authorization) as the listed drug, the average denial rate of each such utilization management tool for each such biosimilar biological product during the plan year.
(5) Total gross spending on covered Part D drugs by the plan, not net of rebates, fees, discounts, or other direct or indirect remuneration.
(6) The total amount retained by the pharmacy benefit manager or an affiliate of such pharmacy benefit manager in remuneration related to utilization of Part D drugs under that plan, inclusive of bona fide service fees.
(7) The total spending on covered Part D drugs net of rebates, fees, discounts, or other direct and indirect remuneration by the plan.
(8) An explanation of any benefit design parameters under such plan that encourage plan enrollees to fill prescriptions at pharmacies that are an affiliate of such pharmacy benefit manager, such as mail and specialty home delivery programs, and retail and mail auto-refill programs.
(9) The following information:
(i) A list of all brokers, consultants, advisors, and auditors that receive compensation from the pharmacy benefit manager or an affiliate of such pharmacy benefit manager for referrals, consulting, auditing, or other services offered to Part D plan sponsors related to pharmacy benefit management services.
(ii) The amount of compensation provided by such pharmacy benefit manager or affiliate to each such broker, consultant, advisor, and auditor.
(iii) The methodology for calculating the amount of compensation provided by such pharmacy benefit manager or affiliate, for each such broker, consultant, advisor, and auditor.
(10) A list of all affiliates of the pharmacy benefit manager.
(11) The following information about any funds disgorged from the pharmacy benefit manager or any affiliates of such pharmacy benefit manager to the Part D plan sponsor consistent with the requirements at § 423.2810(f)(2) from June 1 of the calendar year preceding the deadline for the annual report specified at § 423.2814(a) through May 31 of the calendar year of the deadline for the annual report specified at § 423.2814(a):
(i) The amounts disgorged to the Part D plan sponsor.
(ii) The date of receipt of disgorged funds by the Part D plan sponsor.
(iii) The entity from which such remuneration was derived.
(
printed page 66488)
(iv) The entity that received such remuneration.
(vi) The nature of the violation.
(e)
Summary document.
The summary document described at section 1860D-12(h)(1)(C)(i)(XI) of the Act is the annual report in the format specified by CMS as described at § 423.2814(b).
(f)
Certification.
The annual report must be certified by the Chief Executive Officer, Chief Financial Officer, or General Counsel of such pharmacy benefit manager, or an individual delegated the authority to sign on behalf of one of these officers, who reports directly to the officer.
§ 423.2816
Written explanation of contracts or agreements with manufacturers.
(a)
General.
(1) Not later than 30 days after the finalization of any contract or agreement between a pharmacy benefit manager or an affiliate of such pharmacy benefit manager and a manufacturer (or subsidiary, agent, or entity affiliated with such manufacturer) that makes rebates, discounts, payments, or other financial incentives related to one or more covered Part D drugs or other prescription drugs, as applicable, of the manufacturer directly or indirectly contingent upon coverage, formulary placement, or utilization management conditions on any other covered Part D drugs or other prescription drugs, as applicable, such pharmacy benefit manager must submit to the Part D plan sponsor a written explanation of such contract or agreement.
(2) The written explanation must include the manufacturer subject to the contract or agreement, all covered Part D drugs and other prescription drugs, as applicable, subject to the contract or agreement and the manufacturers of such drugs, and a high-level description of the terms of such contract or agreement and how such terms apply to such drugs.
(b)
Definition—Other prescription drugs
means prescription drugs covered as supplemental benefits under the Part D program or prescription drugs paid outside of the Part D program.
(c)
High-level description of terms.
The high-level description of the terms of such contract or agreement must describe the methodology by which the rebates, discounts, payments, or other financial incentives related to one or more covered Part D drugs or other prescription drugs is directly or indirectly contingent on coverage, formulary placement, or utilization management conditions on any other covered Part D drugs or other prescription drugs.
(d)
Certification.
The written explanation must be certified by the Chief Executive Officer, Chief Financial Officer, or General Counsel of such pharmacy benefit manager, or affiliate of such pharmacy benefit manager, as applicable, or an individual delegated the authority to sign on behalf of one of these officers, who reports directly to the officer.
§ 423.2818
Audit rights.
(a)
General.
Not less than annually, at the request of the Part D plan sponsor, the pharmacy benefit manager must allow for an audit of the pharmacy benefit manager to ensure compliance with all terms and conditions of the written agreement required under § 423.2808 and the accuracy of data reported under § 423.2814.
(b)
Auditor selection.
The Part D plan sponsor must have the right to select an auditor, and the pharmacy benefit manager may not impose any limitations on the selection of such auditor.
(c)
Provision of information.
(1)
General
The pharmacy benefit manager must make available to such auditor all records, data, contracts, and other information necessary to confirm the accuracy of information reported under § 423.2814, subject to reasonable restrictions on how such information must be reported to prevent redisclosure of such information.
(2)
Reasonable restrictions.
Reasonable restrictions—
(i) May address the types of records, data, contracts, and other information to be reported; the manner of reporting such information; and the use, disclosure, and dispensing of such information by the auditor and the Part D plan sponsor; and
(ii) May not include requirements that wholly prevent the auditor from accessing records, data, contracts, and other information that are necessary to confirm the accuracy of information reported under § 423.2814.
(d)
Timing.
The pharmacy benefit manager must provide such information and other information, data, and records relevant to the audit to such auditor within 6 months of the initiation of the audit and respond to requests for additional information from such auditor within 30 days after the request for additional information.
(e)
Affiliate information.
The pharmacy benefit manager is responsible for providing to such auditor information required to be reported under § 423.2814 or under § 423.2818(c) that is owned or held by an affiliate of such pharmacy benefit manager.
(f)
Timing for audits of affiliate pharmacy benefit managers.
If a pharmacy benefit manager providing PBM functions on behalf of the Part D plan sponsor is an affiliate of such Part D plan sponsor, the Part D plan sponsor must conduct an audit of such pharmacy benefit manager annually.
§ 423.2820
Compliance and enforcement.
(a)
Disgorgement of remuneration to CMS.
(1) A Part D plan sponsor must disgorge any amounts disgorged to the Part D plan sponsor by a pharmacy benefit manager or affiliate of such pharmacy benefit manager under § 423.2810(g) to CMS, in a form and manner determined by CMS.
(2) CMS utilizes the information at § 423.2814(d)(11) provided by pharmacy benefit managers under § 423.2814 in order to effectuate disgorgement of funds from Part D plan sponsors to CMS for deposit into the Federal Supplementary Medical Insurance Trust Fund, within the quarter (3 months) that starts on the July 1 data submission deadline at § 423.2814(a).
(b)
Civil money penalty (CMP) pass-through.
The pharmacy benefit manager or affiliate of such pharmacy benefit manager must reimburse the Part D plan sponsor for any CMP imposed on the Part D plan sponsor as a result of the failure of the pharmacy benefit manager or affiliate of such pharmacy benefit manager to meet the requirements of section 1860D-12(h)(1) of the Act that are applicable to such pharmacy benefit manager or such affiliate under the agreement.
(c)
Punitive remedies for breach of contract between Part D plan sponsor and pharmacy benefit manager.
The pharmacy benefit manager or affiliate of such pharmacy benefit manager must be subject to punitive remedies for breach of contract for failure to comply with the requirements applicable under section 1860D-12(h)(1) of the Act.
(d)
Reporting of alleged violations
Alleged violations of the requirements at §§ 423.2810(a) and 423.2814(a) may be reported to CMS on a confidential basis by manufacturers, Part D plan sponsors, pharmacies, and other entities that have contractual relationships with pharmacy benefit managers or affiliates of such pharmacy benefit managers in a form and manner specified by CMS.
(e)
Anti-retaliation and anti-coercion.
Consistent with applicable Federal or State law, a Part D plan sponsor must not do any of the following:
(i) Retaliate against an individual or entity for reporting an alleged violation under paragraph (d) of this section.
(ii) Coerce, intimidate, threaten, or interfere with the ability of an
(
printed page 66489)
individual or entity to report any such alleged violations.
(f)
Certificate of compliance.
Beginning with the contract certification cycle for plan year 2028 and annually thereafter, each Part D plan sponsor must furnish a certificate of compliance with section 1860D-12(h) of the Act in a form and manner specified by CMS.
§ 423.2822
Confidentiality and restriction on use of information.
(a)
Definition
—For purposes of this section,
available for purchase
means available—
(1) In exchange for remuneration; and
(2) Through an agreement for which the purpose is the provision of such information.
(b)
Confidentiality.
Information disclosed by a pharmacy benefit manager, an affiliate of a pharmacy benefit manager, a Part D plan sponsor, or a pharmacy under section 1860D-12(h) of the Act that is not otherwise publicly available or available for purchase may not be disclosed by the Secretary or a Part D plan sponsor receiving the information, except that the Secretary may disclose the information for any of the following purposes:
(1) To carry out Part D of Title XVIII of the Act.
(2) To permit the Comptroller General to review the information provided.
(3) To permit the Director of the Congressional Budget Office to review the information provided.
(4) To permit the Executive Director of the Medicare Payment Advisory Commission to review the information provided.
(5) To permit the Attorney General to conduct oversight and enforcement.
(6) To provide to the Inspector General of HHS in accordance with its authorities under the Inspector General Act of 1978 (
section 406 of title 5, United States Code
), and other applicable statutes.
(c)
Restriction on use of information.
The Secretary, the Comptroller General, the Director of the Congressional Budget Office, and the Executive Director of the Medicare Payment Advisory Commission must not report on or disclose information disclosed in accordance with paragraph (b) of this section to the public in a manner that would identify any of the following:
(1) A specific pharmacy benefit manager, affiliate, pharmacy, manufacturer, wholesaler, Part D plan sponsor, or plan.
(2) Contract prices, rebates, discounts, or other remuneration for specific drugs in a manner that may allow the identification of specific contracting parties or of such specific drugs.

title: Takes of Marine Mammals Incidental To Specified Activities; Taking Marine Mammals Incidental to the U.S. Navy's TRF Wharf Interface Repairs Project at U.S. Naval Submarine Base Kings Bay, Georgia
abstract: NMFS has received a request from the U.S. Navy (Navy) for authorization to take marine mammals incidental to construction activities associated with Trident Refit Facility (TRF) wharf interface repairs project at Naval Submarine Base (NSB) Kings Bay, Georgia. Pursuant to the Marine Mammal Protection Act (MMPA), NMFS is requesting comments on its proposal to issue an incidental harassment authorization (IHA) to take marine mammals incidental to the specified activities. NMFS is also requesting comments on a possible one-time, 1-year renewal that could be issued under certain circumstances and if all requirements are met, as described in Request for Public Comments at the end of this notice. NMFS will consider public comments prior to making any final decision on the issuance of the requested MMPA authorization.
action: Notice; proposed incidental harassment authorization; request for comments on proposed authorization and possible renewal.
dates: Comments and information must be received no later than November 19, 2026.

Background
The MMPA prohibits the “take” of marine mammals, with certain exceptions. Section 101(a)(5)(A) and (D) of the MMPA (
16 U.S.C. 1361
et seq.
) directs the Secretary of Commerce (as delegated to NMFS) to allow, upon request, the incidental, but not intentional, taking of small numbers of marine mammals by U.S. citizens who engage in a specified activity (other than commercial fishing) within a specified geographical region if certain findings are made and either regulations are proposed or, if the taking is limited to harassment, a notice of a proposed IHA is provided to the public for review.
Authorization for incidental takings shall be granted if NMFS finds that the taking will have a negligible impact on the species or stock(s) and will not have an unmitigable adverse impact on the availability of the species or stock(s) for taking for subsistence uses (where relevant). If such findings are made, NMFS must prescribe the permissible methods of taking; other “means of effecting the least practicable adverse impact” on the affected species or stocks and their habitat, paying particular attention to rookeries, mating grounds, and areas of similar significance, and on the availability of the species or stocks for taking for certain subsistence uses (referred to as “mitigation”); and requirements pertaining to the monitoring and reporting of the takings. The definitions of all applicable MMPA statutory terms used above are included in the relevant sections below (see also
16 U.S.C. 1362
;
50 CFR 216.3
,
216.103
).
