Securities and Exchange Commission
[Release No. 34-106675; File No. SR-FINRA-2026-004]
October 15, 2026.
I. Introduction
On February 10, 2026, the Financial Industry Regulatory Authority, Inc. (“FINRA”) filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission (“SEC” or “Commission”), pursuant to Section 19(b)(1) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 (“Exchange Act”)
[
1
]
and Rule 19b-4 thereunder,
[
2
]
a proposed rule change to amend FINRA Rule 2210 (Communications with the Public) to allow a member broker-dealer (“member”) to project performance or provide a targeted return with respect to a security, a securities portfolio, or an asset allocation or other investment strategy in its communications with the public, subject to specified conditions.
[
3
]
The proposed rule change was published for public comment in the
Federal Register
on February 25, 2026.
[
4
]
The comment period closed on March 18, 2026. The Commission received comment letters in response to the Notice.
[
5
]
On April 7, 2026, FINRA consented to extend until May 26, 2026, the time period in which the Commission must approve the proposed rule change, disapprove the proposed rule change, or institute proceedings to determine whether to approve or disapprove the proposed rule change.
[
6
]
On May 18, 2026, the Commission received a letter from FINRA stating, among other things, that it anticipated submitting a response to comments, as well as amendments to the proposed rule change.
[
7
]
On May 20, 2026, the Commission published an order instituting proceedings to determine whether to approve or disapprove the proposed rule change (“OIP”).
[
8
]
The Commission received comment letters in response to the OIP.
[
9
]
On June 30, 2026, FINRA responded to the comment letters received in response to the Notice and OIP
[
10
]
and filed a partial amendment to the proposed rule change
(
printed page 66372)
(“Partial Amendment No. 1”).
[
11
]
The proposed rule change, as modified by Partial Amendment No. 1 (hereinafter referred to as the “proposed rule change” unless otherwise stated), was published for public comment in the
Federal Register
on July 7, 2026.
[
12
]
On July 21, 2026, FINRA consented to extend until October 23, 2026, the time period in which the Commission must approve or disapprove the proposed rule change.
[
13
]
The Commission received comment letters in response to Notice II.
[
14
]
On October 14, 2026, FINRA responded to the comment letters received in response to Notice II.
[
15
]
This order approves the proposed rule change.
II. Description of the Proposed Rule Change
FINRA Rule 2210 generally prohibits communications with the public that predict or project performance.
[
16
]
As discussed below, there are three exceptions to this general prohibition; the proposed rule change would create a fourth exception in limited circumstances.
A. FINRA Rule 2210 (Communications With the Public)
Among other things, FINRA Rule 2210 imposes restrictions on the content of a member's communications with the public. For example, FINRA Rule 2210(d)(1) (General Standards) (hereinafter the “general content standards”) requires, among other things, that: (1) all member communications be based on principles of fair dealing and good faith, be fair and balanced, and provide a sound basis for evaluating the facts in regard to any particular security or type of security, industry, or service;
[
17
]
and (2) the member: (a) not omit any material fact or qualification if the omission, in light of the context of the material presented, would cause the communication to be misleading;
[
18
]
(b) not make any false, exaggerated, unwarranted, promissory, or misleading statement or claim in the communication;
[
19
]
and (c) consider the nature of the audience to which the communication will be directed and provide details and explanations appropriate to the audience.
[
20
]
The general content standards also prohibit a communication prepared by a member from predicting or projecting performance, implying that past performance will recur, or making any exaggerated or unwarranted claim, opinion, or forecast.
[
21
]
This general prohibition, however, does not apply to communications that contain: (1) certain hypothetical illustrations of mathematical principles;
[
22
]
(2) certain investment analysis tools or written reports produced by such investment analysis tools;
[
23
]
and (3) certain price targets contained in research reports on debt or equity securities.
[
24
]
B. The Proposed Rule Change
The proposed rule change would adopt a fourth exception to FINRA Rule 2210(d)(1)(F) to permit members' communications to project performance or provide targeted returns with respect to a security, a securities portfolio, or an asset allocation or other investment strategy (hereinafter, “projected performance or targeted returns”), subject to the conditions described, in turn, below.
[
25
]
1. Written Policies and Procedures
The proposed rule change would require any member that communicates projected performance or targeted returns to adopt and implement written policies and procedures reasonably designed to ensure that the communication is relevant to the likely financial situation and investment objectives of the intended audience of the communication.
[
26
]
FINRA stated that, under such reasonably designed policies and procedures, a communication containing projected performance or targeted returns should only be distributed to investors whom a member reasonably believes have access to resources to independently analyze this information and who have the financial expertise to understand the risks and limitations of these types of presentations (referred to herein collectively as “investors who have the resources and financial expertise”).
[
27
]
FINRA stated that the proposed rule change generally would not permit the inclusion of projected performance or targeted returns in communications for
(
printed page 66373)
a mass audience or intended for general circulation, including a general retail investor audience, as in such mass communications, a member generally could not form any expectation that the communication is relevant to the likely financial situation and investment objectives of the intended audience.
[
28
]
The proposed rule change would not, however, prescribe the ways in which a member may satisfy the policies and procedures requirement; rather, it would provide members with flexibility to develop policies and procedures that best suit their investor base and business models.
[
29
]
For example, FINRA stated that a member firm may wish to partly base its policies and procedures on its past experiences with particular types of investors who seek this information, group investors into categories or types, or restrict its intended audience to investors who have expressed interest or actually invested in particular types of securities.
[
30
]
2. Disclosure Requirements
The proposed rule change would impose two disclosure-related obligations. Specifically, as originally proposed in the Notice, the proposal would have required any member that communicates projected performance or targeted returns to provide sufficient information to enable the intended audience to understand: (1) the criteria used and assumptions made in calculating the projected performance or targeted return, including whether the projected performance or targeted return is net of anticipated fees and expenses;
[
31
]
and (2) the risks and limitations of using the projected performance or targeted return in making investment decisions, including reasons why the projected performance or targeted return might differ from actual performance.
[
32
]
FINRA stated that the first prong of the disclosure requirement would not prescribe the methodology for calculating projected performance or targeted returns; rather, FINRA would expect that a member provide a general description of the methodology used sufficient to enable the intended audience to understand the basis for the methodology, as well as the assumptions underlying the projection or targeted return.
[
33
]
FINRA stated that, absent this required disclosure, it would be more likely that a projection of performance or targeted return would mislead a potential investor.
[
34
]
FINRA also stated that the second prong of the proposed disclosure requirement would help ensure that investors do not unreasonably rely on a projected performance or targeted return given their uncertainty and risks.
[
35
]
In response to comments, however, FINRA amended the original proposal to remove from the first prong the proposed requirement that a member include in its disclosure whether its calculation of the projected performance or targeted return is net of anticipated fees and expenses,
[
36
]
and to remove from the second prong the proposed requirement that a member include in its disclosure reasons why the projected performance or targeted return might differ from actual performance.
[
37
]
FINRA stated that the general content standards, together with the proposed rule change's remaining disclosure requirements, would help ensure that investors receive the information necessary to consider the risks and limitations of such performance information.
[
38
]
3. Reasonable Basis Requirement; Recordkeeping Requirement
As originally proposed in the Notice, the proposal would have required any member that communicates projected performance or targeted returns to have a reasonable basis for the criteria used and assumptions made in calculating the projected performance or targeted return, and retain written records supporting the basis for such criteria and assumptions.
[
39
]
In response to comments, however, FINRA amended the original proposal to remove these requirements,
[
40
]
and instead proposed to amend the recordkeeping obligation under FINRA Rule 2210(b)(4)(A)(iv) to include information concerning the source of any projection of performance or targeted return used in the communication.
[
41
]
As discussed further below, FINRA stated that an express reasonable basis requirement is unnecessary because FINRA Rule 2210's existing general content standards would preclude the communication of unreasonable performance projections or targeted returns.
[
42
]
FINRA also stated that the proposed recordkeeping requirement would be consistent with the other types of records currently required to be maintained pursuant to FINRA Rule 2210(b)(4) and would help regulators to evaluate members' compliance with the terms of the proposed rule change.
[
43
]
III. Discussion and Commission Findings
After careful review of the proposed rule change, comment letters received, and FINRA's response to the comments, the Commission finds that the proposed rule change is consistent with the requirements of the Exchange Act and the rules and regulations thereunder that are applicable to a national securities association.
[
44
]
Specifically, the Commission finds that the proposed rule change is consistent with Section 15A(b)(6) of the Exchange Act, which requires, among other things, that FINRA rules be designed to prevent fraudulent and manipulative acts and practices, to promote just and equitable principles of trade, and, in general, to protect investors and the public interest.
[
45
]
The proposed rule change would create a new, reasonably tailored exception from FINRA Rule 2210's general prohibition on communications that predict or project performance. The proposed rule change would allow members to communicate projected performance or targeted returns, subject to requirements reasonably designed to protect investors and the public interest. In particular, the proposed rule change would, among other things, require members to: (1) adopt and implement written policies and procedures reasonably designed to ensure that the communication is relevant to the likely financial situation and investment objectives of the intended audience; (2) provide sufficient information to enable the intended audience to understand: (a) the criteria used and assumptions made in calculating the projected performance or targeted return, and (b) the risks and limitations of using the projected performance or targeted return in
(
printed page 66374)
making investment decisions; and (3) maintain records including information concerning the source of any projection of performance or targeted return used in their communications.
As explained in detail below, the proposed conditions would help ensure that such communications are provided only to an appropriate audience of investors who have the resources and financial expertise and that such communications are provided with disclosures designed to support informed investment decision making. Further, the existing general content standards—when coupled with the proposed rule change's conditions—should help ensure that communications including projected performance and targeted returns are fair, balanced, and not misleading. Accordingly, and as explained in more detail below, the Commission finds that the proposed rule change is consistent with Section 15A(b)(6) of the Exchange Act. The Commission addresses the proposed rule change's specific provisions, and any related comments, in turn.
A. Scope of the Proposed Exception to the General Prohibition on Communications That Predict or Project Performance
As described above, the proposed rule change would permit members to communicate projected performance or targeted returns under certain conditions.
[
46
]
FINRA stated that some of its members' customers, including institutional investors and other sophisticated investors, request projected performance or targeted returns to help them make informed investment decisions, but FINRA Rule 2210 currently prohibits members from providing such information.
[
47
]
FINRA stated that, on the other hand, investors can obtain such performance information from other market participants, including registered investment advisers,
[
48
]
unregistered intermediaries, and issuers.
[
49
]
FINRA stated that such different regulatory treatment can: (1) incentivize issuers to avoid offering securities through registered broker-dealers,
[
50
]
and (2) cause investor confusion because investors may receive different types of information about the same investments depending on the financial professional with whom they engage.
[
51
]
For these reasons, FINRA stated that an additional exception to the general prohibition on projecting or predicting performance in member communications is warranted.
[
52
]
A number of commenters supported the proposed rule change.
[
53
]
These commenters stated that the proposed rule change would help investors make more informed investment decisions,
[
54
]
reduce investor confusion,
[
55
]
remove an incentive for issuers to avoid using broker-dealers to distribute their offerings,
[
56
]
encourage capital formation,
[
57
]
and promote regulatory harmonization by aligning more closely with the IA Marketing Rule.
[
58
]
Other commenters opposed the proposed rule change.
[
59
]
One of these
(
printed page 66375)
commenters stated that the proposed rule change would expose investors to substantial risk of misleading and unbalanced sales presentations;
[
60
]
another commenter stated that the proposed rule change would weaken FINRA Rule 2210 and is not in the public interest.
[
61
]
Other commenters recommended various modifications to the scope of information covered by the proposed rule change. Several commenters requested that FINRA broaden the scope of information excepted.
[
62
]
In particular, some commenters recommended modifications to further align the scope of information covered with the IA Marketing Rule.
[
63
]
One of these commenters recommended that FINRA amend the proposed rule change to permit the communication of all types of hypothetical performance.
[
64
]
Alternatively, this commenter recommended that, at a minimum, FINRA permit members to communicate certain types of hypothetical performance, including extracts from composites, composites of extracts, or track records developed based on the aggregation of actual positions across various accounts and/or funds.
[
65
]
Commenters similarly recommended that FINRA permit members to communicate backtested and model performance,
[
66
]
related performance,
[
67
]
and extracted performance.
[
68
]
One commenter requested that FINRA create a tiered regulatory framework that covers projected performance and targeted returns as well as educational, distribution, and cash-flow illustrations and imposes varying levels of restrictions on each category of communication.
[
69
]
One commenter recommended that FINRA remove targeted returns from the proposed rule change, stating that targeted returns should not have been covered by FINRA Rule 2210's prohibition in the first place and therefore should not be subject to the proposed rule change.
[
70
]
Another commenter requested that FINRA create “a proportionate framework that recognizes the difference between a generalized target return and a detailed projection.”
[
71
]
Commenters also requested that FINRA provide guidance on the application or impact of the proposed rule change under specific circumstances, such as the presentation of portfolio or investment characteristics,
[
72
]
the presentation of gross versus net-of-fees performance,
[
73
]
and the presentation of internal rates of return.
[
74
]
In response to commenters who opposed the proposed rule change, FINRA stated that the investor protection requirements specific to the proposed rule change, including the policies and procedures requirements and the disclosure obligations, provide appropriate investor protection.
[
75
]
Because these proposed conditions would operate alongside the existing general content standards, FINRA stated that the proposed rule change would not reduce investor protection.
[
76
]
With respect to requests to modify the scope of communications covered by the proposed rule change, FINRA declined to amend the proposed rule change. In particular, FINRA declined to remove “targeted returns” from its scope or subject projected performance and targeted returns to different obligations, stating that FINRA continues to believe that investors may not always understand or appreciate the distinction between projected performance and targeted returns, so the same conditions should apply to these communications under FINRA Rule 2210.
[
77
]
FINRA also stated that it has long taken the position that Rule 2210(d)(1)(F) prohibits communications that contain targeted returns.
[
78
]
In addition, FINRA declined to modify the proposed rule change to cover additional types of performance at this time, stating that requests to do so are beyond the scope of the proposed rule change.
[
79
]
FINRA stated that the proposed rule change represents an incremental change, declined to address the merits of the requests to broaden the scope of the information covered, and noted that this does not foreclose future potential amendments to adopt standards for other performance categories.
[
80
]
FINRA also declined the request to create a tiered regulatory framework that would also address educational,
(
printed page 66376)
distribution, and cash-flow illustrations.
[
81
]
FINRA stated that such a framework would require unnecessary categorization, definitional distinctions, and differing regulatory treatment that would create burdens and complexity that could frustrate members' understanding of and compliance with the proposed rule change.
[
82
]
Finally, FINRA acknowledged commenters' requests for guidance, and stated that, if the Commission approves the proposed rule change, it will consider providing additional guidance as appropriate.
[
83
]
The proposed rule change reasonably expands the exceptions to FINRA's prohibition on communications that predict or project performance to cover projected performance and targeted returns in certain narrowly defined circumstances and subject to conditions that are reasonably designed to protect investors. As described in detail below, the proposed rule change is reasonably designed to help ensure that such communications are: (1) relevant to the likely financial situation and investment objectives of the intended audience (
i.e.,
investors who have the resources and financial expertise); and (2) made with disclosures that would equip the intended audience to evaluate the risks and limitations of such information.
[
84
]
In addition, the proposed rule change would require members to maintain records concerning the source of any projection of performance or targeted return used in the communication.
[
85
]
Currently, other market participants, including issuers and investment advisers, can provide projected performance and targeted returns to investors, subject to certain conditions. Because FINRA Rule 2210 prohibits members from communicating projected performance or targeted return information, certain investors may be confused by the different information they may receive about the same investment from different market participants. The proposed rule change would help to reduce this confusion—subject to conditions designed to protect investors, as discussed further below—by permitting investors to receive additional information and make more informed investment decisions.
Furthermore, by limiting the exception to projections of performance and targeted returns (and not expanding to include at this time additional categories of performance information suggested by commenters, such as backtested, model, related, and extracted performance), the proposed rule change incrementally permits members to disseminate additional categories of performance information, while allowing FINRA to gain regulatory experience with its members' provision of projected performance and targeted return information to investors to evaluate whether future changes, including expansion of the exception, would be appropriate. FINRA stated that it would not foreclose the possibility of future amendments to address additional categories of performance information, and that it would consider providing additional guidance on the application of the proposed rule change to certain categories of information, as appropriate, if the Commission approves the proposed rule change.
It is likewise reasonable to subject projected performance and targeted returns to the same requirements, as this treatment is consistent with how FINRA has interpreted the general prohibition on predicting or projecting performance and recognizes that the distinction between targeted returns and performance projections is not always clear to investors.
For these reasons, the proposed rule change is reasonably designed to prevent fraudulent and manipulative acts and practices, to promote just and equitable principles of trade, and, in general, to protect investors and the public interest.
B. Conditions of the Proposed Exception
As described above, the proposed rule change would allow members to communicate projected performance or targeted returns, subject to conditions reasonably designed to protect investors and the public interest. As originally proposed in the Notice, the proposal would have required members to: (1) adopt and implement written policies and procedures reasonably designed to ensure that the communication is relevant to the likely financial situation and investment objectives of the intended audience of the communication;
[
86
]
(2) provide sufficient information to enable the intended audience to understand: (a) the criteria used and assumptions made in calculating the projected performance or targeted return, including whether the projected performance or targeted return is net of anticipated fees and expenses;
[
87
]
and (b) the risks and limitations of using the projected performance or targeted return in making investment decisions, including reasons why the projected performance or targeted return might differ from actual performance;
[
88
]
and (3) have a reasonable basis for the criteria used and assumptions made in calculating the projected performance or targeted return, and retain written records supporting the basis for such criteria and assumptions (“reasonable basis requirement”).
[
89
]
As discussed in more detail below, the Commission received comments on each of these proposed conditions, as well as other comments suggesting additional conditions or different requirements altogether. In response, FINRA determined to amend the proposed rule change to modify the disclosure requirements, remove the reasonable basis requirement, and impose a modified recordkeeping requirement.
[
90
]
1. Written Policies and Procedures
The proposed rule change would require any member that provides a communication containing projected performance or targeted returns with respect to a security, a securities portfolio, or an asset allocation or other investment strategy to adopt and implement written policies and procedures reasonably designed to ensure that the communication is relevant to the likely financial situation and investment objectives of the intended audience of the communication.
[
91
]
FINRA stated that this condition is intended to provide members with the flexibility to develop policies and procedures that best suit their investor base and the business in which they engage.
[
92
]
Nevertheless, FINRA stated that, under such reasonably designed policies and procedures, a communication that contains projected performance or targeted return information should only be distributed where the member reasonably believes that the intended audience has the resources and financial expertise.
[
93
]
FINRA also stated that the
(
printed page 66377)
proposed rule change generally would not permit a member to include projected performance or targeted returns in communications directed to a mass audience or intended for general circulation, including to a general retail investor audience, because a member generally could not form any expectation that the communication is relevant to the likely financial situation and investment objectives of the intended audience.
[
94
]
One commenter stated that the proposed policies and procedures requirement and the proposed disclosure requirement, combined with the existing investor protection obligations in the general content standards would ensure that investors are adequately informed and protected.
[
95
]
Two commenters recommended modifications to the proposed policies procedures requirement.
[
96
]
One commenter recommended that FINRA amend proposed FINRA Rule 2210(d)(1)(F)(iv)(a) to expressly require that a member's written policies and procedures be reasonably designed to ensure that a communication's intended audience possesses the financial expertise and resources to understand the risks and limitations of projected performance or targeted returns.
[
97
]
The commenter stated that given projected performance or targeted return information could be provided to retail investors, members should be expressly obligated to ensure that the intended audience has the resources and expertise to evaluate the information properly, and this modification would help ensure that members carefully consider the intended audience and not engage in direct marketing to certain investors.
[
98
]
By contrast, the other commenter appeared to request the removal of the policies and procedures requirement, stating that the proposed rule change's conditions discourage the communication of projected performance and targeted return information altogether.
[
99
]
This commenter recommended that FINRA amend the proposed rule change to permit the communication of such information to any investor “provided that the assumptions underlying the projections are disclosed and appropriate cautionary language explains their limitations.”
[
100
]
Several other commenters suggested that FINRA provide additional guidance regarding the policies and procedures requirement and the intended audience of the communications.
[
101
]
One commenter requested that FINRA clarify that the proposed rule change would not require members to adopt policies and procedures reasonably designed to ensure that the investors who receive the communication have a mandated level of financial expertise and resources, as such a requirement would be “impractical and unwarranted.”
[
102
]
Another commenter stated that the proposed policies and procedures requirement would be redundant of the suitability requirements under FINRA Rule 2111(b) to the extent a communication is simultaneously subject to those requirements, and that satisfaction of institutional suitability obligations under FINRA Rule 2111(b) should automatically fulfill the proposed rule change's policies and procedures requirement.
[
103
]
In response to the request to modify the rule text to expressly provide that a member's policies and procedures must be reasonably designed to ensure the intended audience possesses the financial expertise and resources to understand the risks and limitations of the projected performance or targeted return, FINRA stated that the proposed rule change takes a similar approach to the one the Commission adopted in the IA Marketing Rule.
[
104
]
Specifically, FINRA observed that the IA Marketing Rule requires investment advisers communicating hypothetical performance information in an advertisement to “[a]dopt[ ] and implement[ ] policies and procedures reasonably designed to ensure that the hypothetical performance is relevant to the likely financial situation and investment objectives of the intended audience of the advertisement.”
[
105
]
FINRA observed that, in the adopting release for the IA Marketing Rule, the Commission stated that this policies and procedures requirement was designed to help ensure that an adviser provides advertisements containing hypothetical performance information only to those investors who have the resources and financial expertise to appropriately consider such information, and that hypothetical performance “may not be relevant to the likely financial situation and investment objectives of and may be misleading for investors that do not have the resources and financial expertise” and “could tell [such] an investor little.”
[
106
]
FINRA stated that the proposed policies and procedures requirement would impose comparable obligations on members that intend to distribute communications that contain projected performance or targeted returns by limiting the distribution of such communications to investors who have the resources and financial expertise.
[
107
]
Providing such information to investors who do not have such resources and expertise, FINRA stated, “could be misleading as such persons may not understand the risks and limitations of relying on such presentations.”
[
108
]
Accordingly, FINRA declined to modify as suggested.
[
109
]
FINRA also addressed the commenter's assertion that this proposed requirement would be duplicative of existing obligations under FINRA Rule 2111(b).
[
110
]
FINRA stated that the proposed rule change would apply to all communications (not just those made to institutional customers) and would not be limited to those made in connection with, a recommendation.
[
111
]
However, to the extent a member wishes to adopt overlapping policies and procedures for compliance with both FINRA Rule 2111(b) and the proposed rule change, FINRA stated that a member may do so, as long as such policies and procedures address the requirements of each rule.
[
112
]
It is reasonable to require members communicating projected performance or targeted returns to adopt and implement written policies and procedures reasonably designed to ensure that such communications are relevant to the likely financial situation and investment objectives of the intended audience of the communication.
[
113
]
The proposed rule
(
printed page 66378)
change provides for flexibility in a member's development of such policies and procedures, which would allow members to account for their investor base and business models, while also requiring that the policies and procedures impose appropriate constraints on the audience that can receive such communications. Notably, this policies and procedures requirement generally would not permit the inclusion of projected performance for a mass audience or general circulation (including to a general retail audience) and is designed to help ensure that communications containing projected performance and targeted return information are only be distributed where the member reasonably believes that the intended audience has the resources and financial expertise.
[
114
]
As a result, FINRA expects that such communications will primarily be distributed to institutional and other sophisticated investors. Further, this approach, including the related interpretations, is generally consistent with the Commission's interpretation of the IA Marketing Rule, thereby fostering greater regulatory uniformity, as appropriate, between the investor protections that apply when broker-dealers and investment advisers provide communications containing projected performance and targeted return information.
Similarly, while there may be some overlap in the obligations imposed by the proposed policies and procedures requirement and existing suitability obligations under FINRA Rule 2111(b), given that the rules serve different purposes, it is reasonable to maintain the separate obligations and not expressly provide that satisfaction of FINRA Rule 2111(b) would satisfy the proposed rule change. Nevertheless, a member seeking compliance efficiencies could adopt dual-use policies and procedures that address the requirements of both the proposed rule change and FINRA Rule 2111(b).
For these reasons, the proposed rule change is reasonably designed to prevent fraudulent and manipulative acts and practices, to promote just and equitable principles of trade, and, in general, to protect investors and the public interest.
2. Disclosure Requirements
As originally proposed in the Notice, the proposal would have required any member communicating projected performance or targeted returns with respect to a security, a securities portfolio, or an asset allocation or other investment strategy to provide sufficient information to enable the intended audience to understand: (1) the criteria used and assumptions made in calculating the projected performance or targeted return, including whether the projected performance or targeted return is net of anticipated fees and expenses; and (2) the risks and limitations of using the projected performance or targeted return in making investment decisions, including reasons why the projected performance or targeted return might differ from actual performance.
[
115
]
Two commenters recommended that FINRA modify the proposal as originally proposed in the Notice to more closely align the proposed disclosure requirements with those of the IA Marketing Rule.
[
116
]
One of these commenters recommended that FINRA remove the requirement to disclose the reasons why the projected performance or targeted return information may differ from actual performance.
[
117
]
This commenter stated that the IA Marketing Rule does not impose such a requirement, so the inclusion of this requirement would disadvantage broker-dealers by requiring them to provide more disclosures than investment advisers.
[
118
]
The other commenter requested that FINRA confirm that members could satisfy the requirement to disclose the reasons why projected performance or targeted return information may differ from actual performance by using “standard or generic risk disclosure language addressing market risk, model risk, assumption uncertainty, and the inherent limitations of forward-looking statements.”
[
119
]
This commenter also requested that FINRA confirm that disclosures prepared in compliance with the IA Marketing Rule would satisfy the proposed disclosure requirements of the proposed rule change.
[
120
]
In response, FINRA amended the proposed rule change to remove the express requirements to disclose “whether the projected performance or targeted return is net of anticipated fees and expenses” and the “reasons why the projected performance or targeted return might differ from actual performance.”
[
121
]
FINRA stated that the general content standards may, depending on the facts and circumstances, require members to include the disclosures that were removed from the initially proposed rule text to ensure that a communication containing a projection of performance or targeted return is fair, balanced, and not misleading.
[
122
]
FINRA further stated that the general content standards, together with the proposed rule change's remaining disclosure requirements, would help ensure that investors receive the information necessary to consider the risks and limitations of performance information.
[
123
]
Separately, FINRA stated that, notwithstanding similar phrasing in the IA Marketing Rule and the proposed rule change, the phrasing is not identical and investment advisers are subject to a separate regulatory regime that may inform distinct regulatory treatment based on the facts and circumstances.
[
124
]
For this reason, at this time, FINRA cannot categorically conclude that disclosures that comply with the IA Marketing Rule would always satisfy the requirements of FINRA Rule 2210.
[
125
]
Commenters generally supported these amendments.
[
126
]
Other commenters opposed the elimination of the proposed express requirements to disclose “whether the projected performance or targeted return is net of anticipated fees and expenses” and the “reasons why the projected performance or targeted return might differ from actual performance.”
[
127
]
One of these commenters stated that if the general content standards already require the same disclosures, then an express requirement would have placed no additional compliance burden on members; if, however, a situation arises in which making these disclosures imposes a heavier compliance burden on a member, then the investors “absolutely should” receive such
(
printed page 66379)
disclosures.
[
128
]
Another commenter stated that investors could be easily misled without disclosures about fees, risks, and why projections might differ from actual performance.
[
129
]
In response, FINRA declined to reintroduce these express disclosure requirements, stating that nothing in the proposed rule change would deprive investors of material information or reduce investor protection.
[
130
]
FINRA stated that the general content standards, which would apply to all communications of projected performance or targeted return information, already prohibit the omission of any material fact or qualification if the omission, in light of the context of the material presented, would cause the communication to be misleading.
[
131
]
FINRA further explained that whether a communication that contains a projected performance or targeted return includes sufficient disclosure to meet the obligations in the proposed rule change and the general content standards will depend on the facts and circumstances of the presentation, including the intended audience receiving the communication.
[
132
]
Specifically, FINRA stated that while it would generally expect that, to meet the disclosure requirement regarding the criteria used and assumptions made, a communication would provide sufficient information for the investor to determine whether a projected performance or targeted return is net of anticipated fees and expenses,
[
133
]
the contours of this disclosure would depend on the facts and circumstances, including for example, the sophistication of the intended audience.
[
134
]
Similarly, FINRA stated that, to comply with the requirement to disclose the risks and limitations, FINRA would generally expect that a communication that presents a projection of performance or targeted return to provide sufficient information to enable the investor to understand the reasons why the projected performance or targeted return may differ from actual performance.
[
135
]
FINRA noted, however, that these disclosures could be tailored to the intended audience.
[
136
]
Ultimately, FINRA stated that the amended disclosure requirements retain the essential elements of the initial proposed rule change, while also providing appropriate flexibility for members to tailor their communications based on the specific communication and its intended audience.
[
137
]
Accordingly, FINRA concluded that the proposed rule change, in combination with the general content standards, will ensure that investors have sufficient information to consider the risks and limitations of relying on such performance projections.
[
138
]
The proposed rule change reasonably requires FINRA members communicating projected performance or targeted returns to provide sufficient information to enable the intended audience to understand: (1) the criteria used and assumptions made in calculating the projected performance or targeted return; and (2) the risks and limitations of using the projected performance or targeted return in making investment decisions. Instead of prescribing the specific content of the required disclosures, the proposed rule change would permit members to tailor the disclosures to their intended audience, consistent with the requirements under the proposed rules, the general content standards, and the federal securities laws. In this way, the proposed rule change appropriately recognizes that the specific disclosures required for each communication of projected performance or targeted return information will depend on, among other things, the projected performance or targeted return information itself, the audience of the communication, and the nature of the security, securities portfolio, or asset allocation or other investment strategy at issue.
[
139
]
Accordingly, while it is expected that a member would need to disclose whether a projected performance or targeted return is net of anticipated fees and expenses and/or the reasons why the projected performance or targeted return might differ from actual performance to meet the disclosure requirements under the proposed rule, the proposed rule change would provide members flexibility to tailor such communications where appropriate depending on the facts and circumstances, including for example, the particulars of the specific communication and the intended audience.
Further, these disclosure requirements would supplement FINRA Rule 2210's existing general content standards, which broadly require, among other things, that member communications, including communications containing a projection of performance or targeted return, are fair and balanced, and prohibit the omission of any material fact or qualification if the omission, in light of the context of the material presented, would cause the communication to be misleading.
[
140
]
As a result, the proposed disclosure requirements, together with the general content standards, should help ensure that investors receive sufficient information to understand the criteria, assumptions, risks, and limitations associated with the projected performance or targeted returns.
[
141
]
For these reasons, the proposed rule change is reasonably designed to prevent fraudulent and manipulative acts and practices, to promote just and equitable principles of trade, and, in general, to protect investors and the public interest.
3. Reasonable Basis Requirement; Recordkeeping Requirement
As originally proposed in the Notice, the proposal included a reasonable basis requirement, which would have required any member that provides a communication containing projected performance or targeted returns with respect to a security, a securities portfolio, or an asset allocation or other investment strategy to have “a reasonable basis for the criteria used and assumptions made in calculating the projected performance or targeted return, and retain[] written records supporting the basis for such criteria and assumptions.”
[
142
]
In response to commenters' recommendations to remove, replace, refine, or further explain this requirement,
[
143
]
FINRA
(
printed page 66380)
amended the proposed rule change to remove it.
[
144
]
Instead, FINRA proposed to amend FINRA Rule 2210(b)(4) to require that members maintain records concerning the source of any performance projection or targeted return used in their communications.
[
145
]
FINRA stated that an express reasonable basis requirement is unnecessary because FINRA Rule 2210's existing general content standards would preclude any unreasonable performance projections or targeted returns.
[
146
]
Specifically, FINRA stated that the general content standards already require, among other things, that all member communications be based on principles of fair dealing and good faith; be fair and balanced; and not make any false, exaggerated, unwarranted, promissory, or misleading statement, claim, opinion, or forecast.
[
147
]
FINRA stated that under these applicable standards, it has not identified a set of facts where a projection of performance or targeted return lacking a reasonable basis could comply with FINRA requirements.
[
148
]
To the extent a member communicates projected performance or targeted return information sourced from third parties, FINRA further stated that it would expect members to continue to meet the requirements of the general content standards and reminded members that these standards prohibit them from, for example, publishing or circulating any communication that the member knows, or has reason to know, contains any untrue statement of material fact or is otherwise false or misleading.
[
149
]
FINRA explained that the level of due diligence necessary to assess presentations of performance calculated by third parties would depend on the facts and circumstances.
[
150
]
While FINRA would not generally expect a member to independently verify all of the criteria and assumptions underlying the calculation of a projection prepared by a third party, it would expect a member to evaluate the source of such information, assess whether the available information in the projection is supported, and satisfy itself that the presentation meets the general content standards of Rule 2210.
[
151
]
Moreover, members would also need to consider the availability of information from the third party and whether such information would be necessary for the member to satisfy its obligations under Rule 2210.
[
152
]
FINRA also stated that amending the proposed rule change to require members to keep records concerning the source of any projections and targeted returns will help substantiate the basis for such performance presentations.
[
153
]
Some commenters supported the removal of the reasonable basis requirement from the proposed rule change and the addition of the new recordkeeping requirement.
[
154
]
Two of these commenters stated that eliminating the reasonable basis requirement would align the proposed rule change more closely with the IA Marketing Rule, thereby permitting dual registrants to reduce compliance costs by leveraging existing compliance infrastructure developed for the IA Marketing Rule.
[
155
]
One commenter also stated that the general content standards would have made the reasonable basis requirement unnecessary and duplicative.
[
156
]
One supportive commenter requested that FINRA provide guidance on what would constitute reasonable assumptions and acceptable methodologies for the calculation of projected performance or targeted return information.
[
157
]
One commenter opposed FINRA's removal of the reasonable basis requirement, stating that FINRA Rule 2210 already imposes an independent reasonable basis requirement in other contexts notwithstanding the existence of the general content standards.
[
158
]
This commenter also stated that if the general content standards effectively impose a reasonable basis requirement on members, an express requirement would have placed no additional compliance burden on members.
[
159
]
This commenter further stated that even if a situation arises in which an express reasonable basis requirement imposes a heavier compliance burden, then it is precisely the burden the member should carry for the protection of investors.
[
160
]
This commenter also opposed the removal of the recordkeeping requirement embedded in the reasonable basis requirement, stating that it would effectively preclude regulators and investors from testing the fairness and reasonableness of such projections.
[
161
]
In response, FINRA reiterated that it was unable to identify a set of facts where a projection of performance or targeted return lacking a reasonable basis could comply with FINRA Rule 2210's existing general content standards, and so accordingly, it does not believe that investor protection is reduced by removing the reasonable basis requirement.
[
162
]
Moreover, FINRA stated that: (1) the proposed recordkeeping requirement—coupled with the existing requirement that member communications provide a sound basis for evaluating the facts in regard to any particular security or type of security—would require members to substantiate the basis for such performance presentations in order to demonstrate compliance with the content standards;
[
163
]
and (2) in most cases, members would be unable to demonstrate compliance with the proposed rule change and the general content standards without records to support the basis for the criteria used and assumptions made in calculating a projection of performance or targeted return.
[
164
]
For these reasons, FINRA stated that the proposed recordkeeping requirement and the general content standards provide robust investor protection.
[
165
]
Furthermore, FINRA stated that the omission of an express reasonable basis requirement and the inclusion of other conditions similar to those in the IA Marketing Rule would reduce compliance uncertainty for member personnel who act both as
(
printed page 66381)
registered representatives and investment adviser representatives, as well as for members that are either dually registered as investment advisers or distribute communications containing projections or targeted returns that are available to both member customers and advisory clients.
[
166
]
For these reasons, FINRA declined to reintroduce the reasonable basis requirement into the proposed rule change.
[
167
]
With respect to requests for guidance on the reasonableness of specific assumptions used to calculate projected performance or targeted returns, FINRA stated that the long-established content standards in current FINRA Rule 2210 provide sufficient principles for members to assess the reasonableness of the criteria used and assumptions made in a projection of performance or targeted return.
[
168
]
FINRA added that whether a projection of performance or targeted return is reasonable under these general content standards will depend on the facts and circumstances of the presentation.
[
169
]
Finally, FINRA indicated that if the Commission approves the proposed rule change, it will consider what additional guidance may be warranted.
[
170
]
It is reasonable to remove the reasonable basis requirement from the proposed rule change and to require members to maintain records concerning the source of any performance projection or targeted return used in their communications. The general content standards—combined with the recordkeeping requirement—effectively require members to substantiate the basis of any performance projection or targeted return prior to communicating it to investors, as it would be difficult for a member to demonstrate compliance with the proposed rule change and the general content standards without records supporting the basis for the criteria used and assumptions made in calculating the projected performance or targeted return information.
[
171
]
Under these circumstances, an express reasonable basis requirement would be duplicative of the general content standards.
For these reasons, the proposed rule change is reasonably designed to prevent fraudulent and manipulative acts and practices, to promote just and equitable principles of trade, and, in general, to protect investors and the public interest.
4. Other Comments
A number of commenters recommended other changes to the proposed rule change, including additional conditions or alternative approaches altogether, as well as the inclusion of compliance safe harbors.
With respect to additional conditions, one commenter recommended that—to the extent a member communicates projected performance or targeted return information to retail customers—FINRA amend the proposed rule change to limit such communications to those made in support of, or in connection with, a recommendation of any securities transaction or investment strategy involving securities (including account recommendations) that is subject to Regulation Best Interest.
[
172
]
FINRA declined to make this change, stating that the general content standards and the conditions of the proposed rule change provide appropriate investor protection to retail investors in the absence of a recommendation covered by Regulation Best Interest.
[
173
]
FINRA reiterated that under the proposed policies and procedures requirement, communications containing projected performance or targeted returns should only be distributed to investors who have the resources and financial expertise,
[
174
]
and could not be included in communications directed to a mass audience or for general circulation, including a general retail investor audience.
[
175
]
It is reasonable that the proposed rule change does not limit a member's ability to communicate projected performance or targeted returns to retail investors to only those circumstances where the communications are made in support of, or in connection with, a recommendation subject to Regulation Best Interest. As discussed above, the proposed policies and procedures requirement is designed to limit communications containing projected performance or targeted returns to investors who have the resources and financial expertise. In addition, the proposed rule change would impose disclosure obligations that require FINRA's members to provide sufficient information to enable the intended audience to understand the criteria, assumptions, risks, and limitations associated with such information. Taken together with the general content standards of FINRA Rule 2210, these requirements both limit the scope of retail investors who would be eligible to receive these communications to those who are in a position to understand these communications and their associated limitations and would help ensure that any retail investor who receives such a communication would have the information to evaluate it.
With respect to commenters that recommended alternative approaches, one commenter requested that FINRA subject capital acquisition brokers (“CABs”) and non-CAB members to the same or similar rules related to the communication of projected performance and targeted return information about unregistered securities to institutional investors.
[
176
]
A second commenter requested that FINRA regulate the use of registered index-linked annuity (“RILA”) illustrations in a manner similar to variable annuity communications pursuant to FINRA Rule 2211 (Communications with the Public About Variable Life Insurance and Variable Annuities).
[
177
]
In both instances, FINRA declined to do so. FINRA stated that CABs are subject to a separate rulebook that is specifically limited to firms that elect to operate as CABs with specified limitations on their activities.
[
178
]
Accordingly, FINRA disagreed that the communication standards designed for the limited activities of a CAB would be appropriate for a non-CAB member under FINRA Rule 2210.
[
179
]
FINRA also stated that to the extent the commenter was requesting an amendment to FINRA Rule 2211, such a request is outside the scope of the proposed rule change.
[
180
]
It is reasonable to impose different regulatory obligations on CAB and non-CAB members related to the communication of projected performance or targeted returns to institutional investors about unregistered securities. CABs are subject to a separate FINRA rulebook that imposes more limited regulatory obligations that are commensurate with
(
printed page 66382)
their limited activities. For that reason, communication rules that are designed for a CAB's limited business model are inappropriate for non-CAB members that may engage in more expansive business activities. Similarly, the imposition of FINRA Rule 2210's additional restrictions upon CABs would tend to erode the regulatory benefit that the more limited CAB rulebook was designed to provide to members who limit their activities and elect CAB status. In addition, it is reasonable not to amend FINRA Rule 2211 as part of the proposed rule change given it is outside the scope of the proposal.
Another commenter recommended—based on requirements in the Uniform Prudent Investor Act (“UPIA”)—that FINRA require the communication of multiple possible outcomes “as an array of probability in different economic conditions” based on statistical norms instead of a single performance projection or targeted return.
[
181
]
In response, FINRA stated that the UPIA is a model law that establishes general standards for trustee conduct when investing trust property, and therefore FINRA does not believe that proposed rule change is appropriate for application of the model law.
[
182
]
FINRA acknowledged that the provision of multiple possible outcomes may be valuable in some instances but declined to require in every instance that members provide projections of performance or targeted returns in a specific manner or that such presentations be based on specific, differing market conditions.
[
183
]
FINRA stated that the disclosures required under the proposed rule change would provide sufficient information to investors and would also provide members flexibility to tailor their communications based on the intended audience of the communication.
[
184
]
It is reasonable that the proposed rule change does not require the disclosure of multiple possible outcomes, as recommended by the commenter. The proposed rule change and the general content standards impose a principles-based framework for the content of member communications containing projected performance or targeted return information. For this reason, it is reasonable to expect that the members communicating projected performance or targeted return information will present such information and any corresponding disclosures in a way that equips the intended audience to meaningfully understand its risks and limitations. Depending on the facts and circumstances, a member may wish to simultaneously provide multiple projections or targets, but FINRA Rule 2210 need not require such presentations in every circumstance.
Further, a commenter suggested that FINRA provide examples or safe harbors for the types of recipients to whom a communication of projected performance or targeted return could be sent under the proposed rule change, including a safe harbor that expressly permits dual registrants to use communications prepared in compliance with the IA Marketing Rule.
[
185
]
FINRA responded that it does not believe that it is necessary to provide any specific safe harbors or additional guidance at this time.
[
186
]
With respect to requests for safe harbors tied to the type of recipient, the methodologies used, or the disclosures made, FINRA stated that the proposed rule change is intended to provide members with the flexibility to develop policies and procedures that best suit their investor base and the business in which they engage (
e.g.,
policies and procedures based in part on the member's past experiences with particular types of investors who seek this information).
[
187
]
For this reason, FINRA stated that whether a communication containing a projection of performance or a targeted return complies with FINRA Rule 2210 will depend on the facts and circumstances.
[
188
]
FINRA stated, however, that if the Commission approves the proposed rule change, it will consider whether additional guidance or amendments would be appropriate.
[
189
]
The proposed rule change reasonably provides a principles-based approach for members to determine the appropriate audience for these communications. Eliminating this flexibility in favor of predefined categories or safe harbors would fail to account for the fact that the circumstances of each communication—including the nature of the communication; the security, securities portfolio, or asset allocation or other investment strategy at issue; and the nature of the intended audience—will be relevant to whether a particular communication would comply with this proposed rule change. As such, it is reasonable to decline to establish specific safe harbors based on categorical, ex ante classifications of investors eligible to receive projected performance or targeted return information.
[
190
]
FINRA also stated that if the Commission approves the proposed rule change, FINRA will consider whether guidance is needed in the future.
[
191
]
For these reasons, the proposed rule change is reasonably designed to prevent fraudulent and manipulative acts and practices, to promote just and equitable principles of trade, and, in general, to protect investors and the public interest.
IV. Conclusion
For the reasons set forth above, the Commission finds that the proposed rule change, as modified by Partial Amendment No. 1, is consistent with Section 15A(b)(6) of the Exchange Act, which requires, among other things, that FINRA rules be designed to prevent fraudulent and manipulative acts and practices, promote just and equitable principles of trade, and, in general, protect investors and the public interest.

In accordance with the requirements of the Federal Advisory Committee Act, the Millennium Challenge Corporation (MCC) Advisory Council was established as a discretionary advisory committee on July 14, 2016. AGENCY:
Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration (FMCSA), Department of Transportation (DOT).
ACTION:
Notice of availability of supplemental information; request for comments.
SUMMARY:
This notice advises the public of new information that FMCSA believes is relevant to the application from Grote Industries, LLC (Grote) for an exemption from the requirement that exterior lighting devices on commercial motor vehicles (CMVs) be steady-burning. If granted, the exemption would allow motor carriers to operate CMVs equipped with auxiliary warning lamps controlled by Grote's Rear-End Collision Warning (RCW) system. Following publication of the Agency's notice seeking comment, Grote provided additional information to FMCSA staff concerning the design and operation of the RCW system, including the color and activation sequence of the auxiliary warning lamps, the interaction between the RCW and brake-activated warning functions, system operation on combination vehicles, and the operation of the radar detection system. FMCSA is making this supplemental information available in the docket and provides an opportunity for public comment.
DATES:
Comments must be received on or before November 19, 2026.
ADDRESSES:
You may submit comments identified by Docket Number FMCSA-2026-0100 by any of the following methods:
Federal eRulemaking Portal:
www.regulations.gov
.
See the Public Participation and Request for Comments section below for further information.
Mail:
Dockets Operations, U.S. Department of Transportation, 1200 New Jersey Avenue SE, W58-213, West Building, Washington, DC 20590-0001.
Hand Delivery or Courier:
1200 New Jersey Avenue SE, W58-213, West Building, Washington, DC 20590-0001, between 9 a.m. and 5 p.m., Monday through Friday, except Federal holidays.
Fax:
(202) 493-2251.
Each submission must include the Agency name and the docket number (FMCSA-2026-0100) for this notice. Note that DOT posts all comments received without change to
www.regulations.gov
,
including any personal information included in a comment. Please see the Privacy Act heading below.
Privacy Act:
In accordance with
49 U.S.C. 31315(b)
, DOT solicits comments from the public to better inform its exemption process. DOT posts these comments, including any personal information the commenter provides, to
www.regulations.gov
,
as described in the system of records notice DOT/ALL-14 FDMS (Federal Docket Management System (FDMS)), which can be reviewed at
https://www.transportation.gov/​individuals/​privacy/​privacy-act-system-records-notices
.
The comments are posted without edit and are searchable by the name of the submitter.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Mr. David Sutula, Chief, Vehicle and Roadside Operations Division, Office of Carrier, Driver, and Vehicle Safety, FMCSA;
MCPSV@dot.gov
.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
I. Public Participation and Request for Comments
FMCSA encourages interested persons to participate in this proceeding by submitting comments and related materials regarding Grote's supplemental information discussed in this notice.
A. Submitting Comments
If you submit a comment, please include the docket number for this
(
printed page 66386)
notice (FMCSA-2026-0100), indicate the specific section of this document to which the comment applies, and provide a reason for your suggestions or recommendations. You may submit your comments and material online or by fax, mail, or hand delivery, but please use only one of these means. FMCSA recommends that you include your name and a mailing address, an email address, or a phone number in the body of your document so the Agency can contact you if it has questions regarding your submission.
To submit your comment online, go to
https://www.regulations.gov/​docket/​FMCSA-2026-0100/​document
,
click on this notice, click “Comment,” and type your comment into the text box on the following screen.
If you submit your comments by mail or hand delivery, submit them in an unbound format, no larger than 8
                    1/2
                     by 11 inches, suitable for copying and electronic filing.
FMCSA will consider all comments and material received during the comment period. Comments received after the comment closing date will be filed in the public docket and will be considered to the extent practicable.
B. Confidential Business Information (CBI)
CBI is commercial or financial information that is both customarily and actually treated as private by its owner. Under the Freedom of Information Act (
5 U.S.C. 552
), CBI is exempt from public disclosure. If your comments responsive to the notice contain commercial or financial information that is customarily treated as private, that you actually treat as private, and that is relevant or responsive to the notice, it is important that you clearly designate the submitted comments as CBI. Please mark each page of your submission that constitutes CBI as “PROPIN” to indicate it contains proprietary information. FMCSA will treat such marked submissions as confidential under the Freedom of Information Act, and they will not be placed in the public docket of the notice. Submissions containing CBI should be sent to Brian Dahlin, Chief, Regulatory Evaluation Division, Office of Policy, FMCSA, 1200 New Jersey Avenue SE, Washington, DC 20590-0001 or via email at
brian.g.dahlin@dot.gov
.
At this time, you need not send a duplicate hardcopy of your electronic CBI submissions to FMCSA headquarters. Any comments FMCSA receives not specifically designated as CBI will be placed in the public docket for this notice.
C. Viewing Comments and Documents
To view comments, as well as any documents mentioned in this preamble as being available in the docket, go to
https://www.regulations.gov
,
insert FMCSA-2026-0100 in the keyword box, select the document tab and choose the document to review. To view comments, click this notice, then click “Browse Comments.” If you do not have access to the internet, you may view the docket by visiting Dockets Operations in the DOT West Building, 1200 New Jersey Avenue SE, W58-213, Washington, DC 20590-0001, between 9 a.m. and 5 p.m., Monday through Friday, except Federal holidays.
II. Legal Basis
FMCSA has authority under
49 U.S.C. 31136(e)
and
31315(b)
to grant exemptions from the Federal Motor Carrier Safety Regulations (FMCSRs). FMCSA must publish a notice of each exemption request in the
Federal Register
(
49 CFR 381.315(a)
). The Agency must provide the public an opportunity to inspect the information relevant to the application, including the applicant's safety analysis. The Agency must provide an opportunity for public comment on the request.
The Agency reviews the application, safety analyses, and public comments submitted and determines whether granting the exemption would likely achieve a level of safety equivalent to, or greater than, the level that would be achieved absent such exemption, pursuant to the standard set forth in
49 U.S.C. 31315(b)(1)
. The Agency must publish its decision in the
Federal Register
(
49 CFR 381.315(b)
). If granted, the notice will identify the regulatory provision(s) from which the exempted party will be exempt, the effective period, and all terms and conditions of the exemption (
49 CFR 381.315(c)(1)
). If the exemption is denied, the notice will explain the reason for the denial (
49 CFR 381.315(c)(2)
). The exemption may be renewed (
49 CFR 381.300(b)
).
III. Background
On December 10, 2025, Grote submitted an application for a five-year exemption from
49 CFR 393.25(e)
, which generally requires exterior lamps on CMVs to be steady-burning. Grote requested the exemption on behalf of motor carriers seeking to use auxiliary warning lamps in conjunction with Grote's RCW system. Grote's application described one or more auxiliary lamps positioned on the rear or sides of a CMV or trailer. The application described a rear-facing radar system that calculates the time-to-collision (TTC) of vehicles approaching from behind and also contemplated use of the system on the side of a CMV for side-impact protection during parking maneuvers.
In its application, Grote stated that the RCW signal circuit would activate when TTC was less than or equal to a threshold corresponding to a substantial risk of an impending collision, typically between 2.1 and 4.0 seconds. Grote proposed two possible auxiliary-lamp operating sequences. Under one sequence, red lamps would flash between four and sixteen times during a four-second period and then burn steady red while the RCW signal remained active. Under the alternative sequence, amber lamps would operate as SAE J595 Class 3 or Class 2 strobe lamps for up to four seconds and then burn steady red while the RCW signal remained active. Grote further stated that the auxiliary lamps could also be used in combination with brake and marker signal circuits.
On February 9, 2026, FMCSA published a notice of Grote's application and requested public comment (
91 FR 5798
). The notice described the RCW system as activating the auxiliary lamps when a TTC threshold was reached and stated that, following the initial flashing or strobing sequence, the lamps would burn steady red while the collision risk persisted.
On March 4, 2026, FMCSA extended the comment period by 60 days, through May 10, 2026, after the Commercial Vehicle Safety Alliance requested additional time to review the application (
91 FR 10674
).
During the comment period, interested parties raised questions and concerns regarding, among other issues, the relationship between the proposed RCW system and forward collision warning technology, the meaning conveyed to following motorists by the auxiliary warning lamps, and the proposed transition from flashing or strobing warning lamps to a steady-burning red indication. CVSA expressed concern that following motorists could interpret steady-burning red lamps as an indication that the CMV was braking and recommended that the RCW system not transition from flashing amber to steady-burning red for a warning condition unrelated to brake application.
IV. Supplemental Information Provided by Grote
Following the close of the comment period, FMCSA staff sought clarification from Grote regarding the design and operation of the RCW system. FMCSA's questions addressed the operation and sequencing of the auxiliary warning
(
printed page 66387)
lamps, the relationship between the RCW function and Grote's auxiliary brake-warning function, the priority between those functions when both are activated, installation on various CMV types and combinations, and operation of the radar detection system.
Grote subsequently provided the following supplemental information:
A. RCW Warning-Lamp Operation and Color
Grote clarified that when operating as part of the RCW system, the auxiliary warning lamps pulse in amber for up to four seconds with each activation of the RCW signal circuit and do not transition to a steady-burning red indication. Grote explained that the transition from amber pulsation to steady-burning red is associated with the brake-activated auxiliary pulsating lamp function, not the RCW warning function.
This supplemental information differs from the description in the original application and February 9, 2026, notice, which stated that after the initial flashing or strobing RCW warning sequence, the auxiliary lamps would transition to steady-burning red while the RCW signal remained active.
B. Functional Priority and Interaction With Auxiliary Brake-Activated Warning Lamps
Grote explained that the RCW system uses the same auxiliary lamps used by its brake-activated auxiliary pulsating lamp system.
When an RCW event and a braking event occur at the same time, Grote stated that the brake-activated function takes precedence over the RCW function. Thus, when the service brakes are applied during an RCW event, the auxiliary lamps would transition from the RCW warning sequence to the applicable brake-activated warning sequence. Any steady-burning red indication would therefore be associated with brake application rather than with the RCW warning function.
The original application stated generally that the RCW auxiliary lamps could be used in combination with brake and marker signal circuits but did not describe the operational priority between those functions. Grote's supplemental explanation provides additional information concerning that hierarchy.
C. Radar Detection and Activation
Grote stated that the RCW system uses a self-contained, rear-facing radar system capable of detecting approaching vehicles at distances of approximately 200 meters. The system continuously evaluates the relative motion of an approaching vehicle and calculates TTC. When the calculated TTC reaches the programmed activation threshold, the RCW system automatically activates the auxiliary amber warning lamps.
Grote further stated that the RCW system does not require the CMV driver to activate or otherwise interact with the system and that operation of the RCW radar would not interfere with other radar-based vehicle detection systems.
D. Scope and Combination Vehicles
Grote clarified that it intends the requested exemption to apply to all CMVs. For combination vehicles consisting of more than one trailing unit, including doubles and triples, Grote stated that the RCW system would be installed and operated on the rear-most unit of the combination.
E. Supplemental Materials
FMCSA has placed in the docket a memorandum summarizing the meeting between FMCSA staff and Grote during which Grote provided the operational clarifications described above. The memorandum also includes a chart provided by Grote illustrating the operation of the RCW system and its interaction with the brake-activated auxiliary lamp function.
The memorandum to the docket is titled “Ex Parte Communication with Grote Industries, LLC Regarding Rear-End Collision Warning Lamp System.”
V. Reopening of Comment Period and Request for Comments
FMCSA believes interested persons should have an opportunity to review and comment on this new information before the Agency makes a decision on Grote's exemption request. Comments submitted in response to this notice must be limited to addressing any relevant information summarized in this notice and in the Memorandum to the Docket identified above. Comments addressing other matters will not be considered by FMCSA.

Under
part 235 of title 49 Code of Federal Regulations
(CFR) and
49 U.S.C. 20502(a)
, this document provides the public notice that by letter dated July 20, 2026, IORY petitioned FRA seeking approval to discontinue or modify a signal system. FRA assigned the petition Docket Number FRA-2026-1981.
Specifically, IORY requests to discontinue the centralized traffic control (CTC) signal system in Cincinnati, Ohio. The subject area is on main tracks Nos. 1 and 2, between control point (CP) East Norwood (milepost (MP) 10.9) and CP NA Tower (MP 7.5) on the Midland Subdivision and between CP Oakley (MP 10.1) and CP Ridge (MP 10.6) on the Oasis Subdivision.
IORY explains that the absolute signals and power-operated switches at CPs East Norwood, Bond Hill, Oakley, and Ridge would be removed. Further, all electric locks in the subject area will be removed, and the signal appliances will be removed from service. In its petition, IORY notes that the “current traffic density and operating characteristics of the territory no longer require” CTC for the safe movement of trains, as the line has no opposing train movements or fleeted operations. IORY adds that replacement parts for the obsolete CTC system are no longer manufactured, and repair options are limited. Finally, IORY states that the proposed operating method of converting the area to yard limit authority will “facilitate more efficient yard operations . . . and reduce the duration of occupancy at adjacent highway-rail grade crossings.”
A copy of the petition, as well as any written communications concerning the petition, is available for review online at
